105115.m: Menisci spread the pressure in the knee over a larger area.

105116.q: Which cruciate ligament tears much more often?
105116.e: The anterior (front) cruciate ligament is under heavy strain when you twist or stop suddenly. Tearing it is one of the most common serious knee injuries in sport.
105116.m: The anterior cruciate ligament tears much more often than the posterior one.

105117.q: Which movement does the anterior cruciate ligament prevent?
105117.e: The anterior cruciate ligament runs at an angle from the shin bone backwards and upwards to the thigh bone. This stops the shin bone from sliding forwards.
105117.m: The anterior cruciate ligament stops the lower leg from sliding forwards.

105118.q: How does a doctor check whether the anterior cruciate ligament is torn?
a: She carefully pulls the lower leg forwards
She taps the heel with a hammer
She listens to the knee with a stethoscope
105118.e: If the shin bone can be pulled unusually far forwards, the anterior cruciate ligament is no longer holding. Often an MRI scan is done as well.
105118.m: A loose shin bone shows a torn cruciate ligament.

105119.q: In which sport, popular in Switzerland, are especially many cruciate ligaments torn?
105119.e: When skiing, the skis can twist the knee while the body keeps moving. Football also causes many cruciate ligament tears.
105119.m: Skiing and football are typical sports for cruciate ligament tears.

105120.q: In an operation, what is a torn cruciate ligament often replaced with?
a: A piece of the patient’s own tendon
105120.e: Often a tendon from the thigh or part of the kneecap tendon is used. It is anchored in the knee as a new ligament.
105120.m: A new cruciate ligament is often made from the body’s own tendon.

105121.q: What do people often notice at the moment a cruciate ligament tears?
a: An audible pop in the knee
105121.e: Many people report a bang or pop in the knee. Afterwards the knee usually swells quickly and feels unstable.
105121.m: A cruciate ligament tear is often noticed as a pop in the knee.

105122.q: What helps athletes prevent a cruciate ligament tear?
a: Strong leg muscles and a good warm-up
Only doing sport in the evening
105122.e: Strong thighs and calves support the knee. If you warm up and land jumps cleanly, you twist your knee less often.
105122.m: Strong leg muscles protect the cruciate ligaments.

105123.q: How many cruciate ligaments does a knee joint have?
105123.e: Each knee has an anterior (front) and a posterior (back) cruciate ligament. Together they keep the knee stable forwards and backwards.
105123.m: Each knee has a front and a back cruciate ligament.

105124.q: Unlike a tendon, what does a ligament connect?
105124.e: Ligaments hold bones together at joints. Tendons, on the other hand, pass the force from a muscle to a bone.
105124.m: Ligaments connect bones, tendons connect muscles to bones.

105125.q: What are ligaments mainly made of?
a: Tough connective tissue with collagen fibres
105125.e: Ligaments are made of tightly packed collagen fibres. They are very strong when pulled but only stretch a little.
105125.m: Ligaments are made of strong collagen fibres.

105126.q: How is a torn outer ankle ligament usually treated today?
a: Without surgery, with a splint and physiotherapy
With a plaster cast for a whole year
Not at all, you must keep training straight away
105126.e: Most torn outer ankle ligaments heal well with a supporting splint and targeted exercises. An operation is rarely needed.
105126.m: A torn outer ankle ligament usually heals without surgery.

105127.q: What can happen if a torn ligament heals badly?
a: An unstable joint that keeps giving way
A stiff joint that can never bend again
105127.e: If a ligament stays too long or loose, it no longer holds the joint properly. You then twist it again more easily.
105127.m: A badly healed ligament can make the joint unstable.

105128.q: Roughly how long does a torn ligament take until it can carry weight again?
105128.e: Ligaments have a poor blood supply and heal slowly. It usually takes around six weeks or longer until they hold well again.
105128.m: A torn ligament needs around six weeks to heal.

105129.q: What is the technical term for a dislocated joint?
105129.e: In a luxation, the joint surfaces lose contact with each other. A fracture, on the other hand, is a broken bone.
105129.m: A luxation is a dislocated joint.

105130.q: What is the technical term for putting a dislocated joint back in place?
105130.e: In a reduction, the doctor puts the head of the joint back into its socket, often with painkillers.
105130.m: A reduction puts the joint back in its place.

105131.q: What is it called when a joint is only partly dislocated?
105131.e: In a subluxation, the joint surfaces still partly touch. Often the joint pops back by itself.
105131.m: In a subluxation the joint is only partly dislocated.

105132.q: Which joint easily dislocates in toddlers if they are pulled up sharply by the arm?
a: The head of the radius at the elbow
105132.e: In small children the head of the radius still sits loosely in its holder. A sudden jerk makes it slip partly out, and the child then keeps the arm still.
105132.m: Never pull toddlers up sharply by the arm, or the head of the radius can slip out.

105133.q: In which direction does the kneecap almost always move when it dislocates?
105133.e: The pull of the thigh muscles draws the kneecap slightly outwards. That is why it almost always dislocates to the outer side.
105133.m: When it dislocates, the kneecap usually moves outwards.

105134.q: Why should you not put a dislocated joint back yourself?
a: You could injure nerves, blood vessels or bones
The joint will never go back in
It is forbidden to give first aid
105134.e: Nerves and blood vessels often run next to the joint. There may also be a fracture that only shows up on an X-ray.
105134.m: A dislocated joint needs a doctor.

105135.q: Which parts of a joint are often injured as well in a dislocation?
105135.e: For the bone to jump out of its socket, the capsule and ligaments must be strongly stretched or torn.
105135.m: In a dislocation, the capsule and ligaments often tear too.

105136.q: Why does a shoulder dislocate more easily again after the first time?
a: The capsule and ligaments stay stretched or torn
The upper arm bone gets longer
105136.e: If the injured supporting tissues do not heal tightly together, the joint is less stable. This is common, especially in young people.
105136.m: After a first shoulder dislocation, the joint is often less stable.

105137.q: What happens in a joint with osteoarthritis?
a: The bones become as soft as rubber
105137.e: Osteoarthritis is wear and tear of the joint. The cartilage becomes thinner and cracked until bone can rub on bone.
105137.m: In osteoarthritis, the joint cartilage wears away.

105138.q: What does the ending “-itis” in the word arthritis mean?
105138.e: Arthritis is an inflammation of a joint, osteoarthritis is wear and tear. The two are often confused.

105139.q: In which people does osteoarthritis occur most often?
105139.e: Osteoarthritis is joint wear that develops over many years. That is why it mainly affects older people.

a: A smooth layer on the ends of the bones in a joint
A muscle that moves the joint
A ligament that connects two bones
A fluid in the bone marrow
105140.e: Joint cartilage covers the ends of the bones and makes sure they glide smoothly over each other. In osteoarthritis it wears away.
105140.m: Joint cartilage lets the bones in a joint glide.

105141.q: Which risk factor puts strain on knees and hips and encourages osteoarthritis?
105141.e: Every extra kilogram presses on the joints with every step. That is why being overweight speeds up cartilage wear.
105141.m: Being overweight strains the joints and encourages osteoarthritis.

105142.q: What is a typical early sign of osteoarthritis?
a: Pain in the first steps after a rest
A joint that is always cold
105142.e: This is called start-up pain. After a few minutes of movement it often gets better.
105142.m: Start-up pain after a rest is a typical sign of osteoarthritis.

105143.q: What can often be seen on an X-ray in osteoarthritis?
a: A joint space that has become narrower
105143.e: Cartilage does not show up on an X-ray. When it gets thinner, the bones move closer together and the gap between them looks narrower.
105143.m: A narrow joint space on an X-ray points to osteoarthritis.

105144.q: Which sports are often recommended for osteoarthritis in the knee or hip?
105144.e: These sports move the joints evenly without hard jolts. That keeps muscles and cartilage in good shape.
105144.m: Cycling and swimming are gentle on joints with osteoarthritis.

105145.q: Which two parts of the hip joint does a total hip replacement replace?
a: The hip socket and the head of the thigh bone
The kneecap and the top of the shin bone
The meniscus and the cruciate ligament
105145.e: In a total hip replacement, an artificial socket is placed in the pelvis. A stem with a ball replaces the head of the thigh bone.
105145.m: A total hip replacement replaces the socket and head of the hip joint.

105146.q: What is the most common reason for a hip replacement?
105146.e: When the cartilage is badly damaged, every step hurts. An artificial joint can then take away the pain and improve movement.
105146.m: Most hip replacements are done because of osteoarthritis.

105147.q: Which metal are many implant stems that sit in the thigh bone made of?
105147.e: Titanium is light, very strong and well tolerated by the body. The bone can even grow onto its surface.
105147.m: Many implant stems are made of well-tolerated titanium.

a: A plaster cast for the leg
105148.e: In a hip replacement, surgeons replace the diseased hip joint with an artificial one made of metal, ceramic or plastic.
105148.m: A hip replacement is an artificial hip joint.

105149.q: In which two ways is a hip replacement fixed in the bone?
a: With bone cement or by growing in without cement
With screws from outside through the skin
Only by muscles, with no fixing at all
105149.e: Cemented implants are firm straight away. With cement-free implants, the bone grows into the rough surface.
105149.m: Hip replacements are either cemented or grow into the bone without cement.

105150.q: What does the prefix “endo” in the word endoprosthesis mean?
105150.e: An endoprosthesis is placed inside the body. An artificial leg that is fitted from outside, on the other hand, is an exoprosthesis.
105150.m: An endoprosthesis sits inside the body.

105151.q: In many cases, how long does a modern hip replacement last?
a: Always only until the next winter
105151.e: Thanks to good materials, many hip replacements work for decades. If one becomes loose, it can be replaced.
105151.m: Many hip replacements last twenty years or longer.

105152.q: What material is the artificial head of the hip or the gliding surface of the socket often made of?
105152.e: Ceramic is very hard and smooth, and a special plastic called polyethylene glides well. This means little wear.
105152.m: The hip head and socket are often made of smooth ceramic or plastic.

105153.q: Which complication is especially feared in the first weeks after a hip replacement?
105153.e: Until the muscles and capsule have healed, the artificial head can jump out of the socket. That is why extreme movements are avoided at first.
105153.m: After the operation you must avoid extreme hip movements so the implant does not dislocate.

105154.q: Which animals can also place their thumb opposite their other fingers?
105154.e: Many monkeys and apes also have an opposable thumb. In humans, however, it is especially long and flexible.
105154.m: Many monkeys and apes can also place their thumb opposite their fingers.

105155.q: Which joint can move more, an ellipsoid joint or a ball-and-socket joint?
105155.e: A ball-and-socket joint like the shoulder moves around three axes and can also rotate. An ellipsoid joint has only two axes.
105155.m: A ball-and-socket joint can move more than an ellipsoid joint.

105156.q: What can help with severe osteoarthritis in the knee or hip when nothing else works?
105156.e: If the joint is badly worn, it can be replaced by an implant made of metal and plastic. Afterwards the pain is usually much less.
105156.m: An artificial joint can help with severe osteoarthritis.

105157.q: How can you often tell from the outside that a shoulder is dislocated?
a: The shoulder looks angular with a dent
The shoulder turns completely blue and cold
The shoulder becomes as soft as rubber
105157.e: When the head of the upper arm bone jumps out of the socket, the round shape of the shoulder is missing. A hollow forms below the top of the shoulder.
105157.m: A dislocated shoulder often looks angular and has a dent.

105158.q: What can happen if a torn-off piece of meniscus gets trapped in the knee?
a: Suddenly the knee can no longer be fully straightened
The knee becomes longer for good
The foot goes to sleep for ever
105158.e: The loose piece catches between the bones and blocks the joint. This is called a locked joint.
105158.m: A trapped piece of meniscus can lock the knee.

105159.q: What is a ligament injury called when the ligament is only overstretched but not torn?
105159.e: In a sprain the fibres are overstretched but still whole. It usually heals faster than a tear.
105159.m: A sprained ligament is overstretched but not torn.

105160.q: Which ligament in the knee is injured especially often when skiing?
105160.e: In a fall, the knee often bends inwards while the ski turns outwards. This overstretches or tears the ligament on the inside of the knee.
105160.m: When skiing, the inner ligament of the knee is often injured.

105161.q: Which imaging method shows torn ligaments especially well?
105161.e: An MRI shows soft tissues such as ligaments, cartilage and menisci very precisely. An X-ray, on the other hand, mainly shows bones.
105161.m: Ligaments show up well on an MRI, bones on an X-ray.

105445.q: How does the epidermis protect the body?
a: It keeps out germs and dirt
It pumps blood around the body
105445.e: The epidermis, the outer layer of skin, is a dense protective layer. It stops germs getting in and the body drying out.
105445.m: The epidermis protects against germs and drying out.

105446.q: What is the technical term for the outer layer of the skin?
105446.e: In technical language, the outer layer of skin is called the epidermis. The word comes from Greek and means “on the skin”.
105446.m: Experts call the outer layer of skin the epidermis.

105447.q: Unlike the dermis, what does the epidermis not contain?
105447.e: The epidermis has no blood vessels of its own. It is supplied with nutrients by the dermis below, which is why a very shallow scratch does not bleed.
105447.m: There are no blood vessels in the epidermis.

105448.q: What is the top layer of the epidermis, the horny layer, made of?
105448.e: The horny layer contains flat, dead cells full of keratin. They form a tough protective layer and gradually flake off.
105448.m: The horny layer is made of dead, hardened cells.

105449.q: Where are the new cells of the epidermis made?
a: In the lowest layer, the basal layer
In the horny layer at the very top
105449.e: In the basal layer, cells divide all the time. The new cells move upwards, harden and are finally shed.
105449.m: New skin cells are made at the very bottom of the epidermis.

105450.q: After roughly how many weeks has the epidermis completely renewed itself?
105450.e: A newly made cell takes about a month to reach the surface and flake off. So the epidermis renews itself roughly every four weeks.
105450.m: The epidermis renews itself about once a month.

105451.q: Where on the body is the epidermis thickest?
a: On the soles of the feet
105451.e: On the soles of the feet and the palms, the horny layer is especially thick because it has to withstand a lot of pressure and rubbing. On the eyelids, by contrast, the skin is very thin.
105451.m: The soles of the feet have the thickest epidermis in the body.

105452.q: Which protein makes the cells of the horny layer firm and tough?
105452.e: The horny cells are filled with keratin. Hair and fingernails are made of the same horny substance.
105452.m: Keratin makes the horny layer of the skin firm.

105453.q: What is an important part of house dust?
105453.e: Every day a person loses countless tiny flakes from the horny layer. They make up part of house dust and are food for dust mites.
105453.m: Part of house dust is shed skin cells.

105454.q: What are the three layers of the skin, from the outside in?
a: Horny skin, muscle skin, bone skin
105454.e: On the very outside is the epidermis, below it the tough dermis. At the bottom is the subcutis, with lots of fat.
105454.m: The dermis lies between the epidermis and the subcutis.

105455.q: Why is the dermis called “leather skin” in German?
a: Because leather is made from it in animals
Because it is brown like leather
Because only people with leather shoes have it
105455.e: When animal hides are tanned, it is mainly the tough dermis that is turned into leather. That is where the German name for this layer comes from.
105455.m: Leather is made from the dermis of animals.

105456.q: Which fibres make the dermis hard to tear?
105456.e: The dermis is largely made of collagen fibres. They make the skin strong when pulled and very tough.
105456.m: Collagen fibres make the dermis strong.

105457.q: What is found in the dermis and supplies the skin with nutrients?
105457.e: The epidermis has no blood vessels of its own. It is supplied by the tiny blood vessels in the dermis.
105457.m: The dermis is full of tiny blood vessels.

105458.q: What happens to the fibres of the dermis in old age?
a: They become weaker and wrinkles form
105458.e: Over the years, the body makes less collagen and fewer elastic fibres. The skin becomes slacker and wrinkles form.
105458.m: Weaker fibres in the dermis lead to wrinkles.

105459.q: What lies in the dermis and tells the brain about touch?
105459.e: The dermis contains many nerve endings and touch receptors. They sense touch, pressure, warmth, cold and pain.
105459.m: The touch receptors in the dermis sense touch.

105460.q: What are stretch marks on the skin?
105460.e: If the skin is stretched a lot very quickly, for example during a growth spurt, fibres in the dermis can tear. This shows up as stripes.
105460.m: Stretch marks are tears in the dermis.

105461.q: In which layer of skin are the hair roots?
105461.e: Hair roots sit deep in the dermis, some reaching into the subcutis. There they are supplied by tiny blood vessels.
105461.m: Hair roots sit deep in the dermis.

105462.q: What is the subcutis mainly made of?
105462.e: The subcutis is the lowest layer of the skin and is mainly made of loose connective tissue and fatty tissue.
105462.m: The subcutis is mainly made of fat.

105463.q: What job does the fat in the subcutis have?
a: It protects against cold and stores energy
105463.e: The fat under the skin works like an insulating layer against the cold. It is also an energy store for the body.
105463.m: The fat in the subcutis keeps you warm and stores energy.

105464.q: Where on the body does the subcutis have almost no fat?
105464.e: On the eyelids the skin is very thin and has hardly any fat underneath. On the tummy, bottom and thighs, by contrast, the layer of fat is often thick.
105464.m: The eyelids have almost no fat under the skin.

105465.q: Where do many people with diabetes inject their insulin?
105465.e: Insulin is injected with a short needle into the fatty tissue under the skin, often on the tummy. From there it slowly passes into the blood.
105465.m: Insulin is injected into the layer under the skin.

105466.q: Why is the fat pad under the skin of the heel important?
a: It cushions the pressure when walking
105466.e: The fat pad on the heel is especially thick. It works like a shock absorber with every step.
105466.m: The fat pad on the heel cushions every step.

105467.q: Which sea animals have an especially thick layer of fat under their skin against the cold?
105467.e: Whales and seals have a thick layer of fat called blubber. This layer under the skin keeps them warm in cold seawater.
105467.m: Thick blubber under the skin protects whales and seals from the cold.

a: It connects the dermis to the muscles and bone lining
It connects the epidermis to the hair
It connects the eyes to the brain
It connects the bones to the teeth
105468.e: The subcutis lies between the dermis and the coverings of the muscles below. Because it is loosely built, the skin can be moved in many places.
105468.m: The subcutis connects the skin to the body so that it can move.

105469.q: Where are the sense receptors that are especially good at feeling vibrations?
105469.e: Deep in the subcutis there are sense receptors that react especially to vibrations, for example when your phone buzzes in your trouser pocket.
105469.m: Vibrations are felt by sense receptors deep in the skin.

105470.q: What does an oil gland (sebaceous gland) make?
105470.e: Oil glands make sebum, a mixture of fats. It keeps skin and hair supple.

105471.q: Where do most oil glands release their sebum?
105471.e: Most oil glands open into the hair follicle, the sheath around the hair. From there, the sebum reaches the surface of the skin.
105471.m: Oil glands usually open next to a hair.

105472.q: Where do people have no oil glands?
a: On the palms and soles of the feet
105472.e: The palms and soles of the feet have no hair and no oil glands. On the face and scalp, by contrast, there are especially many.
105472.m: The palms and soles of the feet have no oil glands.

105473.q: Why does hair get greasy if you do not wash it for a long time?
a: Because oil glands keep producing more oil
Because the hair itself makes fat
105473.e: The oil glands of the scalp keep releasing sebum. It spreads along the hair, so over time the hair looks greasy.
105473.m: Oil from the scalp makes unwashed hair greasy.

105474.q: In which parts of the body are there especially many oil glands?
105474.e: There are especially many oil glands in the so-called T-zone of forehead, nose and chin, and on the chest and back. The skin gets shiny faster there.
105474.m: The face, chest and back have many oil glands.

105475.q: What can form if the opening of an oil gland gets blocked?
105475.e: If sebum builds up in the hair follicle, a blackhead forms. If bacteria get in too, it can turn into an inflamed spot.
105475.m: Blocked oil glands lead to blackheads and spots.

105476.q: What job does sebum have on the skin?
a: It forms a protective film against drying out
105476.e: Together with sweat, sebum forms a thin protective film on the skin. It keeps the skin supple and holds back many germs.
105476.m: Sebum protects the skin from drying out.

105477.q: What is the oil from the glands on the edge of the eyelids for?
a: It stops the tear fluid from evaporating too quickly
It helps the eyes see better
105477.e: The glands on the edge of the eyelid release oil into the tear film. This keeps the eye moist for longer.
105477.m: Oil from the eyelid edge stops the tear film from evaporating.

105478.e: Sweat evaporates on the skin. As it does so, it takes heat away from the body, which cools down.

105479.q: Where do people who sweat excessively often sweat most?
a: On the hands, feet and armpits
105479.e: With excessive sweating, the sweat glands work much harder than needed, often on the hands, feet or armpits. Doctors can treat this.
105479.m: Some people sweat too much, often on their hands and feet.

105480.q: What do the larger sweat glands in the armpits release as well?
105480.e: The armpits have special sweat glands that also release scent substances. Bacteria break down what they release, and that is how armpit odour forms.
105480.m: Sweat glands in the armpits release scent substances.

105481.q: Why does fresh sweat hardly smell, but old sweat smells strongly?
a: Sweat turns into fat in the air
The skin makes scent substances later
The water in the sweat goes off
105481.e: Fresh sweat has almost no smell. Only when bacteria on the skin break it down do they make the smelly substances.
105481.m: Sweat odour is caused by bacteria.

105482.q: Roughly how many sweat glands does a person have?
105482.e: Spread over the whole skin, a person has several million small sweat glands. Together, in heat or during sport, they can make several litres of sweat a day.
105482.m: People have millions of sweat glands.

105483.q: Why do dogs pant when it is hot?
a: Because they sweat almost only on their paws
Because they have too many sweat glands
Because they are pretending to be thirsty
105483.e: Dogs have sweat glands almost only on their paws. They mainly cool down by panting, as water evaporates from the tongue and airways.
105483.m: Dogs cool down by panting instead of sweating.

105484.q: What is the cooling called that happens when sweat evaporates and takes heat from the body?
105484.e: Water needs energy to evaporate. This energy is taken from the skin, which is why it is called evaporative cooling.

105485.q: Why does sweating feel especially unpleasant in humid weather?
a: Sweat evaporates poorly in damp air
You do not sweat at all when it is humid
Sweat turns greasy when it is humid
105485.e: When the air already contains a lot of water vapour, sweat hardly evaporates. It stays on the skin and there is very little cooling effect.
105485.m: In damp air, sweat does not cool you well.

105486.e: Melanin is the most important pigment in skin, hair and eyes. The more melanin, the darker the colour.
105486.m: Melanin is the pigment of the skin.

105487.e: Melanocytes sit in the epidermis. They make melanin and pass it on to the skin cells around them.

105488.q: What does melanin protect the skin from?
105488.e: Melanin absorbs a large part of the UV rays. In this way it protects the genetic material in skin cells from damage.
105488.m: Melanin protects the skin from UV rays.

105489.q: What happens in the skin when you get a tan?
105489.e: UV rays make the melanocytes produce more melanin. So a tan is a protective reaction of the skin.
105489.m: Getting a tan is the skin protecting itself against the sun.

105490.q: What mainly makes dark skin different from light skin?
a: The amount and type of melanin
105490.e: People of all skin colours have about the same number of melanocytes. In dark skin, however, they make more and darker melanin.
105490.m: Skin colour depends on the amount of melanin.

105491.q: What is the name of an inborn condition in which the body makes little or no melanin?
105491.e: In albinism, melanin is missing from the skin, hair and often the eyes. People with it have very pale skin and must protect themselves well from the sun.

105492.q: What is the dangerous skin cancer that develops from pigment cells called?
105492.e: Melanoma develops from melanocytes that have changed abnormally. Switzerland is one of the countries in Europe with the most cases of melanoma, which is why sun protection is important.

105493.q: Apart from the skin, where else is melanin found?
a: In hair and in the iris
105493.e: Melanin also gives hair and the iris of the eyes their colour. When hair turns grey, it hardly makes any melanin any more.
105493.m: Melanin also colours hair and eyes.

a: A skin condition with blackheads and spots
A fungal infection of the feet
105494.e: With acne, blackheads and inflamed spots appear mainly on the face, chest and back. It is very common in teenagers.
105494.m: Acne shows up as blackheads and spots.

105495.q: At what age does acne occur most often?
105495.e: Hormonal changes in puberty encourage acne. That is why very many teenagers have spots at times, which usually clear up later.
105495.m: Acne is most common in teenagers.

105496.q: What is a blocked skin pore that often looks dark at the top called?
105496.e: A blackhead forms when a hair follicle is blocked by sebum and horny cells. If it is open, the tip turns dark.
105496.m: A blocked skin pore is called a blackhead.

105497.q: Why is an open blackhead dark at the top?
a: The contents change colour in the air
A black hair grows inside it
105497.e: The dark colour does not come from dirt. The plug of sebum, horny cells and melanin turns dark when it meets the air.
105497.m: Blackheads are not dark because of dirt.

105498.q: Which glands play the main part in causing acne?
105498.e: In acne, the oil glands make too much sebum and the opening of the hair follicle becomes clogged with horny cells. It gets blocked and blackheads form.
105498.m: Acne starts with blocked oil glands.

105499.q: Why should you not squeeze spots?
a: The inflammation can spread and leave scars
It turns the skin brown for good
Then no hair grows there any more
105499.e: Squeezing can push pus deeper into the skin. The inflammation then often gets worse and scars can remain.

105500.q: What do the bacteria involved in acne spots feed on?
105500.e: These bacteria live in the hair follicles of the skin and feed on sebum. In blocked pores they multiply and encourage inflammation.

105501.e: Severe acne is best treated by a skin doctor, called a dermatologist. There are effective creams and medicines.
105501.m: A skin doctor can help with severe acne.

105502.q: What can severe, untreated acne leave behind?
105502.e: Deep inflammation can destroy tissue in the dermis. After healing, scars then remain, which is why early treatment is worthwhile.

105503.q: With which childhood illness do you get an itchy rash with small blisters all over your body?
105503.e: Chickenpox is caused by a virus. Typical signs are itchy blisters that appear all over the body and later crust over.
105503.m: Chickenpox causes itchy blisters all over the body.

105504.q: Which viral illness in small children causes blisters on the hands, feet and in the mouth?
105504.e: Hand, foot and mouth disease is caused by viruses and mainly affects children under ten. Typical signs are blisters on the palms, soles of the feet and in the mouth.
105504.m: Hand, foot and mouth disease causes blisters on the hands, feet and in the mouth.

105505.q: Which illness can be caused by the same virus decades after chickenpox?
105505.e: After the illness, the chickenpox virus stays in nerve cells. If it becomes active again later, painful shingles develops.
105505.m: The chickenpox virus can cause shingles later.

105506.q: What causes a rash with weals when you touch stinging nettles?
a: The stinging hairs of the plant
105506.e: The stinging hairs of the nettle break off and inject irritating substances into the skin. Itchy, burning weals appear.
105506.m: The stinging hairs of nettles cause weals.

105507.q: What is a rash with itchy weals, often caused by an allergy, called?
105507.e: Hives, technical term urticaria, look like the result of touching stinging nettles. They are often triggered by allergies, for example to foods or medicines.

105508.q: Which metal in belt buckles and jeans buttons often causes a contact rash?
105508.e: Nickel is one of the most common causes of a contact allergy. Where nickel stays on the skin for a long time, an itchy eczema can develop.

105509.q: In which illness does the red rash typically start behind the ears?
105509.e: With measles, the blotchy rash usually starts behind the ears and on the face. Then it spreads over the whole body.
105509.m: The measles rash starts behind the ears.

105510.q: Which illness with a rash is caused by bacteria and often shows a “strawberry tongue”?
105510.e: Scarlet fever is caused by streptococci, which are bacteria. Typical signs are a fine rash and a red, bumpy strawberry tongue.
105510.m: Scarlet fever can often be recognised by the strawberry tongue.

105511.q: What is typical of atopic eczema?
105511.e: In atopic eczema, the protective function of the skin does not work properly. The skin is dry, gets inflamed easily and is very itchy.
105511.m: Atopic eczema causes dry, itchy skin.

105512.e: Atopic eczema is a skin condition that is not contagious. So you cannot catch it from other people.

105513.q: What can trigger a new flare-up of atopic eczema?
a: Stress or dry air from the heating
105513.e: Stress, infections or dry air in winter can irritate the sensitive skin. Then the eczema flares up again.
105513.m: Stress and dry air can make atopic eczema worse.

105514.q: Where does atopic eczema often appear in schoolchildren?
a: In the creases of the elbows and the backs of the knees
On the ends of the hair
105514.e: In children and teenagers, the inner bends of the arms and legs are often affected. There the skin rubs and easily gets damp.
105514.m: Atopic eczema often appears in the elbow creases and the backs of the knees.

105515.q: How does atopic eczema usually progress?
a: In flare-ups with better and worse times
105515.e: Atopic eczema typically comes in flare-ups. A flare-up can be triggered by stress, infections or dry air from the heating, for example.

105516.q: What is especially important for daily skin care with atopic eczema?
105516.e: Rich moisturising creams strengthen the damaged protective layer of the skin and ease the dryness. Hot showers and scrubbing dry the skin out even more.
105516.m: With atopic eczema, the skin needs plenty of rich cream.

105517.q: Which illnesses often occur together with atopic eczema?
a: A broken bone and a strain
105517.e: Atopic eczema, hay fever and allergic asthma are known as atopic conditions. They often occur in the same families or in the same person.
105517.m: Atopic eczema often occurs with hay fever and asthma.

105518.q: Why does scratching make atopic eczema worse?
a: It irritates the skin and makes the itching stronger
It makes the skin too greasy
105518.e: Scratching damages the skin and encourages inflammation. This makes it itch even more, creating a vicious circle.
105518.m: Scratching makes the itching of atopic eczema stronger.

105519.e: Common warts are caused by papillomaviruses. The idea that toads pass on warts is an old myth.

105520.e: Wart viruses are passed on by direct contact or via objects. Small injuries to the skin make infection especially easy.

105521.q: What are warts on the sole of the foot that hurt when you walk called?
105521.e: Verrucas, or plantar warts, grow inwards on the sole of the foot because of the body’s weight. That is why they press and hurt when you walk.
105521.m: Verrucas are on the sole of the foot.

105522.q: Where is it especially easy to catch warts on the feet?
a: Barefoot at the swimming pool and in changing rooms
105522.e: Wart viruses survive well on damp floors in swimming pools and changing rooms. Pool sliders help protect you.
105522.m: Pool sliders protect against warts at the swimming pool.

105523.q: What are the small black dots you often see in a verruca?
105523.e: The dark dots are small blood vessels in which the blood has clotted. Warts do not have real roots.
105523.m: Black dots in warts are tiny blood vessels.

105524.q: What does a skin doctor often use to freeze a stubborn wart?
105524.e: Liquid nitrogen is about minus 196 degrees Celsius. It destroys the wart tissue, which then falls off.

105525.q: What happens to many warts in children, even without treatment?
105525.e: Over time the immune system fights the wart viruses. That is why many warts in children disappear by themselves after months or a few years.
105525.m: Many warts disappear on their own.

105526.q: In which layer of skin do wart viruses multiply?
105526.e: Wart viruses infect cells of the epidermis and make them grow wildly. This creates the hard, rough bump.

a: Pressure and rubbing, for example in tight shoes
105527.e: A corn forms when a patch of skin is pressed or rubbed for a long time. A common cause is shoes that are too tight.

105528.q: Where do corns form most often?
a: On the back of the hand
105528.e: Corns mainly form on and between the toes. There, shoes press on bony bumps.
105528.m: Corns are usually on the toes.

105529.q: Why does a corn hurt when you walk?
a: A hard core presses deep down on nerves
It contains small splinters of bone
105529.e: In the middle of a corn, a hard core grows inwards like a thorn. It presses on the nerves below and hurts with every step.
105529.m: The hard core of a corn presses on nerves.

105530.q: Where does the German name for a corn, “Hühnerauge” (chicken’s eye), come from?
a: From its look, with a pale ring and a dark core
Because it is treated with eggs
105530.e: With its round edge and the core in the middle, it looks like a bird’s eye. Otherwise it has nothing to do with chickens.
105530.m: A corn looks like a bird’s eye.

105531.q: What should you avoid doing with a corn?
a: Cutting it off yourself with scissors
105531.e: If you cut it yourself, you can hurt yourself and get an infection. It is better to take the pressure off the spot and have the core removed by a professional.
105531.m: You should not cut a corn off yourself.

105532.q: What is a wide patch of thickened hard skin without a hard core, caused by pressure, called?
105532.e: A callus is a broad thickening of the horny layer, for example on the hands of craftspeople. Unlike a corn, it has no core pressing down deep.
105532.m: A callus is thickened hard skin without a core.

105533.q: What helps most to stop a corn coming back?
a: Scratching the spot open every day
105533.e: As long as the pressure continues, the corn keeps forming again. Well-fitting shoes and pads take the pressure off the spot.

105534.e: Podiatrists specialise in caring for and treating feet. They remove the hard core gently.

105535.q: Into which layer of skin is the ink injected for a tattoo?
105535.e: The ink has to reach the dermis. If it were only in the epidermis, it would flake off after a few weeks as the skin renews itself.
105535.m: Tattoo ink sits in the dermis.

105536.q: Which people of New Zealand have a long tradition of face tattoos?
105536.e: The traditional tattoos of the Māori are called tā moko. They show a person’s origins and status and are still worn today.
105536.m: The Māori in New Zealand wear traditional face tattoos.

105537.q: Which famous glacier find from the Ötztal Alps has more than 60 tattoos?
105537.e: The glacier mummy Ötzi is more than 5000 years old. More than 60 tattoos made of lines and crosses were found on his skin.

105538.q: From which language does the word “tattoo” come?
105538.e: The word goes back to “tatau” from Tahiti. Sailors with James Cook brought it to Europe in the 18th century.
105538.m: The word tattoo comes from Polynesia.

105539.q: What are tattoos usually removed with today?
105539.e: Laser light breaks the ink particles into smaller pieces. The body can then gradually remove them, which usually takes several sessions.
105539.m: Tattoos are removed with a laser.

a: A painting on the skin that disappears after a while
105540.e: Henna only colours the upper layers of the skin. As the epidermis renews itself, it fades after a few weeks. People are warned against “black henna” with added substances, because it can cause allergies.
105540.m: A henna tattoo does not last for ever.

105541.q: Why should you keep a fresh tattoo out of the sun and not go swimming?
a: It is a wound that has to heal first
It then starts to itch like a wart
105541.e: When you get a tattoo, the skin is injured thousands of times. Until the wound has healed, germs in the water and sunlight can lead to infections and damage to the colours.
105541.m: A fresh tattoo is a wound.

105542.q: Which cells of the immune system take up tattoo ink in the skin?
105542.e: Scavenger cells, also called macrophages, swallow the ink particles. Because they cannot break them down, the ink stays visible in the dermis.
105542.m: Scavenger cells hold the tattoo ink in place.

105832.q: What is the tube-shaped pocket in the skin that a hair sits in called?
105832.e: The hair follicle wraps around the hair root like a small tube. In it, the hair is made and anchored.
105832.m: Every hair sits in a hair follicle.

105833.q: Which small muscle on the hair follicle makes the hair stand up when you are cold?
105833.e: A tiny muscle is attached to the hair follicle. When it contracts, the hair stands up and you get goose bumps.
105833.m: The hair erector muscle makes hairs stand up in the cold.

105834.q: Which cells in the hair follicle make sure a new hair can grow after one falls out?
105834.e: There are stem cells in the upper part of the hair follicle. They can divide again and again and build a new hair root.
105834.m: Stem cells in the hair follicle make new hair growth possible.

105835.q: What are the thick hairs on a cat’s muzzle called, whose follicles are surrounded by especially many nerves?
105835.e: Whiskers, also called vibrissae, are touch hairs. Their follicles have lots of nerves, so the cat can feel the slightest air movements and obstacles in the dark.

105836.q: What are the fine, short, pale little hairs called that grow on the cheeks and arms, for example?
105836.e: Vellus hairs are thin, short and hardly coloured, and they cover large parts of the skin. Hair on the head and eyebrows, by contrast, is thicker and strongly coloured.
105836.m: The fine fuzz on the skin is made of thin, pale little hairs.

105837.q: Do unborn babies in the womb already have hair?
a: Yes, a fine fuzz that usually falls out before birth
No, hair only grows after birth
Yes, thick hair on the head that never falls out
105837.e: Even an unborn baby grows a very fine fuzz all over its body. It is called lanugo and usually falls out before birth.
105837.m: Unborn babies have a fine fuzz of hair.

105838.q: Why can you feel even a very light touch on a single hair?
a: There are nerve endings around the hair follicle
The tip of the hair is a sense organ
The hair conducts electricity to the brain
105838.e: A fine network of nerve endings lies around every hair follicle. When the hair moves, the movement is detected at the root and reported to the brain.
105838.m: Hairs work like little feelers because their follicles are surrounded by nerves.

105839.q: What is an inflammation of the hair follicle, usually caused by bacteria, called?
105839.e: In folliculitis, hair follicles become inflamed, often because of bacteria. Small red bumps or tiny spots of pus appear around a hair.
105839.m: Folliculitis is an inflammation of hair follicles.

105840.q: Which property of keratin means hair does not dissolve when you wash it?
a: It does not dissolve in water
105840.e: Keratin is a fibrous protein that does not dissolve in water. It can soak up a little water and swell, but it stays stable.
105840.m: Keratin does not dissolve in water.

105841.q: Which group of substances does keratin belong to?
105841.e: Keratin is a protein made of long chains of amino acids. These chains are twisted into very strong fibres.
105841.m: Keratin is an especially strong protein.

105842.q: Which parts of animals are also mainly made of keratin?
a: The shells of beetles and crabs
105842.e: Hooves, claws, feathers, reptile scales and the outer covering of horns are made of keratin. Snail shells are made of lime, beetle shells of chitin.
105842.m: Hooves, claws and feathers are made of keratin, like our hair.

105843.q: Which chemical element in keratin is responsible for burnt hair smelling so unpleasant?
105843.e: Keratin contains many building blocks with sulphur. When it burns, sulphur compounds form that smell strong and unpleasant.
105843.m: The sulphur in keratin makes burnt hair stink.

105844.q: Which bonds in keratin are broken during a perm and joined again in a new shape?
105844.e: Sulphur bridges hold the keratin chains in their shape. A perm breaks them chemically, the hair is wound round curlers and the bridges are joined again in the new shape.
105844.m: A perm changes the sulphur bridges in keratin.

105845.q: Which cells of the epidermis make keratin?
105845.e: Keratinocytes are the most common cells in the epidermis. They make keratin and slowly move up to the surface as they do so.
105845.m: Keratinocytes are the cells that make keratin.

105846.q: Which layer of the skin is made of dead cells full of keratin?
105846.e: The horny layer is the outermost layer of the epidermis. Its dead, keratin-rich cells protect the body against water loss and germs.
105846.m: The horny layer protects the skin with dead keratin cells.

105847.q: What is the process called in which cells fill up with keratin and die?
105847.e: In keratinisation, cells fill with keratin, lose their nucleus and die. This is how hair, nails and the horny layer of the skin are formed.
105847.m: In keratinisation, living cells turn into firm horn.

a: The scales of the outermost layer of hair lie flat
105848.e: The outermost layer of a hair is made of keratin scales like roof tiles. When they lie flat, the hair reflects the light and shines.
105848.m: Flat hair scales make hair shine.

105849.q: What is the thickened lower end of the hair root called?
105849.e: The hair bulb is the onion-shaped swelling at the end of the hair root. There, the cells that the hair grows from divide.
105849.m: The hair bulb is at the lower end of the hair root.

105850.q: What does the hair papilla bring to the growing cells of the hair root?
105850.e: The hair papilla reaches up into the hair bulb from below and contains tiny blood vessels. Through it, the hair root gets oxygen and nutrients.
105850.m: The hair papilla supplies the hair root with blood.

105851.q: Which part of a hair is made of living cells?
105851.e: Living cells only divide in the hair root. As soon as they are pushed upwards, they harden and die, which is why having your hair cut does not hurt.
105851.m: Only the root of a hair is alive.

105852.q: What is the part of the hair that sticks out of the skin and can be seen called?
105852.e: The hair shaft is the visible hair above the skin. The hair root, on the other hand, is hidden in the hair follicle.
105852.m: The visible part of a hair is called the hair shaft.

105853.q: Where are the pigments made that give hair its colour?
a: In pigment cells in the hair root
105853.e: Pigment cells called melanocytes sit in the hair bulb. They pass the pigment on to the new hair cells as they form.
105853.m: Hair colour is made down in the hair root.

105854.q: Why can the police get DNA more easily from a hair pulled out with its root than from a cut hair?
a: The root contains cells with a nucleus
The root is longer than the shaft
105854.e: Cells with a nucleus, which holds the genetic information, are attached to the hair root. In the hardened hair shaft, hardly any of this is left.
105854.m: For a DNA trace, the hair root is more valuable than the shaft.

105855.q: What usually happens if you pull out a hair but the hair follicle stays undamaged?
a: A hair never grows there again
105855.e: As long as the hair follicle is intact, it makes a new hair. Only when the follicle is destroyed does nothing grow there any more.
105855.m: A pulled-out hair grows back from a healthy follicle.

105856.q: Where do cells divide so that a hair gets longer?
a: At the tip of the hair
In the middle of the hair shaft
On the scalp next to the hair
105856.e: Down in the hair root, cells divide very quickly and push the hair upwards. That is why a hair grows from the bottom and not at the tip.
105856.m: A hair grows from the root.

105857.q: Roughly how many hairs from the head does a healthy person lose each day?
105857.e: Losing about 50 to 100 hairs a day is normal. Most of these hairs are replaced by new ones growing back.
105857.m: Losing up to about 100 hairs a day is normal.

105858.q: In alopecia areata (patchy hair loss), what attacks the hair roots?
105858.e: In alopecia areata, the immune system wrongly turns against the hair roots. Round bald patches appear, which often grow back.
105858.m: In patchy hair loss, the body’s defences attack the hair roots.

105859.q: Which deficiency is a common cause of increased hair loss?
105859.e: Hair roots need a lot of iron because their cells divide quickly. That is why more hair often falls out when there is not enough iron.
105859.m: Iron deficiency can lead to hair loss.

105860.q: Why does hair fall out during many cancer treatments with chemotherapy?
a: The medicines damage cells that divide quickly
105860.e: Chemotherapy targets cells that divide quickly, like cancer cells. The cells of the hair roots also divide quickly and are affected; after treatment, the hair usually grows back.
105860.m: Chemotherapy also affects the fast-growing cells of the hair roots.

105861.q: After a high fever or severe stress, hair often falls out with a delay. After about how long?
105861.e: The strain sends many hairs into the resting phase at the same time. This lasts a few months, so the hair only falls out about 2 to 3 months later.
105861.m: Hair loss after a fever or stress often only shows months later.

105862.q: What happens to a hair before it falls out?
a: It stops growing and only sits loosely
It suddenly becomes twice as thick
105862.e: Every hair has a growth phase and then a resting phase. In the resting phase it no longer grows and finally falls out. A new hair pushes up behind it.
105862.m: A hair falls out at the end of its resting phase.

105863.q: Which organ can cause hair loss if it is overactive or underactive?
105863.e: The hormones of the thyroid gland control metabolism, including in the hair roots. If it works too hard or too little, the hair can thin.
105863.m: Thyroid problems can make hair fall out.

105864.q: What should you do if you lose an unusual amount of hair over a long time?
a: Have a doctor find out the cause
105864.e: Heavy or long-lasting hair loss can have many causes, such as deficiencies or illnesses. A doctor can find them with tests.
105864.m: If you notice unusual hair loss, a medical check-up helps.

105865.q: What are the bald areas at the temples called, which often appear first when someone starts going bald?
105865.e: In inherited hair loss, the hairline often moves back at the temples first. This is called a receding hairline.
105865.m: A receding hairline means the hair moves back at the temples.

105866.q: What is a bald spot on the top of the back of the head called, which recalls a hairstyle monks used to wear?
105866.e: Monks used to have a round patch on the back of the head shaved bald, called the tonsure. The bald patch that forms on top of the head in many men looks similar.
105866.m: The tonsure is a bald patch on the top of the head.

105867.q: What mainly decides whether a man goes bald?
105867.e: The most common baldness comes from inherited hair loss: from birth, the hair roots are sensitive to certain hormones made by the body. Hats or washing play no part in it.

105868.q: Why is the skin of a bald head especially at risk in summer?
a: It has no sun protection from hair
It is thicker than other skin
It has a poorer blood supply
105868.e: Hair shades the scalp. Without it, UV rays hit the skin directly, which is why a hat or sun cream is important.
105868.m: A bald head needs a hat or sun cream in summer.

105869.q: What is usually moved in a hair transplant?
a: The person’s own hair roots from the back of the head
105869.e: In a hair transplant, the person’s own hair follicles are taken from the back of the head and put into bald areas. There they keep growing.
105869.m: In a hair transplant, your own hair moves to a new place.

105870.q: Why does a ring of hair often remain at the back and sides of many bald heads?
a: The hair roots there are less sensitive by inheritance
You lie on it at night
105870.e: The hair roots at the back and sides of the head do not react to the hormones involved in inherited hair loss. That is why a ring of hair often remains there.
105870.m: The ring of hair stays because its roots are tougher.

105871.q: Roughly what share of men have visible inherited hair loss by the age of 50?
105871.e: Inherited hair loss is very common. By about 50, around half of all men are affected to a greater or lesser degree.
105871.m: About one man in two has hair loss by 50.

105872.q: Where does the hair usually get thinner when women have inherited hair loss?
a: At the parting on top of the head
Only at the nape of the neck
105872.e: In women, the hair usually thins over a wide area around the parting. Going completely bald is rare for them.
105872.m: In women, the hair usually gets thinner at the parting.

105873.q: Why does hair turn grey with age?
a: The hair roots make less pigment
105873.e: In the hair roots, pigment cells make the pigment melanin. With age these cells work less, and colourless hairs grow.
105873.m: Grey hair appears when the hair roots make less pigment.

105874.q: Do more grey hairs grow back if you pull out a grey hair?
a: No, only one hair grows from each follicle
Yes, two or three grow back
Yes, all the neighbouring hairs turn grey
105874.e: A hair follicle only ever makes one hair, and pulling one out does not affect the neighbouring follicles. Getting more grey hair comes only from getting older.
105874.m: Pulling out grey hairs does not make more grey hairs grow.

105875.q: Why does a hair without pigment look white?
a: Tiny air bubbles scatter the light
105875.e: Colourless hair contains tiny pockets of air. They scatter the light in all directions, a bit like snow, which is why the hair looks white.
105875.m: Air in the hair makes colourless hairs look white.

105876.q: Can a dark hair that has already grown turn grey overnight?
a: No, only hair that grows back is colourless
105876.e: The hair shaft is dead, and its pigment stays. A hair only turns grey if it grows out of the root already colourless.
105876.m: A hair that has grown does not lose its colour overnight.

105877.q: If you look closely, what is “grey” hair usually?
a: A mixture of coloured and white hairs
Hair with grey dust on it
105877.e: A single hair is usually either still coloured or already white. Only the mixture of both looks grey from a distance.
105877.m: Hair looks grey because of the mix of coloured and white hairs.

105878.q: From what age do many people get their first grey hairs?
105878.e: Many people get their first grey hairs between about 30 and 40. Exactly when depends strongly on their genes.
105878.m: The first grey hairs often appear between 30 and 40.

105879.q: Why do grey roots show again a few weeks after grey hair has been dyed?
a: The hair growing back is still colourless
The dye moves into the scalp
The dye is destroyed by light
The hair rejects the dye straight away
105879.e: Hair dye only works on hair that has already grown. Colourless hair keeps growing out of the root, and it can be seen at the scalp as roots.
105879.m: Dyed hair grows back in its natural colour at the root.

105880.q: What is the pigment called that gives hair and skin their colour?
105880.e: Melanin is made in special cells of the skin and hair roots. Depending on its type and amount, hair is blond, brown, black or red.

105881.q: Roughly what share of the hairs on the head are in the growth phase at the same time?
105881.e: Every hair has its own rhythm. The vast majority are growing, and only a small number are resting or about to fall out, which is why all your hair never falls out at once.
105881.m: Most hairs on the head are growing at the same time, only a few are resting.

105883.q: Roughly how long does the growth phase of a hair on the head last?
105883.e: A hair on the head usually grows for between 2 and 6 years without a break. Then it moves into the transition and resting phases.
105883.m: A hair on the head grows for several years.

105884.q: A hair grows 1 cm per month. How long is it after 3 years of non-stop growth?
105884.e: 3 years are 3 times 12, so 36 months. At 1 cm per month, the hair grows 36 times 1 cm, so 36 cm.
105884.m: To work out hair length, multiply the growth per month by the number of months.

105885.q: Why do eyelashes and eyebrows stay much shorter than the hair on your head?
a: Their growth phase is much shorter
They are not made of keratin
105885.e: Eyelashes and eyebrows only grow for a few months, then they fall out and are replaced. Hair on the head, by contrast, keeps growing for years.
105885.m: The short growth phase keeps eyelashes and eyebrows short.

105886.q: Lena’s hair is 20 cm long and grows 1.2 cm per month. How long is it after 10 months without a haircut?
105886.e: In 10 months the hair grows 10 times 1.2 cm, so 12 cm. 20 cm plus 12 cm makes 32 cm.
105886.m: Add the growth of all the months to the starting length.

105887.q: A person has 100,000 hairs on their head, and each grows 0.3 mm per day. How many metres of hair grow altogether per day?
105887.e: 100,000 times 0.3 mm makes 30,000 mm. Since 1000 mm make one metre, that is 30 m.
105887.m: Lots of small lengths add up to a long distance.

105888.q: A hair stops growing and rests for a while. What usually happens next?
a: It falls out and a new hair grows
It keeps growing twice as fast
It turns into a sweat gland
It stays on the head for ever
105888.e: Every hair goes through growth, a short transition and a resting time. Then it falls out, and a new hair grows from the same hair follicle.
105888.m: After its resting time, a hair falls out and is replaced.

105889.q: What is the skin under the nail called, on which the nail plate rests?
105889.e: The nail plate lies firmly on the nail bed and slowly slides forwards over it as it grows.
105889.m: The nail lies on the nail bed.

105890.q: Why does a healthy fingernail look pink?
a: Blood vessels in the nail bed show through
The nail plate is coloured pink
Light is bent red in the nail
105890.e: The nail plate is almost see-through. Below it lies the nail bed, which has a good blood supply, and its colour shows through.
105890.m: The pink of nails comes from the blood in the nail bed.

105891.q: In which area is the nail plate made?
a: In the nail matrix at the base of the nail
At the tip of the nail
At the side edge of the nail
105891.e: The nail matrix lies under the skin at the base of the nail. Its cells harden and push the nail plate forwards.
105891.m: The nail grows from the nail matrix at the base of the nail.

105892.q: What colour do nails often turn when the blood carries too little oxygen, for example in severe cold?
105892.e: Blood low in oxygen is darker. The nail bed then looks bluish through the see-through nail plate.
105892.m: Bluish nails show there is little oxygen in the blood.

105893.q: What job does the cuticle at the base of the nail have?
a: It protects the nail matrix from germs
It makes the nail grow faster
105893.e: The cuticle seals the gap between the skin and the nail. This means fewer germs reach the sensitive nail matrix.
105893.m: The cuticle seals the base of the nail against germs.

105894.q: How do toenails grow compared with fingernails?
105894.e: Toenails only grow about half as fast as fingernails. That is why a whole toenail takes around one to one and a half years to grow back.
105894.m: Toenails grow more slowly than fingernails.

105895.q: Roughly how long does it take for a whole fingernail to grow back?
105895.e: The nail slowly grows forwards from the nail matrix to the tip. It takes about half a year until it is completely renewed.
105895.m: A fingernail renews itself in about half a year.

105896.q: What forms when you trap your finger hard and blood flows under the nail?
a: A dark bruise under the nail
105896.e: The blow tears tiny vessels in the nail bed. The blood collects under the nail plate and shows through dark red to black.
105896.m: Trapping your finger can cause a bruise under the nail.

105897.q: What makes an ingrown toenail more likely?
a: Cutting the nail round instead of straight
105897.e: If the corners are cut round, the nail can grow sideways into the skin and make it inflamed. That is why toenails are cut straight.
105897.m: Cut toenails straight so they do not grow in.

105898.q: Which germs usually cause nail fungus?
105898.e: Nail fungus is usually caused by thread fungi that feed on keratin. Less often, yeasts or moulds are involved.
105898.m: Nail fungus is usually caused by thread fungi.

105899.q: Where do people especially often catch nail or foot fungus?
a: Barefoot at indoor pools, saunas and showers
105899.e: Fungal spores survive well on damp floors. If you walk barefoot there, you can easily pick them up; pool sliders protect you.
105899.m: Pool sliders protect against fungi at pools and in showers.

105900.q: What kind of surroundings do nail fungi especially like?
105900.e: Fungi grow best in damp warmth, for example in tight, sweaty shoes. Airy shoes and dry feet make life hard for them.

105901.q: How can you often recognise nail fungus?
a: The nail becomes yellowish, thick and brittle
The nail becomes shiny and pink
The nail grows twice as fast
The nail becomes see-through and soft
105901.e: With nail fungus, the nail usually turns whitish to yellowish brown. It becomes thicker and crumbly and can come away from the nail bed.
105901.m: A yellow, thick and brittle nail can be a sign of nail fungus.

105902.q: Why does treating nail fungus often take many months?
a: The healthy nail has to grow back slowly
The medicines only work after years
The fungus hides in the bone
105902.e: The infected nail does not become healthy again; it has to be replaced by healthy nail growing back. Because nails grow slowly, this takes time.
105902.m: Nail fungus is only cured when a healthy nail has grown back.

105903.q: Which skin condition often comes before nail fungus on the toes?
105903.e: Athlete’s foot between the toes is very common. If it is not treated, the fungi can spread to the toenails.
105903.m: Untreated athlete’s foot can spread to the nails.

105904.q: How can you catch nail fungus from other people?
a: By shaking hands on the phone
105904.e: Fungal spores cling to towels, socks and shoes. That is why you should not share these things with others.
105904.m: Your own towels and shoes protect you from nail fungus.

105905.q: Are fingernails or toenails more often affected by nail fungus?
105905.e: Toenails often spend a long time in warm, damp shoes and grow slowly. That is why they are infected much more often than fingernails.
105905.m: Nail fungus mainly affects the toenails.

105906.q: What helps in everyday life to prevent nail fungus?
a: Drying your feet and the gaps between your toes well
Letting your nails grow as long as possible
105906.e: Dry skin between the toes gives fungi little to hold on to. Fresh socks every day and airy shoes also help.

105907.q: What can trigger a new flare-up of psoriasis?
105907.e: Psoriasis often comes in flare-ups. Infections, stress or certain medicines can trigger a new flare-up.
105907.m: Stress and infections can make psoriasis worse.

a: Yes, through shared plates and cups
105908.e: Psoriasis develops within the body itself, triggered by the immune system and an inherited tendency. You cannot catch it from people who have it.

105909.q: On which parts of the body does psoriasis appear especially often?
a: Earlobes and tips of the toes
105909.e: Typical patches appear on the outer sides of the elbows and knees and on the scalp. But other areas can be affected too.
105909.m: Psoriasis often appears on the elbows, knees and scalp.

105910.q: What happens differently in the skin with psoriasis?
a: The epidermis renews itself far too quickly
The skin makes no more cells
The skin loses all its hair
The skin is broken down by fungi
105910.e: Normally the epidermis renews itself in around four weeks. With psoriasis this happens in a few days, so the cells pile up and form scales.
105910.m: With psoriasis, the epidermis grows back far too quickly.

105911.q: What do typical patches of psoriasis look like?
105911.e: The patches have sharp edges, are red and slightly raised. On top lie shiny, silvery scales.
105911.m: Silvery scales on red skin are typical of psoriasis.

105912.q: How do the fingernails often change with psoriasis?
a: They all fall off at once
105912.e: Many people with it have pitted nails with small dents in the nail plate. Yellowish-brown patches, known as oil spots, also occur.
105912.m: Pits in the nails can be a sign of psoriasis.

105913.q: Which additional problem can some people with psoriasis have?
105913.e: In some people with psoriasis, the joints also become inflamed. This is called psoriatic arthritis.
105913.m: Psoriasis can also inflame the joints.

105914.q: Which treatment for psoriasis uses light in a targeted way?
105914.e: In light therapy, the skin is exposed to UV light in a controlled way. This slows down the excessive inflammation and the rapid cell division.
105914.m: Controlled UV light can ease psoriasis.

105915.q: What part does the immune system play in psoriasis?
a: It wrongly triggers inflammation in the skin
People with psoriasis have none at all
It only attacks fungi in the skin
It has nothing to do with it
105915.e: In psoriasis, the body’s defences overreact and cause inflammation in the skin. Flare-ups can be triggered by infections or stress, for example.
105915.m: Psoriasis is an inflammation that comes from the immune system.

a: A spot where the hair grows in a spiral
A bald spot on the head
105916.e: At a hair whorl, the hair follicles are angled so that the hairs grow in a circle around a central point.
105916.m: At a hair whorl, the hair grows in a circle.

105917.q: Where do most people have their hair whorl?
a: On the top of the head towards the back
In the middle of the forehead
At the nape of the neck
105917.e: The typical hair whorl is on the top of the back of the head. From there the hair spreads out in all directions.
105917.m: The hair whorl is usually on the top of the back of the head.

105918.q: In which direction does the hair whorl turn in most people?
105918.e: Studies show that in most people the whorl on the back of the head turns clockwise. In a minority it turns anticlockwise.

105919.q: What is it called when someone has two hair whorls on their head?
105919.e: Some people have two whorls next to each other on the back of the head. This is called a double crown; the hair there is often hard to style.
105919.m: Two hair whorls are called a double crown.

105920.q: Why is it hard to comb hair at a whorl in a different direction?
a: The direction of growth is fixed by the hair follicles
The hair there is electrically charged
105920.e: The hair follicles sit at an angle in the skin and set the direction of growth. Combing cannot change this for good.
105920.m: The angled follicles decide which way the hair grows.

105921.q: For which animal are hair whorls traditionally recorded in its passport for identification?
105921.e: In a horse passport, the position of the hair whorls is drawn in as well as the markings. They are different on every horse and do not change.
105921.m: Horses can also be recognised by their hair whorls.

105922.q: When is it decided where a person’s hair whorl will be?
105922.e: The hair follicles and their direction already form in the unborn child. That is why the hair whorl stays in the same place for life.
105922.m: The hair whorl forms before birth.

105923.q: How are head lice usually passed on?
a: By jumping from head to head
Through water in the swimming pool
105923.e: Head lice can neither jump nor fly. They mainly crawl onto another head when hair touches directly.
105923.m: Head lice move from head to head when hair touches.

105924.q: People with which natural hair colour usually have the most hairs on their head?
105924.e: Blond hairs are especially thin, but usually more of them grow, often around 150,000. Redheads have thicker hairs, but fewer of them.
105924.m: Blond people usually have the most but thinnest hairs on their head.

a: A shampoo with an anti-fungal ingredient
105925.e: Special anti-dandruff shampoos contain ingredients against the yeast fungus on the scalp. This calms the skin, and it makes fewer flakes.
105925.m: Anti-dandruff shampoos work against the fungus on the scalp.

105926.q: Which kind of living thing often encourages greasy dandruff?
105926.e: A yeast fungus that feeds on sebum lives on the scalp. If it multiplies a lot, it irritates the skin and more flakes form.
105926.m: A yeast fungus on the scalp can encourage dandruff.

105927.q: What is the line called where the scalp on the forehead meets skin without hair?
105927.e: The hairline is the line where the hair on the head begins. When hair loss starts, it can move backwards.
105927.m: Where the hair begins on the forehead is the hairline.

105928.q: What do head lice feed on?
105928.e: Head lice bite into the scalp several times a day and suck blood. Their saliva causes the typical itching.
105928.m: Head lice suck blood from the scalp.

105929.q: Why does a small cut on the scalp often bleed a lot?
a: The scalp has an especially good blood supply
The blood in the head is thinner
Blood does not clot on the head
105929.e: The scalp is supplied by many blood vessels that feed the hair roots. That is why even a small wound there bleeds heavily.
105929.m: The scalp has a rich blood supply and bleeds heavily when injured.

105930.q: What is the yellowish, scaly crust called that many babies have on their scalp in the first months of life?
105930.e: Cradle cap is a harmless, greasy flaking of the scalp in babies. It usually disappears by itself after a few months.
105930.m: Cradle cap is a harmless scaly crust in babies.

106224.q: What is the part of a tooth that sticks out of the gum and can be seen called?
106224.e: The crown is the part you see in your mouth and chew with. The root and the socket are hidden in the jawbone.
106224.m: The crown is the visible part of a tooth.

106225.q: Which layer covers the crown of a tooth on the outside?
106225.e: The crown is covered by a hard, shiny layer of enamel. It protects the more sensitive inside of the tooth.
106225.m: Enamel protects the crown like armour.

106226.q: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
106226.e: Tooth enamel is made almost entirely of minerals and is harder than any bone. That is why it stands up to chewing for decades.
106226.m: Tooth enamel is harder than any bone in the body.

106227.q: Which mineral is an important building block of tooth enamel?
106227.e: Tooth enamel is made almost entirely of minerals. The most important building block is calcium together with phosphate.
106227.m: Tooth enamel contains lots of calcium.

106228.q: Why can the body not rebuild lost tooth enamel itself?
a: Finished enamel contains no living cells
Enamel only grows back during sleep
Saliva dissolves new enamel straight away
Enamel only forms again during a fever
106228.e: The cells that build the enamel die as soon as the tooth has come through. That is why a hole in the enamel has to be filled by the dentist.
106228.m: Lost tooth enamel does not grow back.

106229.q: What are the fine grooves on the chewing surface of the back teeth, where decay easily starts, called?
106229.e: Fissures are narrow grooves between the bumps of the back teeth. Food scraps and bacteria easily get stuck there.
106229.m: Decay starts especially easily in the fissures of the back teeth.

106230.q: What are the raised points on the chewing surface of a back tooth called?
106230.e: Back teeth have a wide chewing surface with several cusps. They grind food as if between two millstones.
106230.m: The cusps of the back teeth grind food.

106231.q: What does the dentist do when sealing fissures?
a: She fills the grooves of the chewing surface with plastic
She pulls out a milk tooth
She glues a wire onto the teeth
106231.e: In sealing, the deep grooves of the back teeth are closed with runny plastic. Then bacteria can no longer settle there.
106231.m: Fissure sealing protects the chewing surfaces from decay.

106232.q: What is an artificial cap placed over a badly damaged tooth called?
106232.e: If not enough healthy tooth is left, it is capped with an artificial crown. A bridge, on the other hand, spans a gap between teeth.
106232.m: An artificial crown protects a badly damaged tooth.

106233.q: Which part of the tooth sits in the jawbone and holds the tooth in place?
106233.e: The root sits out of sight in the jawbone. It anchors the tooth so that it does not wobble when you chew.
106233.m: The root anchors the tooth in the jaw.

106234.q: Which hard layer covers the outside of the root of a tooth?
106234.e: The root is not covered with enamel but with a thin, bone-like layer called cementum. The fibres that hold the tooth are anchored in it.
106234.m: The root of a tooth is covered with cementum.

106235.q: What is the hollow in the jawbone that a tooth root sits in called?
106235.e: Each tooth root sits in its own socket, which experts call an alveolus. The socket is part of the jawbone.
106235.m: Each tooth root sits in its own socket.

106236.q: How is a tooth fixed in its socket?
a: With many fine fibres of the root lining
Only by the pressure of the gum
With a kind of glue made of saliva
106236.e: Between the root and the bone lies a lining with thousands of collagen fibres. They cushion the pressure of chewing, which is why a healthy tooth can move just a tiny bit.
106236.m: Fine fibres hold the tooth springily in the jawbone.

106237.q: Why do large back teeth have several roots?
a: They have to withstand strong chewing pressure
So that they fall out more easily
106237.e: You grind food with your back teeth. Several roots spread the strong chewing pressure onto the jawbone.
106237.m: Several roots hold back teeth firmly when you chew.

106238.q: How do nerves and blood vessels get inside a tooth?
a: Through a small opening at the tip of the root
Through the enamel of the crown
Through the gaps between the teeth
106238.e: At the tip of each root there is a tiny opening. There, nerves and blood vessels enter the root canal.
106238.m: Nerves and blood vessels reach the tooth through the tip of the root.

106239.q: Which metal is an artificial tooth root, a dental implant, usually made of?
106239.e: Most dental implants are made of titanium. It is very well tolerated and grows firmly together with the jawbone.
106239.m: Dental implants are usually made of well-tolerated titanium.

106240.q: Why does a milk tooth that has fallen out have almost no root left?
a: Its root was broken down beforehand
Milk teeth never grow with a root
The root stays stuck in the jaw
The root is worn away by chewing
106240.e: When the permanent tooth moves up, the body gradually breaks down the root of the milk tooth. In the end only a little tissue holds the milk tooth, and it wobbles.
106240.m: Before the teeth change, the root of the milk tooth is broken down.

106241.q: Where is the neck of a tooth?
a: Where the crown meets the root
At the tip of the root
In the middle of the chewing surface
106241.e: The neck of the tooth is the narrow area between the crown and the root. In healthy teeth, it lies at the edge of the gum.
106241.m: The neck of the tooth joins the crown and the root.

106242.q: Which two hard substances meet on the outside at the neck of a tooth?
106242.e: The crown is covered with enamel, the root with cementum. The border between the two runs exactly at the neck of the tooth.
106242.m: At the neck of the tooth, the enamel ends and the cementum begins.

106243.q: Why are exposed tooth necks often sensitive to pain?
a: Because unprotected dentine is exposed there
Because especially thick enamel lies there
106243.e: At the neck of the tooth there is no protective enamel. If it is exposed, fine channels in the dentine pass stimuli straight to the nerve.
106243.m: Exposed tooth necks are sensitive because they have no enamel.

106244.q: Which stimulus most often makes sensitive tooth necks hurt?
a: Cold, for example when eating ice cream
Breathing in deeply through the nose
106244.e: Cold, but also sweet or sour things, changes the fluid in the channels of the dentine. This irritates the nerve and causes a short, sharp pain.
106244.m: Sensitive tooth necks react especially strongly to cold.

106245.q: What can cause tooth necks to become exposed?
a: Scrubbing too hard with a hard toothbrush
106245.e: If you scrub with a lot of pressure and a hard brush, you can push the gum back. Gum disease (periodontitis) also makes the gum shrink.
106245.m: Gentle brushing protects the gums and the tooth necks.

106246.q: Why does decay start more easily on an exposed tooth neck than on the crown?
a: Because cementum and dentine are softer than enamel
Because the tooth neck keeps growing back
106246.e: Cementum and dentine contain fewer minerals than tooth enamel. That is why acids from bacteria attack them faster.
106246.m: An exposed tooth neck is especially prone to decay.

106247.q: How do many toothpastes for sensitive teeth help?
a: They seal the fine channels in the dentine
106247.e: Special ingredients settle in the open channels of the dentine and seal them. Stimuli such as cold then reach the nerve less strongly.
106247.m: Toothpaste for sensitive teeth seals open channels in the dentine.

106248.q: How should you brush so that the tooth necks are not damaged?
a: Scrubbing sideways with a lot of pressure
106248.e: If you scrub sideways with a lot of pressure, you can rub notches into the tooth at the neck. Brushing gently with a soft brush protects teeth and gums.
106248.m: Gentle brushing protects the tooth necks.

106249.q: What is the hard substance called that lies under the enamel and makes up most of the tooth?
106249.e: Dentine makes up the main part of the tooth. In the crown it lies under the enamel, in the root under the cementum.
106249.m: Dentine makes up most of a tooth.

106251.q: How hard is dentine compared with tooth enamel and bone?
a: Softer than enamel but harder than bone
106251.e: Dentine contains about 70 per cent minerals, which is less than enamel but more than bone. In return, it is a little more elastic than enamel.
106251.m: In hardness, dentine lies between enamel and bone.

106252.q: What runs through dentine in large numbers?
106252.e: Dentine is crossed by countless tiny channels that reach the pulp. They contain extensions of the cells that make the dentine.
106252.m: Countless fine channels run through dentine.

106253.q: Why do teeth with exposed dentine often hurt when you eat something cold?
a: Fine channels in the dentine pass the stimulus to the tooth nerve
106253.e: Dentine is crossed by tiny channels that reach the pulp. Without the protective enamel, cold and sweet things quickly reach the nerve.

106254.e: Dentine is yellowish. Because enamel is see-through, the dentine helps give the tooth its shade.
106254.m: The yellowish dentine shows through the enamel.

106255.q: What is ivory, the material of elephants’ tusks, made of?
106255.e: Elephants’ tusks are greatly lengthened teeth. Their ivory is mainly made of dentine.
106255.m: Ivory is the dentine of elephant tusks.

106256.q: What happens to the space for the pulp over a lifetime?
a: It gets smaller because new dentine forms
It gets bigger because dentine disappears
It always stays exactly the same size
106256.e: Throughout life, the odontoblasts slowly make more dentine towards the inside. This makes the pulp chamber narrower with age.
106256.m: With age, new dentine makes the pulp chamber narrower.

106257.q: What is the soft tissue inside a tooth called?
106257.e: Inside every tooth lies the dental pulp, a soft tissue. It fills the pulp chamber in the crown and the root canals.
106257.m: The soft dental pulp lies inside the tooth.
