a: They flow back into the body
107415.e: A machine separates the plasma and gives the blood cells back to the donor. That is why you can donate plasma more often than whole blood.
107415.m: When you donate plasma, you get the blood cells back.

107416.q: What are the defence substances in blood plasma that recognise germs called?
107416.e: Antibodies are proteins dissolved in the plasma. They recognise germs and mark them for the defence cells.
107416.m: Antibodies in the blood recognise germs.

107417.q: Which animal is the Rhesus factor named after?
107417.e: The feature was discovered in experiments with blood from rhesus monkeys. That is where the name comes from.
107417.m: The Rhesus factor is named after the rhesus monkey.

107418.q: What does “Rhesus positive” mean in a person?
a: A certain feature sits on the red blood cells
The blood contains no white blood cells
The blood contains especially a lot of iron
107418.e: Rhesus positive means that the red blood cells carry the Rhesus feature. If it is missing, you are Rhesus negative.
107418.m: Rhesus-positive people have the Rhesus feature on their red blood cells.

107419.q: Roughly how many people in Europe are Rhesus positive?
107419.e: Around 85 out of 100 people in Europe are Rhesus positive. Only about 15 per cent are Rhesus negative.
107419.m: Most people in Europe are Rhesus positive.

107420.q: Does a Rhesus-negative person have antibodies against feature D from birth?
a: No, only after contact with Rhesus-positive blood
Only if they have blood group A
107420.e: Anti-D antibodies only form when the immune system meets Rhesus-positive blood. This process is called sensitisation.
107420.m: The body only makes antibodies against the Rhesus feature after contact.

107421.q: Why should a Rhesus-negative person not be given Rhesus-positive blood?
a: They can form antibodies that destroy the foreign blood cells
It gives them a fever straight away
Their heart then beats too slowly
107421.e: The immune system recognises the foreign feature D and forms antibodies. In a later transfusion, the donor cells are then attacked.
107421.m: Rhesus-negative people should only be given Rhesus-negative blood.

107422.q: How do you write blood group A with a positive Rhesus factor in short?
107422.e: The plus sign after the blood group stands for Rhesus positive. A minus sign means Rhesus negative.
107422.m: The plus sign with the blood group means Rhesus positive.

a: Yes, it is inherited from the parents
No, it depends on where you live
107423.e: The Rhesus factor is fixed by the genes and is passed on from parents to children. It stays the same for life.
107423.m: The Rhesus factor is inborn and stays the same for life.

107424.q: Which blood group counts as the universal recipient for red blood cells?
107424.e: People with AB positive have no antibodies against A, B or D. That is why they can be given red blood cells of all groups.
107424.m: People with AB positive can be given red blood cells of all groups.

107425.q: Why can red blood cells of group O be given to many people?
a: They carry no A and no B features
107425.e: The recipient’s antibodies are directed against the features A and B. If these are missing from the cells, there is no clumping.
107425.m: Red blood cells of group O have no A and B features.

107426.q: Which antibodies does a person with blood group O have in their plasma?
107426.e: With blood group O, the features A and B are missing from the cells. That is why the body makes antibodies against both.
107426.m: People with blood group O have antibodies against A and against B.

107427.q: Which antibodies does a person with blood group A have in their plasma?
107427.e: The body does not make antibodies against its own feature A. But it does have antibodies against the foreign feature B.
107427.m: People with blood group A have antibodies against B.

107428.q: Plasma from which blood group is suitable for all recipients?
107428.e: Plasma from group AB contains neither anti-A nor anti-B. That is why it does not attack the cells of any recipient.
107428.m: For plasma, blood group AB is the universal donor.

107429.q: From which blood groups can a person with blood group B be given red blood cells?
107429.e: A person with group B has anti-A in their plasma. So they can only take cells without feature A, which means from B and O.
107429.m: People with blood group B can take red blood cells from B and O.

107430.q: Which blood group is the rarest in Switzerland?
107430.e: Only around one per cent of the population has AB negative. The groups A positive and O positive are the most common.
107430.m: AB negative is the rarest blood group in Switzerland.

107431.q: Why is group O negative blood especially in demand at blood donation services?
a: It is given in emergencies before the blood group is known
107431.e: After serious accidents, there is often no time to find out the blood group. Then injured people are given group O negative blood first.
107431.m: In emergencies, group O negative blood is often used first.

107432.q: From which blood group can a person with O negative be given red blood cells?
a: From O positive and O negative
From A negative and O negative
107432.e: People with O negative have antibodies against A and B and can form antibodies against D. That is why they can only take cells without A, B and D.
107432.m: People with O negative can only take red blood cells from O negative.

107433.q: What happens if someone is given red blood cells of an unsuitable blood group?
a: The blood cells clump together and are destroyed
The blood turns green straight away
The body makes new bones straight away
107433.e: The recipient’s antibodies attach to the foreign cells. These clump together and break apart, which can be life-threatening.
107433.m: With the wrong blood group, the blood cells clump together dangerously.

107434.q: What must match before a blood transfusion?
a: The blood groups of donor and recipient
107434.e: If the blood group does not match, the blood can clump together. That is why it is checked again right beside the patient before every transfusion.
107434.m: In a transfusion, the blood group must match.

107435.q: Why is a little donor blood mixed with the recipient’s blood in the laboratory before a transfusion?
107435.e: If the mixture does not clump, the two blood samples are compatible. This laboratory test is called cross-matching.
107435.m: Before a transfusion, a test checks whether the blood is compatible.

107436.q: Which organisation collects blood donations in Switzerland?
107436.e: The Blood Transfusion Service SRC Switzerland is part of the Swiss Red Cross. Together with regional services, it organises blood donations.
107436.m: In Switzerland, the Blood Transfusion Service of the Swiss Red Cross organises blood donation.

107437.q: What is it called when a person has their own blood taken before a planned operation?
107437.e: In autologous blood donation, your own blood is stored and given back if needed. This avoids any problems with other people’s blood groups.
107437.m: In autologous blood donation, you later get your own blood back.

107438.q: Why is donated blood usually split into its parts?
a: Each patient only gets the part they need
107438.e: Red blood cells, plasma and sometimes platelets are obtained from one donation. In this way one donation often helps several people.
107438.m: A blood donation is split up and can therefore help several people.

107439.q: What is a red cell concentrate?
a: A bag of stored red blood cells
A device for measuring the pulse
107439.e: For a red cell concentrate, the red blood cells are separated from a donation. It is the blood product that is transfused most often.
107439.m: A red cell concentrate mainly contains red blood cells.

107440.q: What is every blood donation tested for in the laboratory before it is used?
a: Germs such as HIV and hepatitis
107440.e: Every donation is tested for blood group and for diseases that can be passed on. This prevents germs being passed to recipients.
107440.m: Every blood donation is checked for germs before it is used.

107442.q: Roughly how many red blood cells does one microlitre of blood contain in adults?
107442.e: A tiny droplet of one microlitre contains around 4 to 6 million red blood cells. They are the most common blood cells.
107442.m: Red blood cells are the most common cells in the blood.

107443.q: What is examined in a blood count?
107443.e: In a blood count, the laboratory counts red and white blood cells and platelets. This can show anaemia or infections, for example.
107443.m: A blood count shows which cells are in the blood.

107444.q: What does the abbreviation “Hb” stand for in a blood count?
107444.e: Hb stands for haemoglobin, the red pigment in blood. A low Hb level can point to anaemia.
107444.m: In a blood count, Hb stands for the red pigment haemoglobin.

107445.q: Are there more red or more white blood cells in the blood?
107445.e: In a tiny drop of blood there are around a thousand times more red than white blood cells. The white ones are still important for the body’s defences.
107445.m: There are far more red than white blood cells in the blood.

107446.q: Why does the doctor sometimes do a blood count when you have an infection?
a: She can see whether there are more white blood cells
She wants to find out the hair colour
She uses it to measure body weight
She uses it to test hearing
107446.e: During an infection, the body makes more white blood cells for defence. The blood count shows this change.
107446.m: With infections, the number of white blood cells often rises.

107447.q: What do scavenger cells in the blood do?
a: They eat bacteria and foreign bodies
107447.e: Scavenger cells are a kind of white blood cell. They take up bacteria and destroy them.

107448.q: Which blood cells protect the body from germs?
107448.e: White blood cells are the body’s defence cells. Some eat germs, others make antibodies.
107448.m: White blood cells are the police in the blood.

107449.q: Which blood cells are called erythrocytes in a blood count?
107449.e: The name comes from the Greek “erythros”, meaning red. In a blood count they are counted and their size is measured.
107449.m: Erythrocytes are the red blood cells.

107450.q: Where are new red blood cells made?
107450.e: Billions of new red blood cells are made in the bone marrow every day. They replace the old ones, which are broken down after about 120 days.
107450.m: Red blood cells are made in the bone marrow.

107451.e: Platelets are pieces pinched off from larger cells. That is why they have no nucleus of their own.

107452.q: Where in the body are platelets made?
107452.e: In the bone marrow, many small platelets are pinched off from large cells. The other blood cells are made there too.
107452.m: Platelets are made in the bone marrow.

107454.q: What happens if someone has too few platelets?
a: They bruise and bleed more easily
They get a fever straight away
They see less well at night
107454.e: Without enough platelets, the blood clots less well. Even small knocks then cause bruises, and wounds bleed for longer.
107454.m: Too few platelets lead to more bleeding.

107455.q: Roughly how long does a platelet live?
a: About a week to ten days
107455.e: Platelets have a short life of around a week. That is why the bone marrow constantly has to make new ones.
107455.m: Platelets only live for about a week.

107456.q: Which well-known medicine stops platelets working and is therefore used to help prevent heart attacks?
107456.e: Acetylsalicylic acid, known as aspirin, stops platelets from sticking together. In a small dose it can prevent blood clots in the vessels.
107456.m: Aspirin stops platelets from sticking together.

107457.q: In which organ are old platelets mainly broken down?
107457.e: The spleen filters aged blood cells out of the blood. Most old platelets are broken down there too.
107457.m: Old platelets are mainly broken down in the spleen.

a: A blood product made from donated platelets
A device for measuring blood pressure
A test to find out the blood group
107458.e: Platelet concentrates are given, for example, to people after chemotherapy who have too few platelets of their own. They help to prevent bleeding.
107458.m: A platelet concentrate contains donated platelets.

107459.q: What forms in a wound so that it stops bleeding?
107459.e: When you are injured, the blood clots. Fine threads of fibrin form a net, and a plug forms that closes the wound.

107460.q: Which small parts of the blood help fibrin to close a wound?
107460.e: Platelets gather at the wound and stick together. Together with the fibrin net, they form a firm plug.

107461.q: What shape does fibrin form in a wound?
107461.e: Fibrin threads join up into a dense net. Blood cells get caught in it, and a firm plug forms.
107461.m: Fibrin forms a net in which blood cells get caught.

107462.q: In which organ is fibrinogen made?
107462.e: The liver makes many plasma proteins, including fibrinogen and other clotting factors. That is why clotting can be disturbed in liver diseases.
107462.m: The liver makes many substances for blood clotting.

107463.q: What happens to the blood clot once the wound has healed?
107463.e: After healing, the body breaks down the fibrin net again. This process is called fibrinolysis.
107463.m: The body dissolves blood clots again after healing.

107465.q: What do surgeons use fibrin glue for?
a: To seal wounds and stop bleeding
107465.e: Fibrin glue copies the last step of blood clotting. It makes a firm clot form on the wound and sticks tissue together.
107465.m: Fibrin glue closes wounds like naturally clotted blood.

107466.q: Why can a small cut stop bleeding after a few minutes?
a: The blood clots and seals it
The heart stops beating for a moment
107466.e: When you are injured, the blood clots. Threads of fibrin form a net and seal the wound.

107467.q: What is the medical term for the bleeding disorder in which blood clots too slowly?
107467.e: In haemophilia, the blood clots too slowly. Even small injuries can therefore bleed for a long time.
107467.m: The medical name for this bleeding disorder is haemophilia.

107468.q: What does not work properly in haemophilia?
107468.e: In haemophilia, the blood clots too slowly. A wound therefore closes only poorly.
107468.m: In haemophilia, the blood clots poorly.

107469.q: What is missing in the blood of people with haemophilia?
107469.e: In haemophilia, a particular protein needed for blood clotting is missing. That is why bleeding is slow to stop.
107469.m: In haemophilia, a clotting substance is missing from the blood.

107470.q: Why do many more boys and men have haemophilia?
a: The gene is on the X chromosome
107470.e: Men have only one X chromosome. If the gene on it is changed, there is no second X to make up for the fault.
107470.m: Haemophilia is inherited via the X chromosome and mainly affects men.

107471.q: Why was haemophilia once called a disease of royal families?
a: It appeared in several European royal families
Only kings were allowed to treat it
You got it from wearing a crown
Only rich people could get it
107471.e: Britain's Queen Victoria carried the gene. Through her descendants, the disease reached the royal families of Spain, Russia and Prussia.
107471.m: Haemophilia spread through European royal families.

107472.q: Can you catch haemophilia from someone?
a: No, people are born with it
107472.e: Haemophilia is passed on through the genes. People have it from birth and cannot infect anyone.
107472.m: Haemophilia is present from birth and is not contagious.

107473.q: How is haemophilia mostly treated today?
a: With injections of the missing clotting factor
With lots of exercise in the sun
With a brace on the teeth
107473.e: People with haemophilia inject the missing factor into a vein regularly or when needed. This lets many of them lead an almost normal life.
107473.m: In haemophilia, the missing clotting factor is injected.

107474.q: Why must people with haemophilia be careful in sports with lots of falls?
a: Even small injuries can bleed for a long time
107474.e: Because the blood clots poorly, bruises can lead to heavy internal bleeding. Swimming or cycling with protection are often good choices.
107474.m: With haemophilia, even small injuries can bleed for a long time.

107475.q: Where does internal bleeding happen especially often in severe haemophilia?
107475.e: Bleeding into the knee, elbow and ankle joints is typical. Without treatment, the joints can be permanently damaged.
107475.m: In haemophilia, the joints often bleed.

107476.q: What does the word “leukaemia” literally mean?
107476.e: The word comes from Greek: “leukos” means white and “haima” means blood. In severe illness the blood can look paler.

107477.q: Which cells multiply out of control in leukaemia?
107477.e: In leukaemia, huge numbers of immature white blood cells are made. They cannot do their jobs and crowd out healthy blood cells.
107477.m: In leukaemia, immature white blood cells multiply out of control.

107478.q: Which type of cancer is most common in children?
107478.e: About a third of all cancers in children are leukaemias. Today most children can be cured.
107478.m: Leukaemia is the most common cancer in children.

107479.q: Why do people donate stem cells for leukaemia patients?
a: So the patients can make healthy blood again
107479.e: In some leukaemias, the diseased bone marrow is replaced. Healthy stem cells from a donor then make healthy blood cells again.
107479.m: Donated stem cells can help leukaemia patients.

107480.q: Which treatment do people with leukaemia receive most often?
107480.e: In chemotherapy, medicines destroy the cancer cells. Depending on the type, other treatments are added.
107480.m: Leukaemia is mostly treated with chemotherapy.

107481.q: Where in the body are the blood cells made that are diseased in leukaemia?
107481.e: Blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the soft inside of the bones. In leukaemia, too many immature white blood cells are made there.
107481.m: Leukaemia starts in the bone marrow.

107482.q: Why are people with leukaemia often pale and tired?
a: Because too few red blood cells are made
Because they get too much sun
Because their heart is too big
107482.e: The cancer cells crowd out the making of healthy blood cells. With too few red blood cells, less oxygen reaches the body.
107482.m: Leukaemia crowds out healthy blood cells and therefore makes people tired.

107483.q: Which leukaemia is most common in older adults in Europe?
107483.e: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, CLL for short, often develops slowly over years. It mainly occurs in people over 60.
107483.m: In older people, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is the most common.

107484.q: Which condition can a severe lack of iron cause?
107484.e: Without enough iron, the body cannot make enough haemoglobin. This leads to iron deficiency anaemia.
107484.m: A lack of iron can lead to anaemia.

107485.q: Which vitamin improves the absorption of iron from plant foods?
107485.e: Vitamin C helps the gut absorb iron from plants better. A glass of orange juice with lentils is therefore a good idea.
107485.m: Vitamin C helps the body absorb iron.

107486.q: Roughly how much iron does an adult's body contain?
107486.e: An adult has only around 3 to 5 grams of iron, about as much as in a small nail. Most of it is in haemoglobin.
107486.m: The body contains only a few grams of iron.

107487.q: Why do you often feel tired when you lack iron?
107487.e: Iron is part of the red blood pigment that carries oxygen. Without enough iron, muscles and brain get less oxygen.
107487.m: A lack of iron makes you tired because less oxygen is carried.

107488.q: Which of these plant foods contains a lot of iron?
107488.e: Pulses such as lentils are good plant sources of iron. Cucumbers and apples, on the other hand, contain little iron.
107488.m: Lentils are a good plant source of iron.

107489.q: Which animal food contains a lot of iron?
107489.e: Red meat such as beef contains a lot of iron that the body can absorb well. Butter, cream and honey contain hardly any iron.
107489.m: Red meat is a good source of iron.

107490.q: Which drink with a meal can reduce the absorption of iron?
107490.e: Tannins in black tea bind iron in the gut. So it is better not to drink it right with iron-rich meals.
107490.m: Black tea with a meal reduces iron absorption.

107491.q: What does the hormone insulin do in the blood?
107491.e: Insulin makes sure that sugar moves from the blood into the cells. This lowers the blood sugar level.

107493.q: Where does the blood get sugar from when you have not eaten for a long time?
107493.e: The liver stores sugar as a reserve. When you do not eat for a long time, it releases some into the blood so that blood sugar does not drop too low.
107493.m: The liver is the body's sugar store.

107494.q: What is the illness called in which blood sugar is permanently too high?
107494.e: In diabetes, insulin is missing or does not work well enough. So too much sugar stays in the blood.
107494.m: In diabetes mellitus, blood sugar is permanently too high.

107495.q: What helps quickly when blood sugar is too low?
a: Glucose tablets or a sugary drink
107495.e: When blood sugar is too low, the brain needs energy fast. Glucose or sugary drinks get into the blood quickly.
107495.m: Glucose helps quickly when blood sugar is too low.

107496.q: Why was the discovery of insulin in 1921 so important?
a: Since then diabetes can be treated
Since then broken bones can be healed
Since then there have been vaccines
Since then people can donate blood
107496.e: Before that, people with type 1 diabetes often died young. With insulin they can live well today.
107496.m: Thanks to insulin, diabetes can be treated.

107497.q: Where in the body is the pancreas, which makes insulin?
a: In the belly behind the stomach
In the head behind the eyes
In the neck next to the larynx
In the leg next to the knee
107497.e: The pancreas lies across the upper belly behind the stomach. It makes insulin and digestive juices.
107497.m: The pancreas lies behind the stomach.

107498.q: Which type of diabetes usually starts in childhood or the teenage years?
107498.e: In type 1 diabetes, the body's own immune system destroys the cells that make insulin. People with it need insulin for the rest of their lives.
107498.m: Type 1 diabetes often starts in children and teenagers.

107499.q: What do many people with diabetes use to check their own blood sugar?
a: A blood glucose meter or sensor
107499.e: A blood glucose meter measures the sugar in a drop of blood from the fingertip. Modern sensors on the skin measure all the time.
107499.m: People with diabetes often measure their blood sugar themselves.

107500.q: What did Karl Landsteiner observe when he mixed blood from different people?
107500.e: Landsteiner saw that some blood samples mix well and others clump together. This is how he discovered the blood groups.
107500.m: Blood that does not match clumps together.

107501.q: Which prize did Karl Landsteiner receive in 1930?
107501.e: For discovering the human blood groups, Landsteiner received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1930.
107501.m: Karl Landsteiner received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1930.

107502.q: Which international day takes place on Karl Landsteiner's birthday, 14 June?
107502.e: World Blood Donor Day honours Landsteiner, who was born on 14 June 1868. On this day, blood donors are thanked.
107502.m: World Blood Donor Day is on 14 June.

107503.q: What did Karl Landsteiner discover around the year 1900?
107503.e: Karl Landsteiner found out that people have different blood groups. He later received the Nobel Prize for this.
107503.m: Karl Landsteiner discovered the blood groups.

107504.q: Why is Landsteiner's discovery so important for blood transfusions?
a: Not all blood suits every person
107504.e: If someone receives blood of an unsuitable blood group, it can be life-threatening. Since Landsteiner, the blood group is checked before every transfusion.
107504.m: Before a blood transfusion, the blood group must match.

107505.q: Which further blood group feature did Landsteiner describe in 1940 together with Alexander Wiener?
107505.e: Together with Wiener, Landsteiner found an additional feature of red blood cells in 1940. This made transfusions even safer.
107505.m: Landsteiner also helped discover the rhesus factor.

107506.q: Which blood group exists besides A, B and AB?
107506.e: In Karl Landsteiner's system there are the blood groups A, B, AB and O. He first called group O “C”.
107506.m: The blood groups are A, B, AB and O.

107507.e: Landsteiner studied medicine in Vienna and worked as a doctor and researcher in pathology. He made his discoveries in the laboratory.
107507.m: Karl Landsteiner was a doctor and researcher.

107807.q: What are the two large branches called into which the windpipe divides at the bottom?
107807.e: The windpipe splits into a right and a left main bronchus. Each leads to one lung.
107807.m: The windpipe divides into two main bronchi.

107809.q: What supports the walls of the larger bronchi so they stay open when you breathe?
107809.e: In the walls of the larger bronchi there are rings and plates of cartilage. They stop the tubes from collapsing.
107809.m: Cartilage keeps the large bronchi open.

107810.q: What is an inflammation of the bronchi called?
107810.e: The ending “-itis” means inflammation. Bronchitis affects the lining of the bronchi and often causes a cough with mucus.
107810.m: In bronchitis, the bronchi are inflamed.

107811.q: What is the examination called in which a doctor looks into the bronchi with a thin tube with a camera?
107811.e: In a bronchoscopy, an endoscope is pushed through the nose or mouth and the windpipe into the bronchi. This lets doctors look at the airways from the inside.
107811.m: A bronchoscopy looks inside the bronchi.

107812.q: Where do the two main bronchi lead?
107812.e: The windpipe divides into a right and a left main bronchus. Each one carries air into one lung.
107812.m: Each main bronchus leads to one lung.

107813.q: What is the mucus in the bronchi for?
a: Dust and germs stick to it
107813.e: The mucus traps dust and germs. Tiny hair-like cilia then move it up to the throat.

107814.q: Why do many long-term smokers cough in the morning?
a: Smoke damages the cilia and mucus builds up
Smoke only dries out the mouth
Smoke cools the lungs too much
107814.e: Tobacco smoke paralyses and destroys the cilia. The mucus is no longer carried away and has to be coughed up.
107814.m: Tobacco smoke damages the self-cleaning of the bronchi.

107815.q: Why are the bronchi also called the bronchial tree?
107815.e: The windpipe divides into two main bronchi, and these divide again and again into smaller branches. It looks like an upside-down tree.
107815.m: The bronchi branch like a tree.

107816.q: What are the finest branches of the bronchi called, just before the air sacs begin?
107816.e: After many branchings, the bronchi become bronchioles. They carry the air all the way to the air sacs.
107816.m: The bronchioles are the finest branches of the bronchial tree.

107817.q: How do the airways change the deeper they go into the lungs?
107817.e: With each branching, the tubes become narrower. The finest bronchioles are thinner than a millimetre.
107817.m: The deeper in the lungs, the thinner the airways.

107818.q: Roughly how wide is a bronchiole?
107818.e: Bronchioles are the airways with a diameter of less than about one millimetre. So they are thinner than a pencil lead.
107818.m: Bronchioles are thinner than a millimetre.

107819.q: What can the smooth muscles in the walls of the bronchioles do?
a: Make the airways narrower or wider
107819.e: When the smooth muscles contract, the bronchioles get narrower. When they relax, air flows more easily.
107819.m: Smooth muscles control how wide the bronchioles are.

107820.q: Where do the finest airways in the lungs end?
107820.e: At the end of the finest bronchioles sit millions of tiny air sacs. There the air you breathe comes very close to the blood.
107820.m: The airways end in the air sacs.

107821.q: What happens in the air sacs of the lungs?
a: Oxygen goes into the blood, carbon dioxide comes out
107821.e: The walls of the air sacs are wafer-thin and surrounded by fine blood vessels. So oxygen can pass into the blood and carbon dioxide into the air.
107821.m: Gas exchange takes place in the air sacs.

107822.q: What is an inflammation of the bronchioles called that mainly affects babies?
107822.e: In bronchiolitis, the fine bronchioles swell and get blocked with mucus. Babies, with their very narrow airways, are especially affected.
107822.m: Bronchiolitis is an inflammation of the finest airways.

107823.q: Why do babies become especially ill when their fine airways are inflamed?
a: They only breathe through their mouth
Their airways are made of cartilage
107823.e: Even a little swelling or some mucus can block a baby's tiny airways. That is why they get short of breath more easily.

107824.q: What is the “Adam's apple” on the neck?
107824.e: The Adam's apple is the front edge of one of the cartilages of the larynx. In men it is usually easy to see.
107824.m: The Adam's apple is part of the larynx.

107825.q: Between which parts of the airways is the larynx?
a: Between the throat and the windpipe
Between the nose and the throat
Between the windpipe and the bronchi
Between the bronchi and the lungs
107825.e: The larynx joins the throat at the top and leads into the windpipe. It forms the entrance to the lower airways.
107825.m: The larynx connects the throat with the windpipe.

107826.q: What in the larynx produces our voice?
107826.e: The vocal folds are in the larynx. When air flows through, they vibrate and make sounds.
107826.m: The voice is made by the vocal folds in the larynx.

107827.q: What is a typical sign of laryngitis?
107827.e: In laryngitis, the vocal folds are also irritated and swollen. That is why the voice becomes hoarse.

107828.q: What is especially typical of croup in young children?
107828.e: In croup, the lining of the larynx below the vocal folds swells, usually because of a virus. A barking cough and noisy breathing, often at night, are typical.
107828.m: You can recognise croup by its barking cough.

107829.q: What do the vocal folds do when we speak?
a: They pull back into the ear
107829.e: When we speak, the vocal folds are brought together. The air we breathe out makes them vibrate, and this creates a sound.
107829.m: Vibrating vocal folds produce the voice.

107830.q: Why do boys' voices get deeper when their voices break?
a: The larynx and vocal folds grow
107830.e: During puberty the larynx grows and the vocal folds get longer. Longer vocal folds vibrate more slowly, so the voice sounds deeper.
107830.m: Longer vocal folds give a deeper voice.

107831.q: What can babies do thanks to their high larynx that adults cannot?
a: Drink and breathe at the same time
107831.e: In babies, the larynx sits high up. Milk can flow past the sides of the entrance to the larynx while air flows through the nose.
107831.m: Babies can drink and breathe at the same time.

107832.q: What job does the epiglottis do?
a: It closes off the windpipe when you swallow
It warms the air you breathe
107832.e: When you swallow, the epiglottis folds over the larynx. This way food goes into the oesophagus and not into the windpipe.
107832.m: The epiglottis protects the windpipe when you swallow.

107833.q: What forms the framework of the epiglottis?
107833.e: The epiglottis contains elastic cartilage. That is why it is flexible and springs back into place after swallowing.
107833.m: The epiglottis is made of flexible, elastic cartilage.

a: Behind the root of the tongue
At the end of the windpipe
107834.e: The epiglottis rises behind the root of the tongue above the entrance to the larynx. From there it can cover the larynx.
107834.m: The epiglottis sits behind the root of the tongue.

107835.q: Which reflex pushes food back out if it slips past the epiglottis into the larynx?
107835.e: If something gets into the larynx, the sensitive lining immediately triggers a cough. The strong blast of air throws the object out.
107835.m: Coughing protects the airways from foreign objects.

107836.q: Why is severe swelling of the epiglottis dangerous?
107836.e: If the epiglottis swells badly during an infection, it can block the way to the windpipe. This is an emergency.
107836.m: Inflammation of the epiglottis is a medical emergency.

107837.q: What protects children well from epiglottitis today?
107837.e: The most common cause was a bacterium that babies are now vaccinated against. Since then the disease has become rare in children.

107838.q: Why should you not laugh or talk with your mouth full?
a: The larynx is open while you do it
The oesophagus is closed while you do it
The stomach closes while you do it
The teeth get in the way
107838.e: When you speak and laugh, air flows through the open larynx. The epiglottis cannot cover it safely then, and food can easily go down the wrong way.
107838.m: The larynx stays open when you speak.

107839.q: What is the gap between the two vocal folds called?
107839.e: The vocal folds form the left and right edges of the glottis. The air you breathe flows through it.
107839.m: The glottis lies between the vocal folds.

107840.q: During which part of breathing do we normally produce our voice?
107840.e: The air flowing out makes the almost closed vocal folds vibrate. This creates the sound.

107841.q: How does the voice get higher?
a: The vocal folds are stretched more tightly
107841.e: Tight vocal folds vibrate faster. More vibrations per second give a higher note.
107841.m: The tighter the vocal folds, the higher the voice.

107842.q: Why do men usually have a deeper voice than women?
a: Their vocal folds are longer and thicker
107842.e: Longer and thicker vocal folds vibrate more slowly. That is why the voice sounds deeper, much like a thick guitar string.
107842.m: Longer vocal folds produce deeper notes.

107843.q: What is a common cause of “singer's nodules” on the vocal folds?
a: Too little sleep at the weekend
107843.e: If you often use your voice too loudly or in the wrong way, you irritate the vocal folds. Small thickenings can form there and make you hoarse.

107844.q: Where in the body are the vocal folds?
a: In the back of the nose
107844.e: The vocal folds are stretched inside the larynx between its cartilages. That is why the larynx is also called the voice box.
107844.m: The vocal folds are in the larynx.

107845.q: How many times per second do the vocal folds vibrate when someone sings a note of 220 hertz?
107845.e: One hertz means one vibration per second. At 220 hertz, the vocal folds therefore vibrate 220 times per second.
107845.m: The pitch matches the number of vibrations per second.

107846.q: How are the vocal folds positioned during quiet breathing?
107846.e: When you breathe, the glottis is wide open so that air can flow freely. Only for speaking are the vocal folds brought close together.
107846.m: When you breathe, the glottis is wide open.

107847.q: By which process does oxygen pass from the air sacs into the blood?
107847.e: Particles move by themselves from a place of high concentration to a place of low concentration. There is more oxygen in the air sacs than in the blood arriving there.
107847.m: In gas exchange, the gases move by diffusion.

107848.q: Roughly how many air sacs does an adult have?
107848.e: The number of air sacs is estimated at around 300 million or more. This creates a huge surface in a small space.
107848.m: The lungs contain hundreds of millions of air sacs.

107849.q: Roughly how large is the surface of all the air sacs together?
107849.e: Spread out, all the air sacs would cover about 100 square metres. That is roughly the floor area of a large flat.
107849.m: The gas exchange surface of the lungs is as large as a flat.

107850.q: What are the finest blood vessels called that wrap around the air sacs like a net?
107850.e: Capillaries are the thinnest blood vessels. Their walls lie close against the walls of the air sacs so that gases can pass quickly.
107850.m: Capillaries wrap around the air sacs.

107851.q: At rest, roughly how long does a red blood cell stay in contact with an air sac?
107851.e: Blood flows quickly through the capillaries of the lungs; at rest the contact time is only about three quarters of a second. It is still enough, because the gases pass across very quickly.
107851.m: Gas exchange in the lungs takes less than a second.

107852.q: Why is the wall between the air sacs and the blood extremely thin?
a: So the gases can pass through quickly
So no germs can get in
107852.e: The dividing wall is thinner than a thousandth of a millimetre. The shorter the path, the faster the gases pass through.
107852.m: A thin wall speeds up gas exchange.

107853.q: Roughly how much oxygen does the air you breathe out contain?
107853.e: The lungs take only about a quarter of the oxygen from the air. So the air you breathe out still contains about 16 per cent oxygen.
107853.m: Breathed-out air still contains about 16 per cent oxygen.

107854.q: Why is carbon monoxide so dangerous for gas exchange?
a: It takes oxygen's place on haemoglobin
It clogs the bronchi with soot
It destroys the ribs at once
It makes the air too damp
107854.e: Carbon monoxide binds much more strongly to the red blood pigment than oxygen does. The blood can then hardly carry any oxygen.
107854.m: Carbon monoxide pushes oxygen out of the blood.

107856.q: Roughly how many breaths per minute does a healthy newborn baby take at rest?
107856.e: Newborn babies breathe much faster than adults, about 40 times per minute. The breathing rate drops with age.
107856.m: Babies breathe much faster than adults.

107857.q: Where is the respiratory centre that controls breathing?
107857.e: In the brainstem, in the medulla oblongata, there are nerve cells that set the rhythm of breathing. That is why we also breathe while asleep.
107857.m: The respiratory centre is in the brainstem.

107858.q: Which change in the blood stimulates breathing the most?
107858.e: Sensors measure the amount of carbon dioxide in the blood. If it rises, we breathe faster and deeper.
107858.m: A lot of carbon dioxide in the blood drives breathing.

107859.q: An adult breathes in 15 times a minute, 0.5 litres of air each time. How much air does he breathe in per minute?
107859.e: You multiply the number of breaths by the amount of air per breath: 15 times 0.5 litres makes 7.5 litres. This is called the minute volume.
107859.m: Minute volume is breathing rate times the volume of each breath.

107860.q: You count 9 breaths from a classmate in 30 seconds. What is her breathing rate per minute?
107860.e: A minute has 60 seconds, twice as long as 30 seconds. 9 times 2 makes 18 breaths per minute.
107860.m: The breathing rate gives the number of breaths per minute.

107861.q: What happens to your breathing rate when you run fast?
107861.e: When you run, your muscles need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide. That is why you breathe faster.
107861.m: When you make an effort, you breathe faster.

a: They breathe out too much carbon dioxide
They no longer take in any oxygen
107862.e: Anyone who breathes too fast and too deeply, for example when upset, gives off too much carbon dioxide. Tingling in the hands and lips and dizziness are typical results.
107862.m: When hyperventilating, you breathe too fast and too deeply.

107863.q: Why do you breathe faster high in the mountains than in the lowlands?
107863.e: At altitude the air pressure is lower, so the air is thinner. With each breath less oxygen reaches the lungs, so you breathe faster.
107863.m: At altitude you have to breathe faster because the air is thinner.

107864.q: Which sound is typical when breathing out during an asthma attack?
107864.e: The narrowed airways only let the air out with difficulty. This creates a whistling or humming sound.
107864.m: Wheezing is a sign of asthma.

107865.q: What happens to the airways during an asthma attack?
107865.e: The muscles around the bronchi tighten, the lining swells and makes thick mucus. Air has trouble getting out.
107865.m: During an asthma attack, the bronchi become narrow.

107866.q: What can trigger an attack in allergic asthma?
107866.e: In allergic asthma, the immune system reacts to harmless substances such as pollen, house dust mites or animal hair. The airways become inflamed and narrow.
107866.m: Pollen can trigger asthma in people with allergies.

107867.q: What is a reliever inhaler for in asthma?
107867.e: The medicine relaxes the muscles around the bronchi within minutes. This lets you breathe better again quickly.
107867.m: A reliever inhaler opens the bronchi quickly.

107868.q: What does a peak flow meter measure?
a: How fast you can breathe out at most
How much sugar is in the blood
107868.e: You blow into the device as hard as you can. If the value drops, the airways are narrower than usual.
107868.m: A peak flow meter shows how clear the airways are.

107869.e: Asthma is a long-term inflammation of the airways, not an infection. You cannot catch it from someone.
107869.m: Asthma is not a contagious illness.

107870.q: What is an inhaler aid called a spacer for?
a: You no longer have to breathe in
107870.e: The spacer is a chamber between the inhaler and the mouth. The spray mist spreads out inside it and can be breathed in calmly instead of getting stuck in the mouth.
107870.m: With a spacer, the medicine gets into the lungs better.

107871.q: What is bronchial asthma, at its core?
a: A long-term inflammation of the airways
107871.e: In asthma, the airways are permanently inflamed and oversensitive. That is why they react to triggers by narrowing.
107871.m: Asthma is a lasting inflammation of the airways.

107872.q: Can a child with well-treated asthma do sport?
107872.e: With the right treatment, most children with asthma can do sport normally. For exercise-induced asthma, an inhaler before training and a good warm-up often help.

107873.q: What is the medical term for an infection of the lungs?
107873.e: “Pneumon” is Greek for lung. Pleurisy affects the lining of the chest, and a pneumothorax is air in the chest cavity.
107873.m: An infection of the lungs is called pneumonia.

107874.q: Which bacteria most often cause pneumonia outside hospital?
107874.e: Pneumococci are the most common bacterial cause of pneumonia caught outside hospital. Their name refers to the lungs.
107874.m: Pneumococci are common causes of pneumonia.

107875.q: Which sounds does a doctor often hear with a stethoscope in pneumonia?
107875.e: When the person breathes, fine crackling sounds can be heard over the inflamed part of the lung. They are called crackles.

107876.q: For whom is pneumonia especially dangerous?
107876.e: In older people and people with a weak immune system, pneumonia more often becomes serious. It can also be dangerous for very young children.
107876.m: Older people are especially at risk from pneumonia.

107877.q: Which examination is often used to confirm pneumonia?
107877.e: On an X-ray, inflamed areas of the lung show up as pale shadows. Listening to the chest and blood tests are added to this.

107878.q: Which symptoms are typical of pneumonia?
a: Fever, cough and shortness of breath
Toothache and ringing in the ears
107878.e: The inflammation in the lungs causes fever and a cough. Because fewer air sacs are working, shortness of breath often comes too.
107878.m: Fever, cough and shortness of breath point to pneumonia.

107879.q: Which vaccine protects against a common form of pneumonia?
107879.e: The pneumococcal vaccine protects against these bacteria. In Switzerland it is recommended for babies and older people.
107879.m: The pneumococcal vaccine helps prevent pneumonia.

107880.q: What collects in the affected air sacs in pneumonia?
107880.e: The inflamed air sacs fill with fluid and immune cells. Hardly any oxygen can then pass into the blood there.
107880.m: In pneumonia, air sacs are filled with fluid.

a: Breathing in other people's tobacco smoke
107881.e: Anyone who stays near people smoking breathes in their smoke too. The same harmful substances get into the lungs.
107881.m: Passive smoking means breathing in other people's tobacco smoke.

107882.q: Where in Switzerland is smoking generally banned to protect people from passive smoking?
107882.e: The federal law on protection against passive smoking has applied since 2010. Smoking is generally banned in enclosed spaces such as restaurants, schools and shops.
107882.m: Smoking is banned in enclosed public spaces.

107883.q: What is the smoke called that rises from the burning cigarette between puffs?
107883.e: Mainstream smoke is drawn in by the person smoking. Sidestream smoke rises freely into the room and is breathed in by everyone there.
107883.m: Sidestream smoke goes straight into the air of the room.

107884.q: Why is sidestream smoke considered especially harmful?
a: Many harmful substances in it are more concentrated
It is hotter than a fire
107884.e: Because the cigarette smoulders at a lower temperature between puffs, the tobacco burns less completely. So many toxins are more concentrated in sidestream smoke.
107884.m: Sidestream smoke is often more toxic than the smoke drawn in.

107885.q: Which airway disease is more common in children who often breathe in second-hand smoke?
107885.e: Tobacco smoke irritates children's sensitive airways. That is why they get asthma and bronchitis more often.
107885.m: Second-hand smoke increases the risk of asthma in children.

107886.q: Why is smoking in a car especially harmful for passengers?
a: The smoke builds up in the small space
The engine draws in the smoke
107886.e: In the cramped interior, harmful substances quickly reach very high concentrations. Even an open window makes little difference.
107886.m: In a car, smoke becomes especially concentrated.

107887.q: In Switzerland, what is a separate, ventilated smoking room in a restaurant called?
107887.e: Federal law generally bans smoking in the enclosed rooms of restaurants. Separate, well-ventilated smoking rooms called fumoirs are allowed.
107887.m: A fumoir is a separate smoking room.

107888.q: Does a window left slightly open protect children in a flat from tobacco smoke?
a: Yes, if it is cold outside
107888.e: Smoke spreads quickly into all rooms, and harmful substances settle in furniture and curtains. Only a smoke-free home gives real protection.
107888.m: Only a smoke-free home really protects children.

107889.q: What is meant by vital capacity?
a: The largest amount of air you can breathe out after breathing in deeply
The amount of air you breathe in and out in one quiet breath
The amount of air that always stays in the lungs after breathing out
The amount of air you breathe in during a whole day
107889.e: You breathe in as deeply as possible and then breathe out as completely as possible. The amount breathed out is the vital capacity.
107889.m: Vital capacity is the largest amount of air you can breathe in and out again.

107890.q: Which device is used at the doctor's to measure vital capacity?
107890.e: With a spirometer you blow into a mouthpiece. The device measures how much air flows and how fast.
107890.m: A spirometer measures the amounts of air in the lungs.

107891.q: Roughly how large is the vital capacity of a healthy adult?
107891.e: In adults, the vital capacity is usually between about 3 and 5 litres. It depends on things such as height, age and training.
107891.m: Adults have a vital capacity of a few litres.

107892.q: Are the lungs completely empty after breathing out as hard as you can?
a: No, about 1 to 1.5 litres of air stay in them
Yes, they are then completely empty
No, they are then still half full of water
107892.e: Even when you breathe out as far as possible, some air stays in the lungs. It stops the air sacs from collapsing.
107892.m: Some air always remains in the lungs.

107893.q: Tidal volume 0.5 litres, inspiratory reserve 3 litres, expiratory reserve 1 litre: what is the vital capacity?
107893.e: The vital capacity is the sum of the tidal volume and both reserve volumes. 0.5 plus 3 plus 1 makes 4.5 litres.
107893.m: Vital capacity is made up of the tidal volume and the two reserve volumes.

107894.q: A person has a vital capacity of 4.5 litres and a residual volume of 1.5 litres. How much air do their lungs hold in total?
107894.e: Total lung capacity is the vital capacity plus the residual air. 4.5 plus 1.5 makes 6 litres.
107894.m: Add the residual air to the vital capacity to get the total lung capacity.

107895.q: What does vital capacity depend on, among other things?
a: Whether you are left- or right-handed
107895.e: Taller people usually have a larger ribcage and larger lungs. Age, sex and training also play a part.
107895.m: Tall people usually have a larger vital capacity.

107896.q: How does vital capacity usually change in old age?
107896.e: With age, the lungs and ribcage become less elastic. That is why you can move less air.
107896.m: Vital capacity falls in old age.

107897.q: How can you easily estimate your own vital capacity at school?
a: Breathe out into an upside-down bottle filled with water
Count your pulse for one minute
Hold your breath and count the seconds
Measure your chest with a tape measure
107897.e: You breathe in deeply and blow through a tube into an upside-down bottle filled with water. The amount of water pushed out equals the air breathed out.
107897.m: Vital capacity can be measured by water displacement.

107898.q: Where in the body is the carbon dioxide made that we breathe out?
107898.e: In cellular respiration, nutrients are broken down using oxygen. This produces carbon dioxide, which travels in the blood to the lungs.
107898.m: Carbon dioxide is made in all cells during cellular respiration.

107899.q: How does carbon dioxide get from the cells to the lungs?
107899.e: Carbon dioxide from the cells is taken up by the blood and carried to the lungs. There we breathe it out.
107899.m: The blood carries carbon dioxide to the lungs.

107900.q: How can you detect carbon dioxide in a school experiment?
a: A glowing splint bursts into flame
107900.e: If you bubble carbon dioxide through limewater, insoluble chalk forms and the water turns milky. A glowing splint that relights, on the other hand, shows oxygen.

107901.q: What does a CO2 traffic light in a classroom show?
a: When the room should be aired
107901.e: As people breathe out, the carbon dioxide level in the room rises. If the light shows yellow or red, you should open the windows, because otherwise tiredness and concentration problems increase.
107901.m: A CO2 traffic light reminds you to air the room.

107902.q: Is carbon dioxide heavier or lighter than air?
107902.e: Carbon dioxide is heavier than air and collects near the floor, for example in fermentation cellars. There it can put people in danger.
107902.m: Carbon dioxide collects near the floor because it is heavier than air.

107903.q: How much of the outdoor air is carbon dioxide?
107903.e: Air is made up mainly of nitrogen and oxygen. Carbon dioxide makes up only about 0.04 per cent.
107903.m: Air contains only very little carbon dioxide.

107904.q: What do green plants do with the carbon dioxide we breathe out?
a: They use it to build sugar
107904.e: In photosynthesis, plants use light, water and carbon dioxide. From these, sugar and oxygen are made.
107904.m: Plants use carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.

108195.q: Which part of the intestine comes directly after the stomach?
108195.e: After the stomach exit, the small intestine begins with the duodenum. There the food mash is mixed with digestive juices.
108195.m: The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine.

108196.q: Where does the duodenum get its name from?
a: It is about twelve finger-widths long
It is about twelve metres long
108196.e: The duodenum is about 25 to 30 centimetres long. That is roughly the width of twelve fingers laid side by side, and its Latin name refers to twelve.
108196.m: The duodenum is about as long as twelve fingers are wide.

108197.q: Which two digestive juices flow into the duodenum?
108197.e: The bile duct and the duct of the pancreas open into the duodenum at a small bump. Their juices help break down fats, proteins and carbohydrates.
108197.m: The bile duct and the pancreatic duct open into the duodenum.

108198.q: What does pancreatic juice do to the acidic food mash in the duodenum?
a: It makes it even more acidic
108198.e: Pancreatic juice contains bicarbonate, which buffers the acid. Only then can the digestive enzymes in the small intestine work properly.
108198.m: Pancreatic juice makes the acidic food mash less acidic.

a: Just after the stomach, at the start of the small intestine
At the end of the large intestine
In the chest next to the heart
In the neck below the larynx
108199.e: The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine. It joins directly onto the stomach exit.
108199.m: The duodenum is the start of the small intestine.

108200.q: Which ring muscle controls when food mash passes from the stomach into the duodenum?
108200.e: The pylorus at the stomach exit keeps opening briefly. This lets the food mash pass into the duodenum in portions.
108200.m: The pylorus lets the food mash into the intestine in portions.

108201.q: What is a common cause of ulcers in the duodenum?
108201.e: A particular bacterium can survive in the lining of the stomach and duodenum and damage it. Then a sore spot forms: an ulcer.
108201.m: Many ulcers in the duodenum are caused by bacteria.

108202.q: Which part of the small intestine follows the duodenum?
108202.e: The small intestine is made up of the duodenum, jejunum and ileum. The jejunum, meaning “empty”, got its name because it was often found empty in people who had died.
108202.m: After the duodenum comes the jejunum.

108203.q: What gives the wall of the duodenum extra protection against acid from the stomach?
108203.e: In the wall of the duodenum there are special glands, Brunner's glands. They make an alkaline mucus that protects the lining from the acid.
108203.m: Alkaline mucus protects the wall of the duodenum.

108204.q: What does the wall of the large intestine look like?
a: It is smooth like a garden hose
It has rings of cartilage like the windpipe
108204.e: The wall of the large intestine is pinched in again and again. In between are pouch-like bulges called haustra.
108204.m: The large intestine has a wall with many bulges.

108205.q: Roughly how long is an adult's large intestine?
108205.e: In adults, the large intestine measures about 1.5 metres. That makes it much shorter but wider than the small intestine.
108205.m: The large intestine is about one and a half metres long.

108206.q: What is the pouch-shaped first part of the large intestine at the lower right of the belly called?
108206.e: The caecum is a pouch-shaped start of the large intestine at the lower right of the belly. This is where the small intestine joins the large intestine.
108206.m: The large intestine begins with the caecum.

108207.q: What is usually actually inflamed in “appendicitis”?
108207.e: In appendicitis, it is almost always the appendix, a small worm-shaped tube on the caecum, that is inflamed. It is then often removed in an operation.
108207.m: In appendicitis, the appendix is inflamed.

108208.q: How does the large intestine run through the belly?
a: Up on the right, across, and down on the left
In many tight loops in the middle
108208.e: The large intestine starts at the lower right, goes up, runs across below the stomach and goes down again on the left. In this way it frames the small intestine.
108208.m: The large intestine runs like a frame around the small intestine.

108209.q: What is the examination called in which a doctor looks at the large intestine with a small camera?
108209.e: In a colonoscopy, a flexible tube with a camera is inserted through the anus. This makes it possible to spot inflammation or growths.
108209.m: A colonoscopy lets you see inside the large intestine.

108210.q: Why is it important that the contents of the large intestine do not flow back into the small intestine?
a: Huge numbers of bacteria live in the large intestine
The large intestine is much hotter
There is stomach acid in the large intestine
The small intestine is already full of air
108210.e: Enormous numbers of bacteria live in the large intestine. A valve at the junction stops them getting back into the small intestine.
108210.m: A valve separates the bacteria-rich large intestine from the small intestine.

108211.q: Besides water, what does the large intestine mainly absorb from its contents?
108211.e: The large intestine mainly absorbs water and mineral salts such as sodium. Most nutrients have already been absorbed in the small intestine.
108211.m: The large intestine takes back water and salts.

108212.q: Roughly where in the belly is the large intestine?
a: It is next to the lungs
108212.e: The large intestine runs like a frame around the loops of the small intestine. It starts at the lower right and ends in the middle of the pelvis.
108212.m: The large intestine lies like a picture frame around the small intestine.

108213.q: Which part of the intestine is the last before the anus?
108213.e: The rectum is the end part of the large intestine. It leads through the anal canal to the anus.
108213.m: The rectum is the last part of the intestine.

108214.q: What job does the rectum do?
a: Store poo until it is passed
108214.e: Poo collects in the rectum until you go to the toilet. It is a stretchy store.
108214.m: The rectum stores poo until you go to the toilet.

108215.q: What is the medical term for the last part of the large intestine, just before the anus?
108215.e: In medicine, this last part is called the rectum. The word comes from the Latin “rectus”, meaning straight.
108215.m: The last part of the large intestine is called the rectum.

108216.q: What triggers the urge to go to the toilet for a poo?
108216.e: When poo collects in the rectum, its wall is stretched. Sensory cells report this to the brain and you feel the urge to go.
108216.m: A full rectum signals the urge to go to the brain.

108217.q: Which sphincter muscle at the anus can be controlled at will?
108217.e: The internal sphincter works automatically. You can tighten the external sphincter on purpose, so you can put off going to the toilet for a while.
108217.m: You can control the external anal sphincter on purpose.

108218.q: Roughly how long is an adult's rectum?
108218.e: The rectum is about 12 to 18 centimetres long. So it is only a short part of the large intestine.
108218.m: The rectum is only about a hand span long.

108219.q: Where in the body is the rectum?
108219.e: The rectum lies in the lower pelvis in front of the sacrum. From there it leads to the anus.
108219.m: The rectum lies low down in the pelvis.

108220.q: Which part of the intestine does the rectum belong to?
108220.e: The rectum is the last piece of the large intestine. In the large intestine, water is taken out of the food mash before the poo collects in the rectum.
108220.m: The rectum is the end part of the large intestine.

a: On the underside of the liver
108221.e: The gall bladder lies in the upper right of the belly on the underside of the liver. It is connected to the liver and intestine by ducts.
108221.m: The gall bladder sits under the liver.

108222.q: What is the job of the gall bladder?
108222.e: The gall bladder collects bile between meals and takes water out of it. This concentrates the bile.
108222.m: The gall bladder is a store for bile.

108223.q: What shape is the gall bladder?
108223.e: The gall bladder is a small, pear-shaped hollow sac. It is about 8 to 10 centimetres long.
108223.m: The gall bladder looks like a small pear.

108224.q: What are the hard deposits called that can form in the gall bladder?
108224.e: Gallstones form when substances in the bile clump together and harden. They can cause severe pain in the upper belly.
108224.m: Gallstones form from substances in the bile.

108225.q: When does the gall bladder contract especially strongly?
108225.e: As soon as fatty food mash reaches the intestine, the gall bladder contracts. Then a lot of bile is released to digest the fat.
108225.m: Fatty food makes the gall bladder empty itself.

108226.q: Can a person live without a gall bladder?
108226.e: With gallstones, the gall bladder is often removed. The liver then releases bile directly and continuously into the intestine.
108226.m: You can live well without a gall bladder.

108227.q: Roughly how much bile can an adult's gall bladder store?
108227.e: The gall bladder is small and holds only about 30 to 50 millilitres. Because it takes water out of the bile, a lot of bile still fits inside.
108227.m: The gall bladder holds only a few tablespoons of bile.

108228.q: What happens to the bile from the gall bladder after a meal?
a: It flows into the small intestine
108228.e: After a meal, the gall bladder contracts. The bile flows into the small intestine and helps digest fat there.
108228.m: Bile helps digest fat in the small intestine.

108229.q: Which component of bile can form gallstones if there is too much of it?
108229.e: Bile contains cholesterol, which is kept dissolved by the bile acids. If there is too much of it, it can crystallise and form stones.
108229.m: Too much cholesterol in the bile can lead to gallstones.

108230.q: How does bile help with digestion?
108230.e: Bile acids break large drops of fat into many small droplets. This lets fat-splitting enzymes work better.
108230.m: Bile makes fat easier to digest.

108231.q: What colour is fresh bile from the liver?
108231.e: Fresh bile is yellow to greenish. The colour comes from bile pigments.

108232.q: What does the body break down when bile pigment is made?
108232.e: Red blood cells live for about four months. When their red pigment is broken down, yellow bile pigment is formed.
108232.m: Bile pigment is made from old red blood cells.

108233.e: Gut bacteria turn the pigments from the bile into brown substances. If bile is missing from the gut, the poo becomes pale.
108233.m: Bile pigments give poo its brown colour.

108234.q: What happens to most of the bile acids after fat has been digested?
a: They go back to the liver
They are stored in the bones
108234.e: Bile acids are absorbed again at the end of the small intestine and carried in the blood to the liver. This cycle is called the enterohepatic circulation.
108234.m: Bile acids are used again and again.

108235.q: What is often the cause when the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow (jaundice)?
a: Bile pigment builds up in the body
Too much sugar in the blood
108235.e: If the liver is ill or the bile cannot drain away, bile pigment collects in the blood. It settles in the skin and eyes and turns them yellow.
108235.m: In jaundice, bile pigment builds up in the body.

108236.q: Roughly how much bile does an adult's liver make each day?
108236.e: The liver makes about half a litre to a litre of bile every day. Some of it is stored for a while in the gall bladder.
108236.m: The liver produces about a litre of bile every day.

108237.q: In which organ are the villi found?
108237.e: The lining of the small intestine is covered with millions of villi. There are no villi in the large intestine.
108237.m: Villi are found only in the small intestine.

108238.q: What are the villi in the intestine for?
108238.e: The villi greatly increase the inner surface of the small intestine. This lets far more nutrients be absorbed into the blood.
108238.m: Villi create a huge surface for absorbing nutrients.

108239.e: Villi are small, finger-shaped bumps on the lining. They stand close together like a velvet carpet.

108240.q: What would happen if the small intestine were completely smooth inside, with no villi?
a: It could absorb far fewer nutrients
You would never be hungry again
108240.e: The villi increase the surface of the small intestine enormously. Without them there would be much less surface through which nutrients pass into the blood.
108240.m: Without villi, the body would absorb far fewer nutrients.

108241.q: Where do sugar and amino acids go after the villi have absorbed them?
108241.e: In every villus there are fine blood vessels. They carry sugar and amino acids through the portal vein to the liver.
108241.m: Nutrients from the villi are carried on in the blood.

108242.e: Fine blood vessels and a lymph vessel run through each villus. They carry away the absorbed nutrients.
108242.m: There are fine blood vessels inside the villi.

108243.q: In which disease are the villi damaged by gluten?
108243.e: In coeliac disease, the immune system reacts to gluten from wheat, rye and barley. The villi shrink, and nutrients are absorbed less well.
108243.m: In coeliac disease, gluten harms the villi.

108244.q: Roughly how tall is a single villus?
108244.e: Villi are about 0.5 to 1.5 millimetres tall. With the naked eye you can just about see them as a velvety surface.
108244.m: A villus is only about a millimetre tall.

108245.q: In which part of the intestine do most gut bacteria live?
108245.e: In the large intestine, bacteria find plenty of time and food. That is why by far the most gut bacteria live there.
108245.m: Most gut bacteria live in the large intestine.

108246.q: Which vitamin is made by gut bacteria?
108246.e: Gut bacteria make vitamin K and some B vitamins. The body needs vitamin K for blood clotting.

108247.q: What can gut bacteria break down that our body cannot digest itself?
108247.e: Fibre from plants reaches the large intestine undigested. There bacteria ferment it and make useful substances.
108247.m: Gut bacteria make use of fibre.

108248.q: Which medicines can upset the gut flora and cause diarrhoea?
108248.e: Antibiotics kill not only germs that cause disease but also useful gut bacteria. This can upset the balance of the gut flora.
108248.m: Antibiotics can also hit the good gut bacteria.

108249.q: Roughly how many bacteria live in a person's body compared with their body cells?
108249.e: An estimate from 2016 comes to around 38 trillion bacteria and around 30 trillion human cells. Most of the bacteria live in the gut.
108249.m: About as many bacteria live in the body as it has cells.

108250.q: What are products or foods with live, useful bacteria called?
108250.e: Probiotics contain live microorganisms, for example lactic acid bacteria. They are found in some yoghurts, for instance.

108251.q: How does healthy gut flora protect against germs that cause disease?
a: It leaves them hardly any space or food
108251.e: The many useful bacteria occupy the gut wall and use up the nutrients. So harmful germs find it harder to settle.
108251.m: Good gut bacteria crowd out harmful germs.

108252.q: Which bacterium normally lives harmlessly in every person's gut?
108252.e: Escherichia coli, E. coli for short, is part of the normal gut flora. Only some strains can make you ill.
108252.m: Escherichia coli is a typical resident of the gut.

108253.q: What does it mean to be constipated?
a: Poo comes rarely and is hard
You get tummy ache when eating
You have hiccups all the time
108253.e: When you are constipated, you go to the toilet rarely and the poo is often hard and difficult to pass. This can cause tummy ache and a feeling of fullness.
108253.m: When you are constipated, going to the toilet is rare and difficult.

108254.q: What is most likely to help against constipation?
108254.e: Fibre binds water and makes poo softer and bulkier. Enough fluid supports this effect.
108254.m: Fibre and water help prevent constipation.

108255.q: Which food helps many people with constipation?
108255.e: Prunes contain a lot of fibre and substances that stimulate the gut. White rice, chocolate and rusks tend to make constipation worse.

108256.q: What are medicines called that help you pass poo?
108256.e: Laxatives make poo softer or stimulate the gut. They should only be taken for a short time and on medical advice.
108256.m: Laxatives help with constipation but are not for everyday use.

108257.q: How does exercise help against constipation?
a: It slows the flow of bile
108257.e: Physical activity such as running or cycling gets the gut moving too. People who sit a lot are more likely to get constipated.
108257.m: Exercise gets the gut moving too.

108258.q: From when do people usually speak of constipation in adults?
a: Going for a poo less than 3 times a week
Going for a poo once a day
Going for a poo twice a day
Going for a poo every morning
108258.e: Anything from about three times a day to three times a week is healthy. Less often than three times a week usually counts as constipation.
108258.m: Going for a poo less than three times a week counts as constipation.

108259.q: Why can it lead to constipation if you often hold in the urge to poo?
a: The urge gets weaker over time
108259.e: If you often hold in the urge, the gut gets used to it. The signal gets weaker and the poo stays in the gut for longer.
108259.m: You should go to the toilet soon after you feel the urge.

108260.q: Which foods contain a lot of fibre?
108260.e: Fibre is found in wholegrain products, vegetables, pulses and fruit. Animal foods contain almost none.
108260.m: Wholegrains, vegetables and fruit provide lots of fibre.

108261.q: What is the biggest danger with severe diarrhoea, especially for young children?
108261.e: With diarrhoea, the body loses a lot of water and salts. Young children can become dehydrated quickly.
108261.m: With diarrhoea, the body risks drying out.

108262.q: What should you do above all when you have diarrhoea?
a: Drink plenty, with a little salt and sugar
Drink nothing at all if possible
108262.e: It is important to replace water and salts. Special rehydration drinks from the chemist contain salts and sugar in the right proportions.
108262.m: With diarrhoea, you must replace lost fluid.

108263.q: Which virus often causes contagious vomiting and diarrhoea, especially in winter?
108263.e: Noroviruses are very contagious and suddenly cause vomiting and diarrhoea. Outbreaks often happen in schools, hospitals and on ships.
108263.m: Noroviruses cause contagious vomiting and diarrhoea.

108264.q: Why should you wash your hands especially thoroughly when you have diarrhoea?
a: So you do not pass the germs on
108264.e: Many germs that cause diarrhoea are very contagious and get onto door handles and food via the hands. Washing your hands with soap breaks this path.
108264.m: Hand washing protects others from diarrhoea germs.

108265.q: What is the best way to protect yourself from contagious diarrhoea germs?
108265.e: Many diarrhoea germs are passed on by dirty hands. Washing your hands with soap after the toilet and before eating protects you well.
108265.m: Washing your hands with soap protects against diarrhoea germs.

108266.q: What is the diarrhoea called that people often get in faraway countries from contaminated food or water?
108266.e: Traveller's diarrhoea is the most common illness on trips to hot countries. It is usually caused by bacteria in water or food.
108266.m: Traveller's diarrhoea often comes from contaminated water or food.

108267.q: According to the World Health Organization, from when is it called diarrhoea?
a: Runny poo at least 3 times a day
108267.e: The WHO defines diarrhoea as three or more watery stools a day. So both how often and how runny it is matter.
108267.m: Runny poo three times a day counts as diarrhoea.

108268.q: Which rule of thumb applies to eating in countries with unsafe drinking water?
a: “Boil it, peel it or forget it”
108268.e: Boiling kills germs, and peeling removes the dirty skin. Raw, unpeeled food and ice cubes are risky.
108268.m: When travelling, it is better to skip anything you cannot cook or peel.

a: Stomach acid flows into the oesophagus
Too little saliva in the mouth
108269.e: In heartburn, acidic stomach contents flow back into the oesophagus. Its lining is not protected against acid and burns.
108269.m: Heartburn is caused by stomach acid in the oesophagus.

108270.q: Where do you typically feel heartburn?
108270.e: The burning rises behind the breastbone, sometimes up into the throat. That is where the oesophagus runs.

108271.q: Which muscle normally stops stomach contents from flowing back into the oesophagus?
108271.e: Where the oesophagus joins the stomach there is a sphincter muscle. If it does not close properly, acid can rise up.
108271.m: A sphincter muscle separates the oesophagus and the stomach.

a: Lying down after a big meal
Going for a walk after eating
108272.e: If you lie down with a full stomach, you make it easier for the acid to rise. Big meals also increase the pressure in the stomach.
108272.m: After a big meal, you should not lie down straight away.

108273.q: How do antacids work against heartburn?
108273.e: Antacids contain alkaline substances. These neutralise some of the stomach acid.
108273.m: Antacids make stomach acid less harmful.

108274.q: What is the medical name for stomach contents flowing back into the oesophagus?
108274.e: Reflux comes from the Latin word for flowing back. If it happens often, it is called reflux disease.
108274.m: Stomach contents flowing back is called reflux.

108275.e: Fatty food stays in the stomach for a long time and can loosen the sphincter to the oesophagus. Spicy food, coffee and chocolate can also cause problems.
108275.m: Very fatty food can trigger heartburn.

108276.q: Why does raising the upper body in bed help against heartburn at night?
a: The stomach then makes no acid
108276.e: If the upper body is higher, the acid has to rise against gravity. It manages this much less well.
108276.m: A raised upper body makes it harder for acid to rise.

108277.q: Which acid is in stomach acid?
108277.e: The stomach lining makes hydrochloric acid. It makes the gastric juice strongly acidic.

108278.q: Roughly what pH does the gastric juice in an empty stomach have?
108278.e: With a pH of about 1 to 2, the empty stomach is very acidic. A pH of 7 would be neutral.

108279.q: Which cells in the stomach lining make the acid?
108279.e: The parietal cells sit in the glands of the stomach lining. They release the acid into the inside of the stomach.

108280.q: What protective job does stomach acid do?
108280.e: Many bacteria and other germs do not survive the strong acid. In this way the stomach protects against germs in food.
108280.m: Stomach acid kills many germs in food.

108281.q: Why does stomach acid not digest the stomach wall itself?
a: A layer of mucus protects it
The stomach is made of bone
The stomach wall is made of fat
108281.e: The stomach lining makes a thick layer of mucus. It keeps the acid away from the cells.
108281.m: Mucus protects the stomach wall from its own acid.

108282.q: Which protein-splitting enzyme is activated by stomach acid?
108282.e: The stomach releases an inactive form called pepsinogen. The acid turns it into the active enzyme pepsin.
108282.m: Stomach acid activates the enzyme pepsin.

108283.q: Roughly how much gastric juice does an adult make each day?
108283.e: The stomach lining makes about 2 to 3 litres of gastric juice every day. It contains acid, mucus and enzymes.
108283.m: The stomach makes several litres of gastric juice every day.

108284.q: What does stomach acid do to the proteins in food?
108284.e: The acid destroys the shape of the proteins; they are denatured. Unfolded proteins are easier for enzymes to break down.
108284.m: Stomach acid unfolds proteins for digestion.

108285.q: What can make the stomach produce gastric juice even before you eat?
a: The smell or sight of food
108285.e: Just smelling, seeing or thinking about food stimulates gastric juice through the nerves. The stomach gets ready for the meal in this way.
108285.m: Even the smell of food gets the stomach going.

a: Wave-like muscle movements in the digestive tract
108286.e: In peristalsis, the muscles of the digestive tract contract in waves. This pushes the contents along bit by bit.
108286.m: Peristalsis pushes food through the body in waves.

108287.q: Why can you swallow even when doing a handstand?
a: The stomach sucks the food in
The tongue pushes it all the way to the stomach
108287.e: The muscles of the oesophagus contract in waves. This movement works even against gravity.
108287.m: Thanks to muscle waves, swallowing works even upside down.

108288.q: Which two muscle layers work together in peristalsis?
108288.e: Circular muscles squeeze the gut, longitudinal muscles shorten it. Together they create a continuous wave.
108288.m: Circular and longitudinal muscles create peristalsis.

108289.q: What is the gut's own network of nerves sometimes called?
108289.e: There are many millions of nerve cells in the gut wall. They control the gut's movements on their own and are therefore also called the belly brain or second brain.
108289.m: The gut has its own nervous system.

108290.q: Where do the rumbling and gurgling noises in your tummy come from?
a: Gut movements push gas and liquid along
The ribs rub against each other
The heart beats against the stomach
108290.e: The muscles of the stomach and gut move gas and liquid along. This creates noises, especially when the stomach is nearly empty.
108290.m: Tummy rumbling comes from the movement of the stomach and gut.

108291.q: What is a dangerous condition called in which the contents of the gut can no longer move on?
108291.e: In a bowel obstruction, the gut is blocked or paralysed. It is an emergency that must be treated quickly in hospital.
108291.m: A bowel obstruction is a medical emergency.

108292.q: What happens to the stomach contents when you are sick?
a: They flow into the large intestine
108292.e: When you vomit, the stomach muscles and the diaphragm contract strongly. The stomach contents are pushed upwards, against the normal direction.
108292.m: When you vomit, transport runs in the wrong direction.

108293.q: Roughly how long does a mouthful take to travel down the oesophagus to the stomach?
108293.e: The oesophagus is about 25 centimetres long. The muscle wave carries a mouthful into the stomach in a few seconds.
108293.m: A mouthful reaches the stomach after a few seconds.

108294.q: Which type of muscle moves the gut without us deciding to?
108294.e: The gut wall is made of smooth muscle. It works by itself, without us controlling it consciously.
108294.m: Smooth muscles move the gut without our help.

108591.q: Which organ is the body's most important detox centre?
108591.e: The liver breaks down many toxins, medicines and alcohol or makes them harmless. Afterwards they can be got rid of via the kidneys or the bile.
108591.m: The liver is the body's great detox centre.

108592.q: Into which substance does the liver turn the toxic ammonia from breaking down protein?
108592.e: Breaking down protein produces toxic ammonia. The liver turns it into harmless urea, which the kidneys remove in urine.
108592.m: The liver turns toxic ammonia into harmless urea.

108593.q: To which organ does blood from the gut flow first, so that absorbed substances can be checked?
108593.e: The nutrient-rich blood from the stomach and gut flows first to the liver. It processes the substances and makes toxic ones harmless.
108593.m: Blood from the gut flows to the liver first.
