109480.m: Raw meat belongs in the coldest part of the fridge.

109481.q: How does nicotine affect the blood vessels?
109481.e: Nicotine makes the blood vessels narrower, so pulse and blood pressure rise. That is why smokers' hands and feet are often cooler.

a: It makes germs that cause disease harmless
109482.e: To disinfect means to reduce germs so much that they can no longer infect anyone. This needs substances such as alcohol that kill germs.
109482.m: Disinfection makes germs that cause disease harmless.

109782.q: What is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye called?
109782.e: The retina lines the back of the inside of the eye. It contains the sensory cells that react to light.
109782.m: The retina is the light-sensitive layer in the eye.

109783.q: How does the image on the retina compare with the object being looked at?
109783.e: The cornea and lens work together like a converging lens in a camera and make an upside-down, smaller image. The brain processes it so that we see the world the right way up.
109783.m: The image on the retina is upside down.

109784.q: What do the sensory cells of the retina do with the light that falls on them?
a: They turn it into electrical signals
They reflect it back to the front
They focus it into a beam
109784.e: The light-sensitive cells react to light and produce nerve signals. These are passed on to the brain.
109784.m: The retina translates light into nerve signals.

109785.q: What is the spot on the retina called where we see most sharply?
109785.e: The yellow spot (macula) lies in the middle of the retina, exactly where the image falls when you look straight at something.
109785.m: We see most sharply at the yellow spot.

109786.q: Which instrument can an eye doctor use to look directly at the retina?
109786.e: With an ophthalmoscope, light is shone through the pupil into the eye, and the back of the eye with its blood vessels can be seen.
109786.m: The back of the eye is examined with an ophthalmoscope.

a: The retina comes away from the wall of the eye
109787.e: In a detached retina, the retina separates from the layer underneath. Warning signs are flashes of light or a shadow in your field of vision; it is an emergency.
109787.m: A detached retina must be treated quickly.

109788.q: From which organ does the retina develop in an unborn baby?
109788.e: In the embryo, the retina grows out as a pouch of the diencephalon, part of the brain. That is why it is considered an outpost of the brain.
109788.m: The retina is an outpost of the brain.

109789.q: Why do eyes sometimes look red in flash photos?
a: The flash reflects off the back of the eye, which has a rich blood supply
The lens colours the light red
The tears glow in the flash
109789.e: In the dark the pupil is wide. The flash falls on the back of the eye, which is full of blood vessels, and is reflected back red.
109789.m: The red-eye effect shows the blood-filled back of the eye.

109790.q: What is the medical term for the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye?
109790.e: The Latin medical term for this layer is retina. That is why eye doctors speak of retinal diseases, for example.
109790.m: The light-sensitive layer of the eye is called the retina.

109791.q: Where is the lens of the eye?
a: Right at the back by the retina
109791.e: The lens lies behind the iris and the pupil. Light falls through the pupil onto the lens.
109791.m: The lens lies directly behind the pupil.

109792.q: What is the eye's ability to focus on near and far objects called?
109792.e: In accommodation, the lens changes how curved it is and so how strongly it bends light. This lets both near and far images form sharply on the retina.
109792.m: Accommodation is the focusing of the eye.

109793.q: Which muscle changes the shape of the lens?
109793.e: The ring-shaped ciliary muscle is connected to the lens by fine fibres. When it tightens, the lens can curve more.
109793.m: The ciliary muscle controls the shape of the lens.

109794.q: How does the lens change when we look at something close up?
109794.e: For close vision, the suspending fibres relax. The elastic lens then curves more and bends the light more.
109794.m: For near things, the lens curves more.

109795.q: What is the condition called in which the lens of the eye becomes cloudy?
109795.e: In a cataract, the lens turns milky. You then see as if through a fog; it mostly affects older people.
109795.m: In a cataract, the lens of the eye becomes cloudy.

109796.q: What is usually done in the common operation on a cloudy lens?
a: It is replaced with an artificial lens
It is replaced with glass from the vitreous body
It is simply removed without a replacement
109796.e: The cloudy lens is removed and replaced with an artificial lens (intraocular lens). This operation is one of the most common of all.
109796.m: A cloudy lens can be replaced with an artificial lens.

109797.q: Why do many people need reading glasses from about the age of 45?
109797.e: With age, the lens loses its elasticity and can no longer curve enough for close vision. This is called age-related long-sightedness.
109797.m: With age the lens gets stiffer, so you need reading glasses.

109798.q: In physics, what kind of lens is the lens of the eye?
109798.e: The lens of the eye curves outwards on both sides. Such lenses bring light together and are called converging lenses.
109798.m: The lens of the eye is a converging lens.

109799.q: What is the lens of the eye suspended from?
109799.e: The lens hangs all round from many fine zonular fibres. These pass the pull of the ring muscle onto the lens.
109799.m: Fine zonular fibres hold the lens in place.

109800.q: Which part of the eye is the clear, curved front?
109800.e: The cornea is right at the front, like a watch glass over the iris and pupil. Light enters the eye through it.
109800.m: The cornea is the clear window of the eye.

109801.q: Which part of the eye bends incoming light the most?
109801.e: About two thirds of the eye's total focusing power comes from the cornea. The adjustable lens, which is used for focusing, provides the rest.
109801.m: The cornea bends light the most in the eye.

109802.q: How does the cornea get nutrients even though it has no blood vessels?
a: From tear fluid and aqueous humour
109802.e: To stay clear, the cornea has no blood vessels. It gets oxygen and nutrients from the tear film and the aqueous humour.
109802.m: The cornea is fed by tears and aqueous humour.

109803.q: What happens when something touches the cornea?
a: The eye sees double for a moment
109803.e: The cornea has a great many nerve endings and is very sensitive. When touched, it triggers the blink reflex, which protects the eye.
109803.m: The sensitive cornea triggers the blink reflex.

109804.q: What is the tough white outer layer of the eye called, which the cornea joins at its edge?
109804.e: The sclera is the “white” of the eye. It wraps around the eyeball and at the front joins the clear cornea.
109804.m: The white of the eye is called the sclera.

109805.q: What does a laser treatment such as LASIK change to correct poor eyesight?
a: The length of the optic nerve
109805.e: The laser removes fine layers of the cornea precisely. This changes its curve, and the image falls sharply on the retina again.
109805.m: An eye laser reshapes the cornea.

109806.q: What is the vision problem called in which the cornea is unevenly curved?
109806.e: In astigmatism, the cornea does not bend light equally in all directions. Points then look like short lines.
109806.m: With astigmatism, points look like lines.

109807.q: Which part of the eye can be transplanted from a donor who has died if it is very cloudy?
109807.e: Cornea transplants have been common for many decades. Because the cornea has no blood vessels, it is rarely rejected.
109807.m: A cloudy cornea can be replaced with a donor cornea.

109808.q: Roughly how thick is the cornea in the middle?
109808.e: The cornea is about 0.5 millimetres thick in the middle and slightly thicker at the edge.
109808.m: The cornea is only about half a millimetre thick.

109809.q: What fills most of the eyeball?
109809.e: The vitreous body lies inside the eye and takes up about two thirds of its volume.
109809.m: The vitreous body fills most of the eyeball.

109810.q: What is the vitreous body mostly made of?
109810.e: The vitreous body is about 98 per cent water. It also contains hyaluronic acid and fine collagen fibres.
109810.m: The vitreous body is almost all water.

109811.q: What is a healthy vitreous body like?
109811.e: The vitreous body is a clear, jelly-like mass. Despite its name, it is not hard.
109811.m: The vitreous body is a clear, jelly-like mass.

109812.q: Between which parts of the eye is the vitreous body?
a: Between the lens and the retina
Between the cornea and the iris
Between the eyelid and the cornea
Between the retina and the sclera
109812.e: After the lens, light passes through the vitreous body and then reaches the retina.
109812.m: The vitreous body lies behind the lens and in front of the retina.

109813.q: What are the little threads you sometimes see floating in front of a bright sky?
a: Shadows of tiny particles in the vitreous body
Specks of dust in the air
109813.e: There are tiny clumps in the vitreous body. They cast shadows on the retina and move along when you move your eyes. They are usually harmless.
109813.m: The floating threads are shadows from the vitreous body.

109814.q: What is one of the jobs of the vitreous body?
a: It gives the eye its round shape
109814.e: The vitreous body fills the eye firmly and so supports the wall of the eye. This lets the eyeball keep its round shape.
109814.m: The vitreous body keeps the eye in shape.

109815.q: What often happens to the vitreous body in old age?
a: It partly turns liquid and shrinks
109815.e: Over the years, the vitreous body partly turns liquid and can pull away from the retina. This is called vitreous detachment.
109815.m: In old age, the vitreous body can turn liquid and pull away.

109816.q: Why is the vitreous body called that, even though it is soft?
a: Because it is clear like glass
Because it is made of sand
109816.e: The vitreous body is a soft, jelly-like mass. But it is as clear as glass (the Latin “vitreus” means glassy), so that light reaches the retina freely.
109816.m: The vitreous body is clear like glass but soft.

109817.q: Which nerve carries signals from the eye to the brain?
109817.e: The optic nerve bundles the nerve fibres from the retina and carries them to the brain.
109817.m: The optic nerve connects the eye with the brain.

109818.q: In which part of the head is the visual cortex?
a: At the back of the head
Behind the eyes in the nose
109818.e: The visual pathway runs from the eye right across the brain to the back of the head. There lies the visual cortex, which turns the signals into images.
109818.m: The visual cortex is at the back of the head.

109820.q: Why does each half of the brain receive images from both eyes?
a: Because the optic nerves partly cross over
Because each eye has two optic nerves
Because the blood spreads the images
Because the eyes take turns to see
109820.e: Behind the eyes, the optic nerves partly cross over. About half of the fibres switch to the other side.
109820.m: The optic nerves partly cross over.

109822.q: The optic nerve is a cranial nerve. What does that mean?
a: It runs directly from the head into the brain
It runs through the spinal cord
It lies in the middle of the heart
109822.e: Cranial nerves come directly from the brain, without going through the spinal cord. In this way, the optic nerve connects the eye with the brain by a short route.
109822.m: The optic nerve runs directly from the eye into the brain.

109823.q: Where does the optic nerve leave the eye?
a: At the back of the eyeball
At the front by the pupil
109823.e: The optic nerve gathers the fibres from the retina and leaves the eyeball at the back. From there it runs to the brain.
109823.m: The optic nerve leaves the eye at the back.

109824.q: What is the result if the optic nerve of one eye is completely cut?
a: The eye sees only in black and white
109824.e: Without the optic nerve, the signals from the retina no longer reach the brain. The eye can then see nothing at all.
109824.m: Without the optic nerve, an eye cannot see.

109825.q: Why can you see nothing at the blind spot?
a: There are no light-sensitive cells there
The retina is coloured black there
There is a blood clot there
109825.e: At the blind spot, the nerve fibres and blood vessels leave the eye. There is no room for sensory cells at this point.
109825.m: There are no sensory cells at the blind spot.

109826.q: Why do we not notice the blind spot in everyday life?
a: The brain fills in the gap
109826.e: The brain fills the missing spot with what can be seen around it. So we do not notice a hole in the picture.
109826.m: The brain simply fills in the blind spot.

109827.q: How can you find your own blind spot?
a: Close one eye, fix on a point and change the distance
Look into a lamp with both eyes
Rub your eyes in the dark
109827.e: You draw a cross and a dot next to it. If you look at the cross with one eye and change the distance, the dot suddenly disappears.
109827.m: A simple paper test lets you find the blind spot.

109828.q: Why is the blind spot called that?
a: Because you see nothing at that spot
Because only blind people have it
Because it only appears at night
109828.e: At the spot where the optic nerve leaves the eye, there are no light-sensitive cells. We do not see an image that falls exactly there.
109828.m: The eye sees nothing at the blind spot.

109829.q: Which animal has no blind spot because its eye is built differently?
109829.e: In octopuses, the nerve fibres lie behind the sensory cells. So they do not have to pass through the retina, and no gap forms.

109830.q: Why do you not notice the blind spot with both eyes open?
a: The other eye sees the missing spot
109830.e: The blind spots of the two eyes are in different places in the picture. What one eye does not see, the other one does.
109830.m: With two eyes, each eye covers the other's gap.

109831.q: How many blind spots does a person with two healthy eyes have?
109831.e: Each eye has exactly one place where the optic nerve leaves. The two gaps are in different places in the picture.
109831.m: Each eye has its own blind spot.

109832.q: What leaves the eye at the blind spot?
109832.e: At the blind spot, the nerve fibres leave the eye as the optic nerve. It carries the images to the brain.
109832.m: The optic nerve leaves the eye at the blind spot.

109833.q: What are the rods in the retina mainly responsible for?
a: Seeing sharply in the centre of vision
109833.e: Rods are very sensitive to light. They make it possible to see at dusk and at night.
109833.m: We see at dusk with the rods.

109834.q: What can rods not tell apart?
109834.e: All rods have the same visual pigment. They only report how much light arrives, not what colour it is.

109835.q: Which sensory cells are there more of in the retina?
a: The same number of rods and cones
109835.e: A retina has around 120 million rods but only about 6 million cones. So rods are the most common light-sensitive cells.
109835.m: There are far more rods than cones in the eye.

109836.q: What happens to the visual pigment in the rods when light falls on it?
a: It breaks down and triggers a nerve signal
It flows out of the eye as a tear
109836.e: The visual pigment, also called visual purple, breaks down when light falls on it. This produces a signal that travels through the optic nerve to the brain.
109836.m: Light splits the visual pigment and triggers a signal.

109837.q: Which vitamin does the body need for the visual pigment of the rods?
109837.e: The visual pigment is made from a substance that comes from vitamin A. Vitamin A is found, for example, in liver and eggs, and as a precursor in carrots.
109837.m: The body needs vitamin A for good eyesight.

109838.q: Roughly how long does it take for the eyes to get fully used to the dark?
109838.e: During dark adaptation, the visual pigment is gradually made again. It takes about half an hour until full sensitivity is reached.
109838.m: Getting used to the dark takes about half an hour.

109839.q: Where are the rods mainly found?
a: At the edge of the retina
Only in the centre of vision
109839.e: Rods are spread mainly over the outer areas of the retina. That is why you see faint stars better if you look just to the side of them.
109839.m: The rods are mainly at the edge of the retina.

109840.q: What is it called when someone sees very poorly at dusk because the rods do not work properly?
109840.e: In night blindness, seeing in dim light works poorly. One possible cause is a lack of a particular vitamin.
109840.m: Night-blind people see poorly at dusk.

109841.q: What are the cones in the retina responsible for?
109841.e: Cones need a lot of light. In return, they can tell colours apart and give a sharp image.
109841.m: We see colours with the cones.

109842.q: How many types of cone does a person with normal colour vision have?
109842.e: There are cones for short-wave, medium-wave and long-wave light, roughly blue, green and red. From their signals, the brain mixes all the colours.
109842.m: Humans have three types of cone.

109843.q: Which sensory cells are there more of in the retina: cones or rods?
109843.e: A retina has around 120 million rods but only about 6 million cones. The rods help us see at dusk.
109843.m: There are far more rods than cones in the retina.

109844.q: Where are the cones packed most densely?
a: At the edge of the retina
109844.e: The fovea in the middle of the retina contains almost nothing but tightly packed cones. At the edge of the retina there are far fewer cones.
109844.m: The cones are packed most densely in the fovea.

109845.q: What is tested with charts full of coloured dots with a number hidden in them?
109845.e: Anyone who has trouble telling certain colours apart cannot see the number among the dots. This is how red-green colour blindness is found, for example.
109845.m: Coloured dot charts test colour vision.

109846.q: Why are men more often red-green colour blind than women?
a: The gene is on the X chromosome
109846.e: Men have only one X chromosome. If the gene on it is changed, there is no healthy second X chromosome to make up for it.
109846.m: Red-green colour blindness is inherited via the X chromosome.

109847.q: Which light can many birds see that is invisible to humans?
109847.e: Many birds have a fourth type of cone. With it they see ultraviolet light, which we cannot see.
109847.m: Many birds can see ultraviolet light.

109848.q: How many types of cone do dogs have?
109848.e: Dogs have two types of cone. They see blue and yellow well but can hardly tell red and green apart.
109848.m: With two types of cone, dogs see fewer colours.

109849.q: Where does the sharp image form in short-sightedness?
109849.e: The light rays meet before they reach the retina. Only a blurred image arrives on the retina itself.
109849.m: In short-sightedness, the focus is in front of the retina.

109850.q: What is usually the cause of short-sightedness?
a: The optic nerve is too thin
109850.e: Usually the eyeball has grown a little too long. Even one millimetre makes a clear difference.
109850.m: An eyeball that is too long makes you short-sighted.

109851.q: Which type of lens is used to correct short-sightedness?
109851.e: A diverging lens is thinner in the middle than at the edge. It spreads the rays out a little so that they only meet on the retina.

109852.q: According to studies, which habit helps to prevent short-sightedness in children?
a: Spending lots of time outdoors in daylight
109852.e: Children who spend a long time outside every day become short-sighted less often. Daylight and looking into the distance have a protective effect.

109853.q: What do short-sighted people see badly without glasses?
a: Things right in front of their nose
109853.e: Short-sighted people see clearly close up, but things in the distance look blurred. They often squint when looking into the distance.
109853.m: Short-sighted people see distant things out of focus.

109854.q: What does the unit dioptre measure?
a: The refractive power of a lens
109854.e: The refractive power in dioptres is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres. The more strongly a lens bends light, the bigger the number.
109854.m: The refractive power of a lens is measured in dioptres.

109855.q: A lens has a focal length of 0.5 metres. How many dioptres does it have?
109855.e: The refractive power is 1 divided by the focal length in metres: 1 ÷ 0.5 gives 2 dioptres.
109855.m: The shorter the focal length, the more dioptres the lens has.

109856.q: What does a long-sighted person mainly see out of focus?
109856.e: Long-sighted people mainly have trouble reading or doing handicrafts. They often see well in the distance.
109856.m: Long-sighted people see close things out of focus.

109857.q: With long-sightedness, where would the sharp image form?
109857.e: The light rays would only meet behind the retina. That is why a blurred image forms on the retina.
109857.m: With long-sightedness, the focal point lies behind the retina.

109858.q: What is usually the cause of long-sightedness?
a: The optic nerve is too long
109858.e: Usually the eyeball is built a little too short. The refractive power is then not enough to make a sharp image of close things.
109858.m: An eyeball that is too short makes you long-sighted.

109859.q: Which type of lens is used to correct long-sightedness?
109859.e: A converging lens is thicker in the middle than at the edge. It increases the refractive power so that the image forms on the retina.

109860.q: Why do many long-sighted children hardly notice their long-sightedness?
a: The lens of their eye can make up for the error
Their retina is not finished yet
109860.e: In children the lens is very elastic and can bulge a lot. In this way it makes up for slight long-sightedness by itself, but this can be tiring.
109860.m: Children can often make up for slight long-sightedness themselves.

109861.q: What problems can uncorrected long-sightedness cause when reading?
109861.e: When looking at close things, the eye always has to work harder than necessary. That is tiring and can cause headaches.
109861.m: Uncorrected long-sightedness can give you headaches.

109862.q: Which vision problem is the opposite of long-sightedness?
109862.e: Short-sighted people see well close up and blurrily in the distance. For long-sighted people it is the other way round.
109862.m: Short-sightedness is the opposite of long-sightedness.

109863.q: How do the eyes of a very long-sighted person look behind their glasses?
109863.e: The lenses work like a magnifying glass. Anyone looking through them at the eyes sees them bigger.
109863.m: Glasses for long-sighted people work like a magnifying glass.

109864.q: What does a contact lens rest on?
a: On the tear film over the cornea
Behind the lens of the eye
109864.e: The contact lens floats on a thin film of tear fluid directly in front of the cornea.
109864.m: Contact lenses float on the tear film.

109865.q: In sport, what is one advantage of contact lenses over glasses?
a: They cannot fall off or steam up
109865.e: Contact lenses sit directly on the eye. They do not slip when you run and do not steam up like glasses.
109865.m: In sport, contact lenses are often more practical than glasses.

109866.q: Why should you never rinse contact lenses with tap water?
a: It makes them as hard as stone
109866.e: Germs such as acanthamoebae can live in tap water. If they get into the eye with the lens, they can cause serious inflammation of the cornea.
109866.m: Contact lenses only belong in the right cleaning solution.

109867.q: What are the two main types of contact lenses?
109867.e: Soft lenses are made of plastic that contains water. Rigid lenses are harder and smaller.
109867.m: There are soft and rigid contact lenses.

109868.q: What are soft contact lenses made of?
109868.e: Soft contact lenses are made of a plastic that absorbs water. That is why they are flexible and comfortable to wear.
109868.m: Soft contact lenses are made of plastic that contains water.

109869.q: Why should you not wear normal contact lenses while sleeping?
109869.e: With your eyes closed, less oxygen reaches the cornea. Together with the lens, this raises the risk of inflammation.
109869.m: You do not sleep in normal contact lenses.

109870.q: What do so-called night lenses (orthokeratology) do?
a: They temporarily reshape the cornea overnight
They colour your eyes while you sleep
109870.e: These special rigid lenses gently press the cornea flatter at night. During the day you can then see clearly for a while without any aids.
109870.m: Night lenses reshape the cornea for the day.

109871.q: What should contact lens wearers always do before putting their lenses in?
109871.e: Clean hands stop germs getting onto the lens and into the eye.
109871.m: You wash your hands before putting in contact lenses.

109872.q: Two lines of the same length have arrowheads pointing in different directions at their ends. What do you see?
109872.e: In the Müller-Lyer illusion, the arrowheads make one line look longer and the other shorter, even though both are the same length.
109872.m: Arrowheads can make lines look longer or shorter.

109873.q: What happens if you look for a long time at a drawn wire cube (Necker cube)?
a: The front and back keep flipping
109873.e: The drawing can be seen in two different 3D ways. The brain switches between them, so the cube flips. It was described in 1832 by the Geneva scientist Louis Albert Necker.
109873.m: The Necker cube is an ambiguous figure.

109874.q: In an ambiguous picture you see either a vase or two faces. Why do you never see both at the same time?
a: The brain decides on figure or background
One eye sees the vase, the other the faces
109874.e: With Rubin's vase, the brain decides what is figure and what is background. It can only show one interpretation at a time.
109874.m: In ambiguous figures, figure and background flip.

109875.q: On a grid of white lines on a black background, you see grey spots at the crossings. Are these spots really there?
a: No, they are created by our visual system
No, they are dust on the screen
109875.e: In the Hermann grid the grey dots do not exist at all. If you look straight at a crossing, the spot there disappears.
109875.m: The Hermann grid shows spots that are not there.

109876.q: Why does the Moon look bigger on the horizon than high in the sky?
a: It is closer to the Earth then
The air magnifies it like a magnifying glass
109876.e: In photos, the Moon on the horizon is not bigger. The Moon illusion happens in our head, probably because we have houses and trees to compare it with.
109876.m: The Moon illusion happens in our brain.

109877.q: You stare at a red dot for a long time and then look at a white wall. Roughly what colour is the afterimage?
109877.e: The sensory cells for red get tired. On the white wall, the other parts of the colour then win, and you see the opposite colour.
109877.m: An afterimage appears in the opposite colour.

109878.q: What are figures like the Penrose triangle called, which you can draw but cannot really build?
109878.e: Impossible figures look correct in 3D at first glance. Only when you look closely do you notice that the corners do not fit together.
109878.m: You can draw impossible figures, but not build them.

109879.q: Two circles of the same size: one is surrounded by big circles, the other by small circles. Which looks bigger?
a: The one surrounded by small circles
The one surrounded by big circles
Neither of them can be seen
109879.e: In the Ebbinghaus illusion, the brain compares with the surroundings. Next to small circles, the middle circle looks bigger.
109879.m: The surroundings affect how big we see something.

109880.q: In an illusion room, people in one corner look like giants and in the other like dwarfs. Why?
a: The room is built crooked but looks rectangular
The people are wearing high shoes
The floor is made of rubber
The lamps make the people bigger
109880.e: The Ames room is built distorted, but through a peephole it looks rectangular. That is why the brain misjudges the size of the people.
109880.m: In the Ames room, the false shape of the room tricks us.

110174.q: Where does the outer ear canal of a human end?
110174.e: The outer ear canal leads inwards from the outer ear to the eardrum. Behind it the middle ear begins.
110174.m: The outer ear canal ends at the eardrum.

110175.q: Roughly how long is the outer ear canal in adults?
110175.e: In adults the outer ear canal is around 2.5 to 3.5 centimetres long. It is slightly curved in an S shape.
110175.m: The outer ear canal is only a few centimetres long.

110176.q: What does earwax do in the ear canal?
a: It protects against dirt and germs
110176.e: Earwax (cerumen) traps dust, keeps the skin supple and slows down bacteria. Over time it moves outwards by itself.
110176.m: Earwax is a natural protection for the ear canal.

110177.q: Why do doctors advise against cleaning the ear canal with cotton buds?
a: The earwax gets pushed further in
110177.e: Cotton buds often push earwax inwards, where it can form a plug. You can also injure the eardrum.
110177.m: Cotton buds do not belong deep in the ear canal.

110178.q: What is the wall of the outer third of the ear canal made of?
110178.e: The outer third of the ear canal has a wall of cartilage; the inner part lies in the temporal bone and is made of bone.
110178.m: The ear canal is cartilage on the outside and bone on the inside.

110179.q: Why should you let your ears dry well after swimming?
a: Damp skin in the ear canal gets inflamed more easily
Otherwise you only hear low notes
110179.e: If water stays in the ear canal, the skin softens. Germs then get in more easily and an ear canal infection can develop.
110179.m: After swimming you should let your ears dry well.

110180.q: What job does the outer ear canal do?
a: It carries sound to the eardrum
110180.e: The ear canal is a short tube leading inwards from the outer ear. Sound travels through it to the eardrum.
110180.m: The ear canal carries sound to the eardrum.

110181.q: Why does the doctor gently pull an adult's outer ear backwards and upwards before looking into the ear?
a: So that the curved ear canal becomes straighter
So that the earwax becomes runny
So that the semicircular canals rest
110181.e: The ear canal is curved. Pulling the outer ear backwards and upwards straightens it, so the eardrum can be seen better.
110181.m: A straightened ear canal gives a view of the eardrum.

110182.q: How many ear bones does each human ear have?
110182.e: In each middle ear lie the hammer, anvil and stirrup. Together they form the chain of ear bones.
110182.m: Each ear has three ear bones.

110183.q: In which part of the ear are the ear bones?
110183.e: The ear bones lie in the air-filled cavity of the middle ear. They connect the eardrum to the inner ear.
110183.m: The ear bones sit in the middle ear.

110184.q: What job do the ear bones do?
a: They pass vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear
110184.e: The eardrum vibrates when sound hits it. The hammer, anvil and stirrup pass this vibration on to the inner ear.
110184.m: The ear bones carry sound into the inner ear.

110185.q: In what order do the ear bones pass sound on from the eardrum?
110185.e: The hammer sits on the eardrum, the anvil lies in the middle, and the stirrup presses on the oval window of the inner ear.
110185.m: Sound goes from hammer to anvil to stirrup.

110186.q: Which ear bone passes the vibrations directly to the inner ear?
110186.e: The hammer sits on the eardrum, the anvil in the middle. The stirrup is the last little bone and pushes the vibrations into the inner ear.
110186.m: The stirrup is the last ear bone before the inner ear.

110188.q: Where is the smallest skeletal muscle in the human body?
110188.e: The stapedius muscle in the middle ear is only a few millimetres long. With very loud noises it tightens and dampens the vibrations a little.
110188.m: The smallest skeletal muscle is in the middle ear.

110189.q: What happens if the stirrup in the ear becomes fixed and can no longer vibrate?
a: You can no longer smell anything
110189.e: The stirrup must vibrate freely to carry sound into the inner ear. If it becomes fixed, less sound arrives. An operation can often help.
110189.m: A fixed stirrup makes hearing worse.

110191.q: Which part of the ear is the hammer firmly attached to?
110191.e: The handle of the hammer is attached to the eardrum. When the eardrum vibrates, the hammer moves with it.
110191.m: The hammer hangs on the eardrum.

110192.q: In which part of the ear is the hammer?
110192.e: The hammer is one of the three ear bones. Together with the anvil and stirrup, it lies in the middle ear, just behind the eardrum.
110192.m: The hammer lies in the middle ear behind the eardrum.

110193.q: What is the rounded upper part of the hammer called?
110193.e: The hammer consists of a head, neck and handle. The head of the hammer lies at the top of the middle ear cavity.
110193.m: The upper part of the hammer is its head.

110194.q: Which ear bone is the hammer connected to by a small joint?
110194.e: There is a tiny joint between the hammer and the anvil. The vibration is passed on through it.
110194.m: The hammer and anvil are connected by a joint.

110195.q: What is the tiny muscle attached to the hammer in the ear for?
a: It dampens the vibration a little with loud noises
110195.e: The tensor tympani pulls on the hammer and tightens the eardrum. It then vibrates less strongly, which protects the inner ear a little from loud sounds.
110195.m: A tiny muscle on the hammer dampens loud noises a little.

110196.q: What can a doctor often see through the eardrum when looking with an otoscope?
110196.e: The eardrum is thin and slightly see-through. The attached handle of the hammer shows on it as a light stripe.
110196.m: You can see the handle of the hammer through the eardrum.

110197.q: Which of the three ear bones is the longest?
a: They are all the same length
110197.e: The hammer is around 8 to 9 millimetres long, the anvil only about 5 to 7 millimetres. The stirrup is the shortest.
110197.m: The hammer is the longest ear bone.

110198.q: Where does the hammer in the ear get its name from?
a: From its shape, which looks like a hammer
110198.e: The little bone looks like a small hammer. The anvil and stirrup are also named after their shapes.
110198.m: The hammer is named after its shape.

110199.q: How big is a newborn baby's anvil compared with an adult's?
a: About a tenth of the size
110199.e: The ear bones are already fully grown and fully turned to bone at birth. They do not grow any more after that.
110199.m: The ear bones are already fully grown at birth.

110200.q: In which part of the ear is the anvil?
110200.e: The hammer, anvil and stirrup lie in the middle ear behind the eardrum. They pass sound on to the inner ear.
110200.m: The anvil lies in the middle ear.

110201.q: Which tool is the anvil in the ear named after?
110201.e: The blacksmith puts the hot iron on an anvil and strikes it with a hammer. The ear bone has a similar shape.
110201.m: The hammer and anvil are named after blacksmith's tools.

110202.q: Which little bone is the long process of the anvil connected to?
110202.e: The long process of the anvil reaches to the head of the stirrup. There is a small joint there.
110202.m: The anvil passes the vibration on to the stirrup.

110203.q: How many ear bones does one ear have?
110203.e: In each middle ear there are three ear bones: the hammer, anvil and stirrup. They are the smallest bones in the body.
110203.m: Each ear has three ear bones.

110204.q: What job do the hammer, anvil and stirrup do?
a: They pass on the vibrations of the eardrum
They protect the ear from water
110204.e: Sound makes the eardrum vibrate. The three ear bones pass these vibrations on, amplified, to the inner ear.
110204.m: The ear bones carry sound into the inner ear.

110205.q: What happens if the connection between the anvil and stirrup is broken after an accident?
a: You hear much worse in that ear
You lose your sense of smell
110205.e: If the chain is broken, the vibration no longer reaches the inner ear properly. This causes conductive hearing loss, which can often be treated with an operation.
110205.m: A broken chain of ear bones makes hearing worse.

110206.q: How many joints does the anvil have with neighbouring ear bones?
110206.e: The anvil is connected by a joint to the hammer and by another to the stirrup. That makes two joints in total.
110206.m: The anvil is joined to two neighbours.

110207.q: In which part of the ear is the cochlea?
110207.e: The cochlea lies in the inner ear, well protected in the petrous bone. There sound is turned into nerve signals.
110207.m: The cochlea lies in the inner ear.

110208.q: What is the cochlea filled with?
110208.e: The passages of the cochlea contain fluids, the perilymph and the endolymph. The stirrup sets them in motion.

110209.q: Which cells in the cochlea turn vibrations into nerve signals?
110209.e: The hair cells carry tiny hairs. When these are bent, the cells send signals to the brain through the hearing nerve.
110209.m: Hair cells turn sound into nerve signals.

110210.q: Roughly how many turns does the human cochlea have?
110210.e: The human cochlea winds about two and a half times around a bony axis. That is why it looks like a snail shell.
110210.m: The cochlea has about two and a half turns.

110211.q: Which sounds do older people often hear worse first?
110211.e: The hair cells for high sounds sit at the start of the cochlea and wear out first. That is why older people often hear high sounds worse.
110211.m: In old age you often hear high sounds worse first.

110212.q: What is converted in the cochlea?
110212.e: In the cochlea, sound waves make a fluid vibrate. Hair cells turn this into nerve signals that go to the brain.
110212.m: The cochlea turns sound into nerve signals.

110213.q: Why is protection from noise so important for the hair cells?
a: Destroyed hair cells do not grow back in humans
Hair cells need noise to grow
Otherwise hair cells move out of the ear
Otherwise hair cells turn into bone
110213.e: Very loud noise can permanently damage the delicate hair cells. In humans they do not form again, so the hearing loss stays.
110213.m: Destroyed hair cells do not come back.

110214.q: Which device can directly stimulate the hearing nerve in the cochlea with electricity in cases of very severe hearing loss?
110214.e: A cochlear implant has an electrode that is inserted into the cochlea. It stimulates the hearing nerve with electrical signals.
110214.m: A cochlear implant does the work of the hair cells.

110215.q: How is the cochlea protected from injury?
a: It lies deep in the hard skull bone
It lies in the soft outer ear
It is surrounded by thick hair
110215.e: The cochlea lies in the petrous bone, part of the skull. It is one of the hardest bones in the body.
110215.m: The cochlea is protected in the hard skull bone.

110216.q: How many semicircular canals does each inner ear have?
110216.e: Each inner ear has three semicircular canals. Together with two little sacs they form the organ of balance.
110216.m: Each inner ear has three semicircular canals.

110217.q: Which movements do the semicircular canals detect?
110217.e: The semicircular canals react to rotation, for example when nodding, shaking or tilting your head. That way the brain knows how the head is turning.
110217.m: The semicircular canals sense turns of the head.

110218.q: How are the three semicircular canals arranged in relation to each other?
a: Roughly at right angles in three planes
One behind the other in a row
In circles one inside the other
110218.e: The three semicircular canals are roughly at right angles to each other. That way every turn in space can be detected.
110218.m: The three semicircular canals cover all three directions in space.

110219.q: What is inside the semicircular canals of the inner ear?
110219.e: The semicircular canals are filled with fluid. When you turn, it lags behind a little and bends tiny sensory hairs.
110219.m: Fluid moves in the semicircular canals.

110220.q: Where in the body are the semicircular canals?
110220.e: The semicircular canals are well protected in the skull bone in the inner ear. The cochlea lies right next to them.
110220.m: The semicircular canals lie in the inner ear.

110221.q: After spinning fast in the playground, why does everything still seem to turn even though you are standing still?
a: The fluid in the semicircular canals keeps moving
Your eyes grow for a moment
The ear canal fills with air
110221.e: Because of its inertia, the endolymph keeps flowing for a moment after you stop. So the brain reports a turn that is no longer happening.
110221.m: After spinning, the fluid in the semicircular canals keeps moving for a moment.

110222.q: Which organ tells the brain whether we are standing upright or lying down?
a: The organ of balance in the inner ear
110222.e: The organ of balance contains tiny chalk crystals that gravity pulls downwards. That way the brain senses how the head is tilted.
110222.m: The organ of balance senses gravity.

110223.q: Through which nerve do the signals from the semicircular canals reach the brain?
110223.e: The vestibular nerve (nervus vestibularis) forms the eighth cranial nerve together with the hearing nerve. It carries the signals from the semicircular canals.
110223.m: The vestibular nerve reports turns to the brain.

110224.q: Besides the semicircular canals, which senses help the brain to keep its balance?
a: The eyes and the position sense in muscles and joints
110224.e: The brain compares the messages from the organ of balance with what the eyes see and what muscles and joints report. That is why you wobble more with your eyes closed.
110224.m: Balance comes from several senses working together.

110225.q: Which two spaces does the Eustachian tube connect?
a: The middle ear and the upper throat
The outer ear and the mouth
The inner ear and the brain
The ear canal and the nose
110225.e: The Eustachian tube, also called the auditory tube, leads from the middle ear cavity to the upper throat behind the nose.
110225.m: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear and the throat.

110226.q: What is the Eustachian tube mainly for?
a: Balancing the pressure in the middle ear
110226.e: When it opens, air can flow into or out of the middle ear. That way the pressure is the same on both sides of the eardrum.

110227.q: What is another name for the Eustachian tube?
110227.e: The Eustachian tube is also called the auditory tube. It connects the middle ear with the upper throat.
110227.m: The Eustachian tube is also called the auditory tube.

110228.q: What helps when your ears start to feel blocked as a plane comes in to land?
a: Holding your breath for a long time
110228.e: When you swallow or yawn, the Eustachian tube opens briefly. This balances the pressure in the middle ear.

110229.q: How do divers balance the pressure in their ears?
a: Pinch their nose and gently push air in
Hold their breath for a long time
110229.e: With your nose pinched, you gently push air through the Eustachian tube into the middle ear. This balances the pressure.
110229.m: You can balance ear pressure by pinching your nose.

110230.q: Why do young children get middle ear infections more often than adults?
a: Their Eustachian tube is shorter and flatter
They do not have an eardrum yet
Their ear canal is full of water
110230.e: In children the Eustachian tube is shorter, narrower and lies flatter. Germs from the throat can get into the middle ear more easily.
110230.m: A short, flat Eustachian tube makes middle ear infections more likely.

110231.q: Why does your ear often feel dull and blocked when you have a bad cold?
110231.e: With a cold, the lining swells and closes the Eustachian tube. Then the pressure can no longer balance out.
110231.m: A blocked Eustachian tube makes the ear feel dull.

110232.q: Roughly how long is the Eustachian tube in adults?
110232.e: In adults the Eustachian tube is around 3.5 centimetres long. Part of it is bone, the larger part is cartilage.
110232.m: The Eustachian tube is only a few centimetres long.

a: A noise in the ear with no outside source
An inflammation of the outer ear
A loud echo in the mountains
110233.e: With tinnitus you hear whistling, rushing or humming, even though no matching sound is coming from outside.
110233.m: Tinnitus is a noise in the ear that only you can hear.

110234.q: Which language does the word “tinnitus” come from?
110234.e: The word comes from the Latin “tinnire”, which means “to ring”.

110235.q: What is a common cause of tinnitus in teenagers?
110235.e: Very loud music in headphones or at concerts can damage the hair cells. Whistling afterwards is a warning sign.
110235.m: Loud music can cause noises in the ears.

110236.q: According to experts, after how long is tinnitus called chronic?
110236.e: Tinnitus that lasts longer than around three months is considered chronic. Before that it is called acute tinnitus.
110236.m: Tinnitus lasting over three months is considered chronic.

110237.q: How can you best protect yourself from tinnitus at a loud concert?
a: With ear protection and distance from the speakers
By standing as close to the speakers as possible
110237.e: Ear protection lowers the sound level in the ear. The further you are from the loudspeakers, the quieter it also gets.
110237.m: Ear protection and distance protect your ears.

110238.q: Is tinnitus a disease in itself or a symptom?
110238.e: Tinnitus is a sign of illness. It can occur, for example, after noise, with sudden hearing loss or with stress.
110238.m: Tinnitus is a symptom, not a disease in itself.

110239.q: What helps many people with long-lasting tinnitus to live better with the noise?
a: Learning to pay less attention to the noise
Blocking their ears with cotton wool for ever
110239.e: With chronic tinnitus, people learn in therapy to pay less attention to the noise. The brain often gets used to it this way.
110239.m: You can learn to pay less attention to tinnitus.

110240.q: What is tinnitus called that only the person affected can hear and nobody else can measure?
110240.e: Almost all ear noises are subjective and arise in the hearing pathway. Objective tinnitus is rare, for example a rushing of blood that others can hear.

110241.q: When do many people affected notice their tinnitus most strongly?
a: In quiet surroundings, for example when falling asleep
110241.e: In silence there are no other sounds to cover the tinnitus. That is why it is often most bothersome in bed at night.
110241.m: In silence, an ear noise is especially noticeable.

a: The length of the ear canal
110242.e: Decibels show how loud a sound is. Pitch, on the other hand, is measured in hertz.

110243.q: Which sound level roughly matches the hearing threshold of a healthy young person?
110243.e: 0 decibels does not mean silence; it is roughly the quietest sound that a healthy young ear can just hear at 1,000 hertz.
110243.m: 0 decibels is at the hearing threshold.

110244.q: Roughly how loud is a normal conversation?
110244.e: A normal conversation at a distance of one metre is around 60 decibels. A vacuum cleaner, at around 70 to 80 decibels, is much louder.

110245.q: Roughly from what sound level does sound start to hurt your ears?
110245.e: The pain threshold is around 120 to 130 decibels, about as loud as a jet plane close up.

110246.q: Why is there an upper volume limit at concerts in Switzerland?
a: So that the musicians use less electricity
So that the loudspeakers last longer
So that the drinks stay cool
110246.e: Very loud music over a long time can permanently damage hearing. That is why a regulation limits the sound level at events.
110246.m: Concerts have a volume limit to protect people's ears.

110247.q: What is the best way to protect your hearing at a loud concert?
a: With a hat over your eyes
110247.e: Earplugs reduce the sound by many decibels. Keeping your distance from the loudspeakers and taking breaks somewhere quiet also help.
110247.m: Ear protection lowers the volume in your ear.

110248.q: Why can listening to music through headphones for a long time at high volume damage your hearing?
a: The louder and longer the sound, the more hair cells are damaged
Headphones cool down the inner ear
110248.e: For hearing damage, what counts is the sound dose made up of level and time. Even from about 85 decibels over a long time, the hair cells can suffer.
110248.m: Loud music does more harm the longer it lasts.

110249.e: Quiet whispering is around 30 decibels, so it is much quieter than a normal conversation.

a: A sudden loss of hearing, usually in one ear
Slow hearing loss in old age
110250.e: With sudden hearing loss, you suddenly hear worse or hardly at all in one ear, usually for no obvious reason.
110250.m: Sudden hearing loss is hearing that goes suddenly.

110251.q: Which part of the ear does sudden hearing loss affect?
110251.e: Sudden hearing loss is a disorder in the inner ear, that is, in the cochlea with its hair cells.
110251.m: Sudden hearing loss happens in the inner ear.

110252.q: What feeling do people often describe with sudden hearing loss?
a: As if there were cotton wool in the ear
As if the ear were itching
As if the ear were ice-cold
As if they could hear better
110252.e: Many feel a dull pressure, as if there were cotton wool in the ear. Often there is also a noise in the ear.
110252.m: Sudden hearing loss often feels like cotton wool in the ear.

110253.q: What should you do if you suddenly can hardly hear anything in one ear?
a: Rinse the ear with cotton buds
110253.e: Sudden hearing loss should be checked by a doctor soon. That way other causes can be ruled out and treatment can be started.
110253.m: With sudden hearing loss, you go to the doctor soon.

110254.q: Which medicine is often used for sudden hearing loss?
110254.e: Cortisone is meant to reduce inflammation and swelling in the inner ear. It is the most common treatment for sudden hearing loss.
110254.m: Sudden hearing loss is often treated with cortisone.

110255.q: Which ear symptom often also occurs with sudden hearing loss?
a: Hair growing in the ear canal
110255.e: Many people with sudden hearing loss also hear whistling or rushing, that is, tinnitus.
110255.m: Sudden hearing loss often comes with a noise in the ear.

110256.q: How is sudden hearing loss different from acoustic trauma caused by a bang?
a: With sudden hearing loss, usually no cause can be found
With sudden hearing loss you hear better
Acoustic trauma only affects the nose
110256.e: Acoustic trauma has a clear cause, for example a firework close to the ear. With sudden hearing loss, the reason is usually not found.
110256.m: With sudden hearing loss, the cause usually stays unknown.

110257.q: How does mild sudden hearing loss turn out in many cases?
a: The ear always stops working completely
110257.e: In mild cases, hearing often improves within days or weeks, even without treatment. It should still be checked by a doctor.
110257.m: Mild sudden hearing loss often heals by itself.

110258.q: Why do you easily feel sick when reading in the car?
a: Your eyes and sense of balance report different things
There is too little light in the car
110258.e: Your eyes see a still book, but the organ of balance in your ear feels movement. This contradiction can make you feel sick.
110258.m: Travel sickness happens when the senses report different things.

110259.q: At what age does sudden hearing loss happen most often?
110259.e: Sudden hearing loss can happen at any age. It most often affects adults around 50; in children it is rare.
110259.m: Sudden hearing loss mostly affects middle-aged adults.

110260.q: Which is a typical sign of travel sickness?
110260.e: Typical signs are feeling sick, looking pale, cold sweat and being sick. When the movement stops, the symptoms usually go away soon.
110260.m: Travel sickness makes you feel sick.

110261.q: What helps against travel sickness in the car?
a: Looking out of the window into the distance
110261.e: If you look forwards into the distance, you see the movement that the organ of balance feels. Then the senses match better.
110261.m: Looking into the distance helps against travel sickness.

110262.q: Where is the best place to sit on a ship if you tend to get seasick?
a: In the middle of the ship
Right at the front in the bow
Right at the top of the mast
Right at the back in the stern
110262.e: In the middle of the ship it rocks the least. At the front and back the up and down movements are stronger.
110262.m: In the middle of a ship it rocks the least.

110263.q: What is the travel sickness called that astronauts can get when weightless?
110263.e: When weightless, the organ of balance is missing the usual signals from gravity. Many space travellers feel sick in the first few days.
110263.m: You can get travel sick in space too.

110264.q: Which age group is especially often affected by travel sickness?
110264.e: Children between about 2 and 12 are especially prone to it. Babies, on the other hand, are rarely affected.
110264.m: Schoolchildren get travel sick especially often.

110265.q: Which plant is often used as a natural remedy for travel sickness?
110265.e: Ginger has been used against nausea for a long time. Studies show a slight effect in some people.
110265.m: Ginger can help with travel sickness.

110266.q: What does spinning dizziness feel like?
a: As if everything were turning in a circle
As if you were very tired
As if your legs had gone to sleep
110266.e: With spinning dizziness, your surroundings or your own body seem to turn, like after a ride on a merry-go-round.
110266.m: With spinning dizziness, everything seems to turn.

110267.q: Why do you still feel dizzy for a moment after a merry-go-round ride?
a: The fluid in the organ of balance keeps turning
Blood only flows into your feet
Your eyes go blind for a moment
110267.e: In the inner ear there are semicircular canals with fluid. After stopping, the fluid keeps moving for a moment, and the brain reports a turn.
110267.m: After spinning, the fluid in the inner ear keeps moving.

110268.q: What helps if you feel dizzy after spinning?
a: Sitting down and looking at a fixed point
Running quickly in the other direction
110268.e: Sitting prevents falls. A fixed point to look at helps the brain find its bearings again.
110268.m: When dizzy, you sit down and look at a fixed point.

110269.q: Why should you not ride a bike if you suddenly feel spinning dizziness?
a: You can lose your balance and fall
110269.e: With spinning dizziness, your sense of balance is no longer right. Anyone who rides a bike then can easily fall.
110269.m: You do not ride a bike when you have spinning dizziness.

110270.q: Which complaint often also occurs with strong spinning dizziness?
110270.e: When the organ of balance and the eyes do not match, many people feel sick. Some even have to be sick.
110270.m: Strong spinning dizziness often makes you feel sick.

110271.q: How do ballet dancers stop themselves getting dizzy during pirouettes?
a: They fix their gaze on a point
110271.e: With “spotting”, the gaze stays on one point for as long as possible and then the head turns quickly. This reduces the dizziness.
110271.m: A fixed point to look at helps against spinning dizziness.

110272.q: Which nerve carries the signals from the organ of balance to the brain?
110272.e: The vestibular nerve connects the organ of balance in the inner ear with the brain. If it is inflamed, strong spinning dizziness can occur.
110272.m: The vestibular nerve tells the brain the position of the head.

110273.q: Where does spinning dizziness often come from?
a: From the organ of balance in the inner ear
110273.e: Very often the cause of spinning dizziness lies in the organ of balance or the vestibular nerve. Less often it comes from the brain.
110273.m: Spinning dizziness often comes from the organ of balance.

110563.q: Why do you breathe in briefly and strongly when sniffing?
a: So that more scent molecules reach the smelling area at the top
So that the nose warms up faster
So that the smell cells rest for a moment
So that less dust gets into the lungs
110563.e: Sniffing creates swirls of air that carry the air up to the roof of the nose. That way more scent molecules reach the olfactory lining.
110563.m: Sniffing brings more scent molecules to the olfactory lining.

110564.q: What must happen to scent molecules before the smell cells can recognise them?
a: They dissolve in the mucus of the olfactory lining
They are warmed in the lungs
They first mix with the blood
They are broken up by the teeth
110564.e: The olfactory lining is covered by a thin layer of mucus. The scent molecules dissolve in it and so reach the smell cells.
110564.m: Scent molecules must first dissolve in the nasal mucus.

110565.q: Roughly how big is the olfactory lining of a human?
a: A few square centimetres on each side of the nose
About the size of a newspaper page
110565.e: The human olfactory lining is only a few square centimetres in size. In many animals with a good sense of smell it is much bigger.
110565.m: Our olfactory lining is only a few square centimetres in size.

110566.q: Where do the smell cells send their signals?
110566.e: The smell cells are connected directly to the brain by nerve fibres. That is where the impression of a smell arises.
110566.m: Smell signals go straight to the brain.

110567.q: How do the flavours reach the olfactory lining when you chew?
a: From behind, via the throat into the nose
Through the Eustachian tube into the ear
Through the blood into the nose
Through the tear ducts of the eyes
110567.e: When you chew and swallow, aromas rise from the mouth through the throat up into the nose. This is called retronasal smelling.
110567.m: When eating, we also smell from behind through the throat.

110568.q: Where in the nose is the olfactory lining?
a: Right at the top in the roof of the nose
At the back of the throat
110568.e: The olfactory lining is only about the size of a stamp and lies right at the top of the nose. That is why you sniff to smell scents better.
110568.m: Smelling happens right at the top of the nose.

110569.q: What does the olfactory lining in the nose detect?
110569.e: The olfactory lining contains smell cells. They recognise scent molecules that get into the nose with the air.

110570.q: What type of cell are smell cells?
110570.e: Smell cells are specialised nerve cells. They pick up scent molecules and send their signal themselves along an extension towards the brain.
110570.m: Smell cells are nerve cells in the nose.

110571.q: What is special about smell cells compared with most other nerve cells?
a: They are constantly replaced by new ones
They are the biggest cells in the body
110571.e: Most nerve cells last a lifetime. Smell cells, on the other hand, die after a few weeks and are formed again from stem cells.
110571.m: Smell cells renew themselves again and again.

110572.q: How many different kinds of smell receptor do humans have?
110572.e: Humans have a few hundred different smell receptors. From their combinations, the brain can tell a huge number of smells apart.
110572.m: With hundreds of receptor types we can tell countless smells apart.

110573.q: Roughly how many smell cells does a human have?
110573.e: There are several million smell cells in the olfactory lining. A dog, however, has many more.
110573.m: We have millions of smell cells.

110574.q: What do scent molecules attach to in the nose?
110574.e: Scent molecules bind to smell receptors on the smell cells. The discovery of these receptors won the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2004.
110574.m: Scent molecules attach to smell receptors.

110575.q: Why do smells often bring back especially strong memories and feelings?
a: Smell signals go directly to the parts of the brain for feelings and memory
The nose is directly connected to the heart
Smells are stored in the stomach
Smell cells have their own memory
110575.e: Smell signals reach the limbic system very directly, and it is important for feelings and memories. That is why a scent can instantly remind you of the past.
110575.m: Scents are closely linked to feelings and memories.

110576.q: What do smell cells have at their end, which sticks out into the nasal mucus?
110576.e: At the end of each smell cell there are tiny hairs called cilia. On them are the receptors that scent molecules attach to.
110576.m: Smell hairs catch scent molecules in the mucus.

110577.q: How many kinds of smell receptor does a single smell cell usually have?
110577.e: Each smell cell is specialised in one type of receptor. The brain recognises a smell from the pattern of which cells are active at the same time.
110577.m: Each smell cell has only one kind of smell receptor.

110578.q: Which cranial nerve connects the smell cells with the brain?
110578.e: The extensions of the smell cells together form the olfactory nerve (nervus olfactorius). It is counted as the first of the twelve cranial nerves.
110578.m: The olfactory nerve is the first cranial nerve.

110579.q: Where are the taste papillae found in humans?
110579.e: The tongue is covered with many small bumps, the papillae. Many of them contain taste buds.
110579.m: Taste papillae are on the tongue.

110580.q: Why does the surface of the tongue feel rough?
a: Because of the many small papillae
110580.e: A great many tiny papillae stand close together on the tongue. They make the surface rough and help with touch.
110580.m: The many papillae make the tongue rough.

110581.q: Which list names the five basic tastes correctly?
110581.e: The tongue recognises five basic tastes. Spicy is not a taste but a pain signal, and warm or cold is a temperature signal.
110581.m: There are five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.

110582.q: What are the tiny structures in the papillae called that contain the taste cells?
110582.e: The taste buds sit in the papillae. Each contains several dozen sensory cells that come into contact with saliva through a small opening.
110582.m: Taste buds contain the sensory cells for taste.

110583.q: Why does food taste of less when you have a bad cold?
a: Because the nose helps with tasting
110583.e: We sense many flavours through the nose. If it is blocked, the tongue only notices the basic tastes.
110583.m: Without your nose, food tastes bland.

110584.q: Why can you taste normally again a few days after burning your tongue?
a: The taste cells are constantly renewed
You get used to the burning
110584.e: Taste cells only live for about two weeks. Then they are replaced by new ones, so your sense of taste recovers.

110585.q: What is the savoury basic taste called that you can taste in stock, cheese or ripe tomatoes?
110585.e: Umami is Japanese and means something like “delicious”. The taste was first studied in a Japanese seaweed broth.
110585.m: Umami is the savoury basic taste.

110586.q: Which basic taste is mainly caused by sodium ions?
110586.e: Table salt is made of sodium and chloride ions. The sodium ions are recognised by certain taste cells.

110587.q: What has to happen to a flavour substance so that the tongue can taste it?
110587.e: Taste cells only recognise substances that are dissolved in saliva. That is why a completely dry tongue tastes almost nothing.
110587.m: You can only taste dissolved substances.

110588.q: In which fruits does capsaicin occur naturally?
110588.e: Capsaicin is the substance that makes chilli peppers hot. The more capsaicin a variety contains, the hotter it is.

110589.q: Which self-defence product often contains capsaicin from chillies as its active ingredient?
110589.e: Pepper spray contains an extract from chilli peppers with a lot of capsaicin. It irritates the eyes, nose and skin so strongly that an attacker can be fended off.
110589.m: Pepper spray works with the hot substance from chillies.

110590.q: Which scale is used to give the heat of chillies?
110590.e: The Scoville scale measures the amount of hot substances in chillies. Bell peppers have a value of 0; very hot varieties have values in the millions.
110590.m: The heat of chillies is measured in Scoville units.

110591.q: Why does milk ease the burning of chilli better than water?
a: Because capsaicin dissolves in fat but hardly in water
Because milk is always colder than water
Because water makes capsaicin chemically stronger
110591.e: Capsaicin is fat-soluble. Fat and certain proteins in milk take it up and wash it away, while water only spreads it around.
110591.m: Milk helps against chilli burn better than water.

110592.q: Which animals hardly feel the heat of capsaicin and so spread chilli seeds?
110592.e: The capsaicin receptor of birds hardly reacts to the substance. They eat the fruits and pass the seeds out again undamaged.
110592.m: Birds eat hot chillies without feeling the burn.

110593.q: What is capsaicin used for in medicine?
a: In plasters and creams against pain
As a sleeping pill for the night
110593.e: Capsaicin first irritates the pain fibres and, with longer use, makes them less sensitive. That is why it is found in heat plasters and pain-relief creams.
110593.m: Capsaicin in plasters can relieve pain.

110594.q: Why does chilli feel hot in your mouth even though it is not warm at all?
a: Capsaicin triggers the same sensors that also react to heat
Chilli rubs against the tongue and makes heat
110594.e: Capsaicin opens a receptor that normally responds to strong heat. That is why the brain reads the signal as burning.
110594.m: Chilli tricks the brain into sensing heat.

110595.q: Which part of a chilli pepper contains the most capsaicin?
110595.e: The pale dividing walls that the seeds hang from contain the most capsaicin. The seeds themselves only become hot because they stick to them.
110595.m: The heat is mainly in the pale inner walls of the chilli.

110596.q: Which two kinds of thermoreceptors does the skin have?
110596.e: The skin has separate sensory cells for cold and for warmth. Together they give us our sense of temperature.
110596.m: The skin senses cold and warmth with different receptors.

110597.q: Which thermoreceptors are more common in the skin?
110597.e: The skin has far more cold spots than warm spots. That is why cooling is noticed especially quickly.
110597.m: The skin has more cold receptors than warmth receptors.

110598.q: Why does a peppermint sweet feel cool in your mouth?
a: The sweet cools the mouth by several degrees
110598.e: Menthol activates a cold receptor without it really getting colder. The brain then reports “cool”.
110598.m: Menthol tricks you into feeling cold.

110599.q: You hold one hand in cold water and the other in warm water, then both in lukewarm water. What do you feel?
a: The hand that was cold feels warm, the other feels cool
Both hands feel exactly the same
Both hands feel nothing at all
Both hands feel it is hot
110599.e: The thermoreceptors mainly report the change compared with before. For the cold hand, lukewarm is warmer; for the warm hand, it is cooler.
110599.m: Our sense of temperature always compares with what came before.

110600.q: Where in the body are the temperature-sensitive nerve cells that monitor the temperature of the blood?
a: In the hypothalamus of the brain
110600.e: The hypothalamus is the body's temperature centre. It measures the blood temperature and triggers sweating or shivering when needed.
110600.m: The hypothalamus controls our body temperature.

110601.q: What is the sense called with which we feel warmth and cold through the skin?
110601.e: We sense warmth and cold with the thermoreceptors in the skin. This is called the sense of temperature.
110601.m: We feel warmth and cold with our sense of temperature.

110602.q: What do you feel when very hot water above about 45 °C touches your skin?
110602.e: From about this temperature, pain sensors also react. The burning warns you of a scald.
110602.m: Too much heat is felt as pain.

110603.q: What do you notice if you touch the skin point by point with a cold metal tip?
a: You only feel cold at certain points
You feel exactly the same cold everywhere
You only feel cold at the hairs
110603.e: The thermoreceptors are not everywhere but at individual cold and warm spots. In between, the skin only reports touch.
110603.m: We feel cold at individual cold spots on the skin.

110604.q: Which sensory cells do pit vipers use to sense the body heat of their prey, even in the dark?
110604.e: Pit vipers have pit organs between the eye and the nostril. These sense heat radiation so precisely that the snake can locate warm prey.
110604.m: Pit vipers sense warm prey with their pit organs.

110605.q: What do nociceptors report to the brain?
110605.e: Nociceptors are pain sensors. The word comes from the Latin “nocere”, meaning to harm.
110605.m: Nociceptors are the body's pain sensors.

110606.q: Which organ has no pain receptors itself?
110606.e: The brain processes pain, but its tissue itself has no pain receptors. A headache arises, for example, in the membranes around the brain and in blood vessels.
110606.m: The brain itself feels no pain.

a: Pain in a part of the body that is no longer there
Pain that only happens in dreams
Pain from light that is too bright
110607.e: After an amputation, people can feel pain in the missing arm or leg. It is thought that mainly the nervous system and the brain create this feeling.
110607.m: Phantom pain arises in the nervous system, not in the missing body part.

110608.q: Which stimuli do nociceptors react to?
a: Strong heat, strong pressure and harmful substances
110608.e: Nociceptors report anything that can damage tissue. This includes extreme temperatures, crushing and irritating chemicals.
110608.m: Nociceptors react to many kinds of dangerous stimuli.

110609.q: Which substances made by the body can dampen pain, for example during great effort?
110609.e: Endorphins work in a similar way to strong painkillers. The body releases them, for example, during stress or long endurance sport.
110609.m: Endorphins are the body's own painkillers.

110610.q: Why is it dangerous if a person cannot feel pain from birth?
a: They often do not notice injuries in time
They can no longer see properly
110610.e: Without pain, the warning signal is missing. People affected injure themselves more often, for example their bones or joints, without noticing.
110610.m: People who feel no pain easily miss injuries.

110611.q: After a knock, you often first feel a sharp, stabbing pain and then a dull pain. Why?
a: The signals travel along nerve fibres of different speeds
The blood slows down part of the pain
110611.e: Thin fibres with a myelin coating carry the first, stabbing pain quickly. Even thinner fibres with no coating at all are slower and deliver the dull pain.
110611.m: Fast and slow pain use different nerve fibres.

110612.q: Why does it often help to rub a spot you have knocked?
a: Touch signals can dampen the passing on of pain in the spinal cord
Rubbing cools the spot a lot
Rubbing makes the skin permanently numb
110612.e: In the spinal cord, touch signals can block the passing on of pain signals. That is why rubbing feels soothing.
110612.m: Rubbing can weaken pain signals in the spinal cord.

110613.q: What does a sensory receptor do with a stimulus?
a: It turns it into an electrical nerve signal
It passes it into the blood
110613.e: Sensory receptors translate light, pressure, scents or temperature into electrical signals. This is the only language the nervous system understands.
110613.m: Receptors translate stimuli into nerve signals.

110614.q: Which stimulus do the receptors in the skin that sense cold and warmth react to?
110614.e: Each type of receptor is specialised in one kind of stimulus. Warmth and cold receptors in the skin react to temperature.
110614.m: Each receptor reacts to a particular kind of stimulus.

110615.q: Which group do the sensory cells for smell and taste belong to?
110615.e: Smell and taste cells react to chemical substances. That is why they are counted as chemoreceptors.
110615.m: Smell and taste are chemical senses.

110616.q: Which receptors does the eye use to take in light?
110616.e: In the retina there are light-sensing cells, the rods and cones. They are called photoreceptors, from the Greek “phos” for light.
110616.m: Photoreceptors in the eye react to light.

110617.q: Why do you stop feeling your socks after a while?
a: The receptors get used to the unchanging stimulus
Blood stops flowing into your feet
110617.e: Many receptors report an unchanging stimulus more and more weakly over time. This getting used to it is called adaptation.
110617.m: After a while we hardly notice unchanging stimuli.

110618.q: Why do you see spots of light when you press firmly on your closed eyes?
a: The pressure stimulates the retina, and the brain reads this as light
More light gets through the eyelids
The blood in the eye starts to glow
110618.e: Even the wrong kind of stimulus, such as pressure, can excite the retina. The brain only knows light signals from there, so it reports spots of light.
110618.m: The brain always reads signals from the eye as light.

110619.q: Where does the actual perception of a stimulus, such as a smell, take place?
110619.e: The receptor only delivers a signal. Only the brain processes it and turns it into a smell, a picture or a feeling.
110619.m: A stimulus is only perceived in the brain.

110620.q: What can sharks sense with special sense organs on their heads?
a: Weak electric fields from prey animals
110620.e: Sharks have many small pores with electroreceptors on their heads. With these they can even find prey hidden in the sand.

110621.q: What is meant by the stimulus threshold?
a: The smallest stimulus strength that can just be noticed
The greatest stimulus strength you can bear
The place where a nerve ends
110621.e: A stimulus must reach a certain minimum strength to be noticed. This limit is the stimulus threshold.
110621.m: We only notice a stimulus above the stimulus threshold.

110622.q: What is a stimulus called that is too weak to be noticed?
110622.e: If a stimulus is below the threshold, it goes unnoticed. It is called subliminal.
110622.m: We do not notice subliminal stimuli.

110623.q: How does the hearing threshold for high sounds usually change with age?
a: It rises, so high sounds are heard less well
It falls, so you hear better
It stays the same all your life
It disappears by the age of 20
110623.e: With age, sensory cells in the inner ear are lost, especially those for high sounds. These sounds then have to be louder to be heard.
110623.m: In old age, high sounds need to be louder for you to hear them.

110624.q: Why does sunburn hurt even when touched lightly?
a: The pain threshold of the inflamed skin has dropped
The skin suddenly has more bones
The sun has removed the nerves
110624.e: Inflamed skin releases substances that make the pain sensors more sensitive. That is why even a T-shirt is enough to cause pain.
110624.m: With inflammation, the pain threshold drops.

110625.q: You only notice a change in weight when about 2 percent is added. How much must be added to 1,000 g?
110625.e: 2 percent of 1,000 g is 20 g. The heavier something is, the more has to be added for you to feel the difference.
110625.m: The stronger a stimulus is, the bigger a change has to be for us to notice it.

110626.q: What happens to the eye's stimulus threshold when you are in the dark for a long time?
a: It falls, so you see fainter light
It rises, so you see worse
It always stays exactly the same
110626.e: In the dark the eye adapts and becomes more and more sensitive. After a while you can make out things you could not see at first.
110626.m: In the dark, the eye becomes more sensitive over time.

110627.q: What does a nerve cell do when a stimulus goes over its threshold?
a: It always sends out a signal at full strength
It sends a signal half as strong
110627.e: A nerve signal is either triggered completely or not at all. This is called the all-or-nothing principle.
110627.m: Nerve cells fire according to the all-or-nothing principle.

110628.q: What does the difference threshold describe?
a: The smallest difference between two stimuli that you can still notice
The difference between day and night
The distance between two nerve cells
The time until a stimulus is forgotten
110628.e: You compare two stimuli, such as two sounds or two weights. The smallest difference you can just recognise is the difference threshold.
110628.m: The difference threshold shows how finely we can compare stimuli.

110629.q: Which kind of stimuli do mechanoreceptors react to?
110629.e: Mechanoreceptors are stimulated by being deformed. They are found in the skin, muscles, ear and blood vessels.
110629.m: Mechanoreceptors sense pressure, touch and stretching.

110630.q: Where does the skin have especially many touch cells?
110630.e: In the fingertips and lips the touch cells are packed very closely. That is why we feel the tiniest differences there, for example when reading Braille.
110630.m: Fingertips and lips are especially sensitive to touch.

110631.q: Why do you hardly feel your clothes on your skin after a short time?
a: The touch cells get used to the unchanging stimulus
The clothes make the skin numb
The clothes get lighter over time
The brain falls asleep in those places
110631.e: Many touch cells mainly report changes. If a stimulus stays the same, they hardly send any signals and we no longer notice it.
110631.m: Touch cells get used to unchanging stimuli.

110632.q: Which sensory cells in the inner ear are mechanoreceptors?
110632.e: In the inner ear, sound waves move tiny hairs on the hair cells. This movement is turned into nerve signals.
110632.m: We hear with mechanoreceptors in the inner ear.

110633.q: With your eyes closed, which sense lets you recognise a coin in your trouser pocket?
110633.e: Touch cells in the fingers feel pressure, shape and surface. That way you recognise the round, flat coin without looking.
110633.m: With the sense of touch you can recognise shapes without looking.

110634.q: What does a mechanoreceptor do when it is pressed?
a: It produces a signal for the nervous system
110634.e: Mechanoreceptors turn pressure or stretching into electrical signals. Nerves carry them to the brain, which turns them into a feeling such as touch.
110634.m: Mechanoreceptors turn pressure into nerve signals.

110635.q: Which animals use long whiskers to sense even the slightest movements of air?
110635.e: Whiskers, or vibrissae, sit in hair follicles with many mechanoreceptors. Cats use them to find their way even in the dark.

110636.q: Why can you feel a mosquito on your arm even if it hardly touches your skin?
a: Sensory cells at the hair roots report every movement of the tiny hairs
The mosquito gives off heat that you feel
Your eyes tell your skin about the mosquito
The mosquito gives an electric shock
110636.e: Around the hair roots there are nerve endings that notice even the tiniest movement of a hair. The hairs work like feelers.
110636.m: Body hairs work like delicate feelers.

110637.q: Which sense organ do fish use to feel water movements and currents?
